s.x: Electricity runs far more than your lights. It pumps and treats tap water, keeps food and medicine cold, and runs fuel pumps and card payments.12 Long blackouts are real and recent. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, Puerto Rico took about 11 months to restore power to the whole island.3 Many blackout deaths come days or months later, from things you can plan for. Cold, interrupted medical care and suspected generator fumes killed people in Texas, Puerto Rico and Spain.4515 This book prints only sourced facts. Every number has a citation, and every source shows its year. No theories and no predictions. In the next hour: store water and check your carbon monoxide (CO) alarm. Aim for 1 gallon (3.8 liters) per person per day, for 2 weeks if you can.67 50 Mpeople lost power in the 2003 US and Canada blackout16 11 mofor Puerto Rico to restore power everywhere after Maria3 246deaths in Texas linked to the February 2021 winter storm4 3 M+US Medicare patients use electricity-dependent medical equipment10

The power grid is a hidden life-support system. Most of what keeps your household alive either arrives through wires or depends on something that does. When the power stops, each system fails on its own clock. Some stop in seconds. Others hold out for hours or days on backup batteries and fuel. Grid power feeds the systems a household depends on. Each one stops, or runs on limited backup, when the grid goes down.129 Tap water Your tap water is moved by electric pumps. Water and wastewater plants are often the biggest energy users in a town. They use about 30–40% of the energy a municipality uses, says the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA, 2024).1 In the February 2021 Texas freeze, more than 14 million people were hit by water outages and boil-water notices after days of power cuts and frozen pipes.8 Store water before you need it: see Storing Water for Months & Years. Cold food and medicine A closed fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours. A full freezer holds about 48 hours and a half-full one about 24 hours, if the doors stay shut.9 Some medicines must stay cool. Find out now how long yours stay safe at higher temperatures.11 Part 3 (Food) and Part 4 (Medicine) cover both in detail. Medical care Medical care depends on power too. After Hurricane Maria, a household survey found that about one third of deaths after the storm were attributed to delayed or interrupted health care.5 In the US, more than 3 million Medicare patients have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment. More than 4.6 million rely on that equipment or on services such as dialysis, oxygen or home health care (HHS emPOWER).10 Fuel, phones and money Gas station pumps need electricity. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) lists fuel pumps, lighting and payment systems among the systems hit by power and telecom outages (2025).2 Phone service fails too. After Maria, surveyed households in Puerto Rico went an average of 41 days without cell phone service.5 Cash machines stop too. The April 2025 blackout in Spain and Portugal knocked out ATMs, traffic lights and subway networks.14 People on powered medical equipmentOxygen concentrators, ventilators, powered wheelchairs and home dialysis all need electricity. In the US, over 3 million Medicare patients use electricity-dependent equipment.10 List everyone in your family and street who does. See Caring for Elderly & Disab

s.h: 🌍 Real grid failures: dates, durations, deaths
s.x: Big blackouts are not rare and not only in the past. Here are the documented events this book learns from, in date order. Sept 1859The largest geomagnetic storm on record sets telegraph paper on fire.22 Mar 1989A solar storm blacks out Quebec: 6 million people, 9 hours.23 Aug 2003Northeast US and Ontario: about 50 million people lose power.16 Sept 2017Hurricane Maria hits Puerto Rico. Full restoration takes about 11 months.3 Feb 2021Texas freeze: more than 4.5 million people lose power; 246 deaths.174 2022–2025Ukraine: occupation and attacks cut available power capacity from about 38 GW to 12 GW.20 May 2024The first G5 "extreme" geomagnetic storm in over 20 years.24 Sept 2024Hurricane Helene: 5.9 million customers lose power; at least 250 US deaths.1918 Apr 2025Mainland Spain and Portugal lose power at 12:33 Spanish time.12 Spain and Portugal, April 2025 On April 28, 2025, at 12:33 Spanish time, mainland Spain and Portugal lost power.12 Subways, traffic lights and ATMs stopped working.14 Full restoration took about 16 hours.13 Early reports linked at least three deaths to the blackout. In Galicia, police investigated carbon monoxide from a generator after an older couple and their adult son died at home.15 The expert panel's final report, published in March 2026, found no single cause. It described a chain of failures with voltage control problems at its center.1213 Texas, February 2021 (Winter Storm Uri) More than 4.5 million people in Texas lost power, some for as long as 4 days. Federal investigators found that frozen equipment at power plants was the largest single cause.17 Texas officially linked 246 deaths to the storm. About two-thirds were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia.4 Water systems failed too, affecting more than 14 million people.8 Hurricane Helene, September 2024 Helene came ashore in Florida's Big Bend as a Category 4 hurricane on September 26, 2024.18 It left 5.9 million electricity customers without power across 10 states.19 The National Hurricane Center counted at least 250 US deaths. That made Helene the deadliest hurricane in the mainland US since Katrina in 2005.18 The Northeast blackout, August 2003 On August 14, 2003, about 50 million people in the US and Canada lost power. The outage cut 61,800 megawatts of electric load across eight US states and Ontario.16 Some parts of the US waited 4 days for power. Parts of Ontario had ro

s.h: 🏝️ Puerto Rico after Maria: 11 months to restore power
s.x: Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico on September 20, 2017.5 About 11 months later, officials said power had been restored to the whole island.3 A Harvard-led team surveyed 3,299 randomly chosen households. Through the end of 2017, homes averaged 84 days without electricity, 68 days without water and 41 days without cell phone service (NEJM, 2018).5 Average time without each service, from landfall to December 31, 2017 (survey of 3,299 homes). In remote areas, 83% of homes had no electricity for the whole period.5 Interrupted medical care was a major killer. About one third of the deaths after the storm in surveyed households were attributed to delayed or interrupted health care.5 The same study estimated 4,645 excess deaths to the end of 2017.5 Counting the dead took nearly a year. The first official toll was 64.5 A George Washington University study, commissioned by the governor, estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018.21 Older adults faced the highest riskThe George Washington University study found that poor and elderly people were most at risk of dying after Maria.21 Plan medicines and care for older relatives first. See Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies. The 30-year viewPuerto Rico needed about 11 months to restore power to every area.3 This book plans for a much longer case: 30 years with no grid, with no repair crews or deliveries to count on. See What Fails When: The 30-Year Timeline.

Solar storms have already caused real blackouts. A big eruption on the Sun can throw a fast cloud of charged gas, called a coronal mass ejection (CME), toward Earth. The great storm of 1859 was caused by a very fast CME.22 The chain from Sun to grid. In 1859, currents in telegraph wires started fires.22 In 1989, swings in Earth's magnetic field tripped breakers on Quebec's grid.23 1859: the Carrington Event On September 1, 1859, astronomer Richard Carrington saw a bright flare on the Sun. The next day, the largest geomagnetic storm on record reached Earth.22 Auroras were seen as far south as the tropics. Currents surged through telegraph wires and set recording paper on fire at telegraph stations.22 1989: Quebec goes dark in 90 seconds In March 1989, a geomagnetic storm tripped protective equipment on Hydro-Québec's grid. Within 90 seconds, 6 million people lost power, and it stayed off for 9 hours (NOAA).23 May 2024: the strongest storm in 20 years On May 10, 2024, a G5 storm arrived. G5 is the top level on the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) 5-level scale, and this was the first G5 in over two decades (NASA, 2025).24 Grid operators reported isolated effects on large power transformers, voltage support equipment, line breakers and filters (NERC, 2024).25 GPS errors sent some self-steering farm tractors off course during spring planting.24 Solar storms only make pretty auroras. In 1989 a solar storm cut power to 6 million people in Quebec.23 In 1859, storm currents set telegraph paper on fire.22 The full science, warning systems and what helps are in Solar Storms & Grid Collapse: The Facts.

s.h: ☠️ The pattern: who died, and how
s.x: In Texas and Puerto Rico, most deaths did not happen when the lights went out. They came over the following days and months, from causes a household can plan for. Cold: about two-thirds of the 246 Texas deaths in 2021 were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia.4 Missed medical care: about one third of the deaths in the Puerto Rico survey were attributed to delayed or interrupted care.5 Generator fumes: in Spain in 2025, police investigated carbon monoxide after a family of three died with a generator running.15 Age and poverty: after Maria, poor and elderly people faced the highest risk.21 Every cause of death, ranked by speed, is in What Kills People First in Disasters. Never run a generator indoors or in a garageNot even with the doors and windows open. Run it outdoors, at least 20 feet (6 meters) from windows, doors and vents, and use a battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarm.7 See Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer. Babies and childrenChildren depend completely on adults for warmth, safe water and safe food. Learn the danger signs in Part 6 before you need them, and plan feeding now: see Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out. Store extra water for pregnancyThe Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises storing more water for pregnant women, for sick people and for hot climates.6 Pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding each have their own chapter in Part 5, starting with Pregnancy Care Without a Hospital. Dogs and petsYour dogs depend on the same water, food and shelter as you. Count every pet when you work out how much water and food to store. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

s.h: 📏 Why this book uses facts only
s.x: Every number in this book has a source you can check. The small number after a sentence links to the source list at the end of the chapter. Official numbers change, so we give the year. Texas first counted 210 storm deaths, then 246 in its final report.4 Puerto Rico's first official count after Maria was 64.5 An independent study later estimated 2,975.21 Early numbers can be far too lowThe Texas count rose by 36 deaths between reports.4 The first Maria count of 64 later sat beside study estimates of 2,975 and 4,645.215 When you read a number, check its date. The first official death toll tells you the real cost. After Maria, the first official toll was 64.5 A study commissioned by the governor estimated 2,975 excess deaths.21 Where this book's facts come from, in order of preference Source typeExamplesUsed for Government and UN bodiesCDC, EPA, FEMA, NOAA, WHO, UNICEFHealth and safety guidance, official data Professional bodiesAmerican Heart Association, Red Cross, AAP, ACOGFirst aid and medical guidelines Peer-reviewed researchNEJM, Lancet, Cochrane reviewsWhat works, and how well Official event reportsFERC, ENTSO-E, National Hurricane CenterCauses, durations, death tolls Major news outletsAP and similarEvent facts only: dates, places, tolls What we leave out: rumors, predictions, unsourced opinions, product claims, prepper blogs, forums and Wikipedia. If a claim could not be checked against a source like those above, it is not in this book. DoCheck who said it and whenPrefer official agencies and studiesWrite the date next to any number you note downExpect early tolls to change Don'tAct on a single unsourced postPass on rumors in a crisisTrust "secret" cures or miracle gearTreat a forecast as a fact How to read a citationA small number like this6 means "source 6 says this". Tap it to jump to the source. Each source shows who published it, the year, and exactly what it supports.

s.x: Light the house with flashlights, not candles. Never run a generator inside a home or garage, even with the doors and windows open.15 Fill every clean container with tap water in the first hour. s.h: ⏱️ The order of actions at a glance First 72 h
s.x: Work in this order: people, light, water, cold food, air, medicines, contact. The fastest dangers come first, and the slow ones wait their turn. Every clock in this chapter comes from official power outage guidance: Ready.gov, the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).12 Write down the time the power went out. Tape it to the fridge door. The food and medicine decisions below all count from that moment. The fridge, freezer and medicine checkpoints come from USDA and Ready.gov guidance.21 Minute 0Safety check. Flashlights on, not candles. Count every person. Make sure no generator, grill or stove is running indoors.14 Hour 1Fill water containers while the taps still run. Read medicine labels. Unplug electronics to protect them from surges when power returns.1 Hour 4The closed fridge reaches its safe limit. If the outage will last longer, move fridge food into coolers with ice.2 Hour 24A half-full freezer reaches its limit. Once the outage passes one day, Ready.gov's rule for refrigerated medicines applies.21 Hour 48A full freezer reaches its limit with the door kept closed.2 Hour 72Switch to the routine in The First 30 Days: water system, toilets, rationing and roles. Print this pageTape the timeline inside a kitchen cupboard. In a real outage, your phone may be dead and this book offline.

Use flashlights, not candles. Ready.gov lists candles as a fire risk during power outages.1 Keep a flashlight with extra batteries for every household member, including children.1 Count everyoneCall each name out loud. If someone is missing, write down where they were last. Turn on flashlightsGive each child their own light and keep them in the same room as an adult. Check the airIf a carbon monoxide (CO) alarm sounds, or anyone feels dizzy, sick or confused, get everyone outside into fresh air and get medical help.4 Unplug electronicsPower can come back with surges or spikes. Disconnect appliances and electronics to avoid damage.1 Write the timeNote the time the power went out on paper. Every food and medicine decision counts from it. Never heat the house with a gas oven or stoveReady.gov and the CDC both say not to use a gas stove or oven to heat your home. It is a carbon monoxide risk.14 See Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer. Run a 15-minute blackout drillOne evening, switch off the lights and phones. Find the flashlights, count heads and fill the water containers. Time it, then fix whatever slowed you down.

s.h: 🚰 Hour 1: capture water while the taps still run
s.x: Fill every clean container now, before the pressure drops. City water can stop when the pumps that move it lose power.9 What happened in the 2003 blackout The Northeast blackout began on August 14, 2003.13 Cleveland's water system shut down when its four major water supply pumps lost power. Taps gave no more than a trickle.9 About 1.5 million people in the Cleveland area lost water. Residents used bottled water for drinking and bathing.1011 The danger did not end when pressure came back. Residents were told to boil drinking water, because the system could have been contaminated when pressure was lost.1011 In Detroit, a boil-water alert covered 4.3 million customers. It was not lifted until Tuesday, August 19, 2003, five days after the blackout began.1213 No one can tell you how long your taps will runThe 2003 blackout caused loss of water service in some areas, not all.9 Treat every minute of pressure as borrowed time. Fill first, then deal with everything else. Fill drinking containers firstUse clean bottles, jugs and pots with lids. Label them "DRINKING". Fill cooking pots and kettlesCover them so dust and insects stay out. Fill the bathtub and bucketsUse this water for flushing and washing. Keep small children away from a full tub. Turn the taps off when flow slowsWrite down the time the pressure dropped. When water returns, follow boil-water noticesDo not drink tap water until officials say it is safe, or until you have treated it.10 See Disinfecting Water. How much does your family need? Use the calculator, then read Storing Water for Months & Years for safe containers and hidden water in the house.  Babies: keep separate water for formulaFill and label one covered container only for mixing formula. If a boil-water notice is issued, do not use tap water for formula until the notice is lifted or the water is treated. See Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

s.h: 🧊 Hours 0 to 48: the fridge and freezer clock
s.x: Keep the doors shut. A refrigerator keeps food safe for up to 4 hours during a power outage if you do not open the door.23 A full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours with the door closed. A half-full freezer holds about 24 hours.23 Use appliance thermometers. The fridge should be at 4°C (40°F) or below, and the freezer at −18°C (0°F) or below.2 USDA hold times with the doors kept closed. Opening the door shortens them.2 What to do when each clock runs out (USDA, Ready.gov) ApplianceSafe forThen Fridge, door closedAbout 4 hoursThrow out perishable food: meat, poultry, fish, soft cheeses, milk, eggs, leftovers and deli items2 Freezer, half fullAbout 24 hoursCheck each item for ice crystals or a temperature of 4°C (40°F) or below2 Freezer, fullAbout 48 hoursSame check as above2 Food at 4°C (40°F) or warmerUnder 2 hoursThrow it away after 2 hours. Also throw out any food with an unusual smell, color or texture1 If the outage will last more than 4 hours, move fridge food into coolers with ice.2 Perishable food left in a fridge with no power for more than 4 hours goes in the trash: meat, poultry, fish, soft cheeses, milk, eggs, leftovers and deli items.2 Frozen food that still has ice crystals, or is at 4°C (40°F) or below, can be safely refrozen.2 Based on USDA power outage rules for refrigerated and frozen food.2 If it tastes fine, it is safe to eat. USDA says never taste food to decide whether it is safe. When in doubt, throw it out.2 For which foods to eat first and what is safe at room temperature, see Food Safety Without a Refrigerator. Two cheap thermometersBuy one appliance thermometer for the fridge and one for the freezer. Without them, you are guessing at the 4°C (40°F) line.2

Read every medicine label in the house. Look for the word "refrigerate". Do it in the first hour, while you can still reach a pharmacist. If a medicine was not kept at its recommended temperature during an outage, the FDA says to check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, doctor or the maker whether it is still usable.8 The one-day rule: if the power is out for more than a day, discard medicine that should be refrigerated, unless the label says otherwise.1 If a life depends on that refrigerated medicine, talk to a doctor or pharmacist and use it only until a new supply is available.1 Insulin Insulin does not fail the moment the fridge stops. Insulin in vials or cartridges, opened or unopened, may be left unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days and still work.7 Pens and some brands have different limits. Check the label of your exact product.7 Above 30°C (86°F), the 28-day figure no longer applies. The FDA gives it only for 15–30°C (59–86°F).7 Read the label for the words "do not freeze" too, and if you keep insulin in a cooler, do not let it touch the ice. When properly stored insulin is available again, the FDA advises replacing vials that were exposed to extreme conditions.7 Once the fridge stops, all insulin is ruined. The FDA says insulin vials and cartridges keep working for up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F).7 Replace vials exposed to extreme conditions once properly stored insulin is available.7 Gather every medicinePut all of them on one table, including children's and pets' medicines. Sort by the labelMake two piles: "refrigerate" and "room temperature". Write a listFor each cold medicine, write the name, the dose and how many days of supply are left. Call while you canAsk a pharmacist or doctor about each cold medicine while the phones work.8 Watch the clockOnce the power has been out for more than a day, apply the one-day rule above to everything that is not life-saving.1 Medical devices and older adultsTalk to your medical provider now about a power outage plan for medical devices that run on electricity and for refrigerated medicines.1 Older adults and young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures.1 See Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies. s.h: ☠️ Carbon monoxide: the danger you cannot see
s.x: Run a generator outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents. Never use one inside a home, garage or carport.4 The US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) is blunt: never use a generator inside a home or garage, even if the doors and windows are open. Point the exhaust away from the house and other buildings.5 Placement rules from the CDC (20 ft from doors, windows and vents), the CPSC (exhaust away from buildings) and the California Department of Public Health (cord over 20 ft, battery CO alarm).456 Place it outsideAt least 6 m (20 ft) from any door, window or vent.4 Point the exhaust awayAim it away from your home and other buildings.5 Use a long cordAn extension cord longer than 6 m (20 ft) keeps the generator at a safe distance.6 Turn on a battery-powered CO alarm insideUse one in your home whenever a generator runs. Ready.gov advises CO alarms with battery backup on every level of the home.61 Never move it indoorsNot into the garage, not into the carport, not even with the doors open.54 A generator is fine in the garage if you leave the big door open. The CPSC says never use a generator inside a home or garage, even if doors and windows are open.5 Do Light rooms with flashlights1 Keep generators outdoors, 6 m (20 ft) from openings4 Run a battery-powered CO alarm6 If home is too hot or cold, go somewhere with heat or cooling, if it is safe to travel1 Don't Use candles for light1 Heat the house with a gas oven or stove1 Run a generator in a garage or carport4 Leave a car engine running in a garage4 Know the warning signs. CO poisoning can cause headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion.4 If you suspect it, get to fresh air first, then get medical help. For alarms, symptoms and safe heating, read Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

Keep phones and other electric equipment charged, and keep gas tanks full. That is Ready.gov's power outage advice, and it only works if you do it before the outage.1 Cash Ready.gov's outage supplies start with flashlights with extra batteries for every household member, plus enough nonperishable food and water.1 Card readers and cash machines need electricity. Keep cash at home in small bills. Phones and batteries Find out now whether your home phone works in a power outage, and how long its battery backup lasts.1 Make a plan for batteries and other alternatives to meet your needs when the power goes out.1 Charge everything nowPhones, power banks, radios and flashlights with rechargeable batteries.1 Stretch the batteryTurn on low-power mode, dim the screen and close apps you do not need. Send one message outTell your out-of-area contact that you are safe and when you will check in next. Charge from a car only outdoorsNever run a car or generator in a garage or carport.4 Switch off between check-insAgree on fixed times to turn phones on, so the batteries last for days. Fuel is a fire and CO hazardA fuel-burning generator belongs outdoors only, with its exhaust pointed away from buildings.5 For storage and safe refueling, see Generators & Fuel Storage.

s.h: 📞 Contact, neighbors and when to leave
s.x: Check on your neighbors. Ready.gov puts this on its list of things to do during an outage.1 Start with older adults and families with young children. They are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures.1 If your home becomes too hot or too cold, and it is safe to travel, go to a place that has heat or cooling.1 Decide this early, while roads and daylight allow it. Use your family planFollow your meeting points and contact list. No plan yet? See The Family Emergency Plan. Set check-in timesAgree when everyone switches phones on. Write the times on paper. Listen for official updatesKeep a battery or hand-crank radio on, so you are not relying on your phone alone. Visit, do not just callKnock on the doors of neighbors who live alone, use medical devices or have babies.1 Keep a paper logWrite the time of each event: power out, water pressure lost, fridge food thrown out.

How long can insulin vials go without a fridge?Up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F). Check the label for pens. Refrigerated medicine after more than a day without power?Discard it unless the label says otherwise. If a life depends on it, ask a doctor or pharmacist and use it until new supply arrives. Can you taste food to check it?No. Never taste. When in doubt, throw it out.

Never ration water. Drink what you need today and look for more for tomorrow. That is FEMA and Red Cross guidance.1 Ration food, not water. Healthy people can live on half their usual food for an extended period. Do not cut food for children or pregnant women.1 Get a toilet and a handwashing station working in week 1. Outbreaks after disasters follow unsafe water, poor sanitation and crowding.4 Store at least 3.8 liters (1 gallon) per person per day. At least 2 quarts (1.9 liters) of that is drinking water, and heat can double the need.316 Count everything on day 4, then every 7 days. Turn every count into one number: days left. Start long-term systems in weeks 3 and 4, while stored supplies still cover you: rain catchment, garden, compost. Neverration water: drink what you need today1 ½of usual food: what healthy people can live on for an extended period12 2 qt(1.9 L) minimum drinking water a day, normally active person1 1 per 20people: toilet planning figure for shared toilets5

The first 72 hours keep you alive tonight. Days 4 to 30 turn quick fixes into daily systems. If you have not done the first 72 hours yet, start with The First 72 Hours. Work one week at a time. Each week has one main job. Finish it before you move on. Week 1 · Days 4–7Water and toilets. Build a daily water routine. Set up a toilet and a handwashing station. Do the first full inventory. Give everyone a role. Week 2 · Days 8–14Sanitation every day, rations set. Use the inventory numbers to set portions. Choose one warm or cool room. Meet your nearest neighbors. Week 3 · Days 15–21Security and community. Start a watch rota, build a neighbor network, repair what broke, recount. Week 4 · Days 22–30Long-term systems. Rain catchment, garden beds, a seed check, compost, and a written plan for month 2. The 30-day map. Weeks 1 and 2 protect water, toilets and food. Weeks 3 and 4 build the systems that replace what runs out. One wall, one sheetTape the week's jobs, the roles and the inventory "days left" numbers on one wall. Everyone checks the wall, not their memory.

s.h: 💧 Week 1: Turn stored water into a water system
s.x: Never ration water. If supplies run low, drink the amount you need today and try to find more for tomorrow.1 Plan on at least 3.8 liters (1 gallon) per person per day. That is the CDC minimum to store. The CDC says to store more for pregnant women, sick people, pets and hot climates.3 Of that, a normally active person needs to drink at least 2 quarts (1.9 liters) each day.12 In very hot weather, water needs can double. Children, nursing mothers and sick people may need more.6 See How Much Water You Really Need. Stored water is a bridge, not a plan. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, surveyed Puerto Rico households went an average of 68 days without water.9 Week 1 is when you find the next source and a way to treat it, while your stores still cover you. Water for 30 days (arithmetic from the planning and drinking figures above; double the drinking column in very hot weather) PeoplePlanning: 1 gal (3.8 L) each a dayDrinking minimum: 2 qt (1.9 L) each a day 130 gal (114 L)15 gal (57 L) 260 gal (227 L)30 gal (114 L) 4120 gal (454 L)60 gal (227 L) 6180 gal (681 L)90 gal (341 L)  Measure what you haveWrite the volume on every container. Add it up in liters and gallons. Work out days leftTotal water ÷ (number of people × 3.8 L or 1 gal). Write the answer on the wall. Choose your next sourceRain, a well, a spring or a stream. See Finding Water When the Taps Stop. Choose and stock a treatmentBoiling, bleach or a filter. See Disinfecting Water. Separate clean from dirtyMark some containers "DRINKING ONLY". Never pour untreated water into them. Log it every dayOne line a day: liters in, liters used, days left. Do not wait for the last containerStart collecting and treating from your next source while you still have a stored reserve. Then one bad day does not become a dry day. Dogs drink from your stores tooAdd a line for each dog on the water log. Measure what your dog drinks on a normal day now, so you have a real number. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

s.h: 🚽 Weeks 1–2: Toilets and handwashing before anything else
s.x: Disease outbreaks after disasters follow conditions, not the calendar. A review in CDC's journal Emerging Infectious Diseases linked outbreak risk to displacement, crowding, safe water and sanitation, the population's underlying health, vaccination coverage and access to health care.4 Displacement is the main risk factor. Disasters that did not displace people rarely led to outbreaks.4 If your home is safe, making it livable keeps your family out of crowded temporary shelters. See Stay or Go? Diarrheal outbreaks can follow contamination of drinking water.4 So the toilet and the water system are one job: waste must never reach what you drink. The same review found the risk of diarrheal outbreaks after disasters is higher in developing countries than in industrialized countries.4 If your water or sanitation was weak before the outage, treat this section as urgent. Your alarm is a condition, not a dateAct on sanitation the day any of these happens: tap water is no longer safe, the toilet stops flushing, or extra people move in. Each is a risk factor named in the review.4 For how fast each disease appears, see Waterborne Diseases. Outbreak risk after natural disasters is tied to these conditions, with displacement the main risk factor.4 A safe home with clean water and a working toilet addresses three of them. Why sanitation matters by week 2 Illness shows up after a delay. The delay between swallowing a germ and the first symptom is called the incubation period. Cholera can start within hours. Symptoms usually begin 2 to 3 days after exposure, but can start in a few hours or take up to 5 days.7 Hepatitis A takes 15 to 50 days, 28 on average.8 Do the arithmetic. A water or toilet mistake on day 4 can bring cholera by day 9, and hepatitis A anywhere from day 19 to day 54. A week 1 mistake can still make someone sick 7 weeks later. Time from exposure to first symptom (CDC and WHO) IllnessFirst symptom afterSpread by CholeraA few hours to 5 days (usually 2–3)7Contaminated food or water10 Hepatitis A15–50 days (average 28)8Close contact, or contaminated food or water8 How many toilets you need Plan one toilet per 20 people, or one per household, when households share.5 In the first phase of an emergency, no toilet should serve more than 50 people.5 Put a handwashing station right next to every toilet. The Sphere humanitarian standards call for handwashing facilities

You cannot ration what you have not counted. Do the first full count on day 4. Recount every 7 days. Turn every count into "days left". Days left = amount on hand ÷ amount used per day. One number per item is easy to read when you are tired. Clear one shelf at a timeGroup like items. Work in pairs: one person counts, one writes. Count food in person-daysOne person-day is enough food for one person for one day at their normal eating. Count waterLiters or gallons, from the water log. Count medicines per personDoses left ÷ doses per day = days left. Do this first for anyone on daily prescriptions. Count everything elseFuel, batteries, lamp oil, soap, bleach, diapers, formula, menstrual products and dog food. Post the numbersWrite each "days left" on the wall sheet. Circle the lowest three. Those are next week's problems. Example inventory sheet (illustration numbers, family of 4) ItemOn handUsed per dayDays left Water454 L (120 gal)15 L (4 gal)30 Food120 person-days4 person-days30 Daily tablets (one person)45 tablets1 tablet45 Lamp oil2 L0.1 L20  Count daily medicines before foodWrite each person's medicine "days left" at the top of the sheet. Then read Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies for what to do as that number falls. Get this before you need itA clipboard, a paper notebook, pencils, a permanent marker and masking tape for labels. Paper inventory works with no power at all.

s.h: 🥫 Week 2: Rationing math (food yes, water no)
s.x: Food can be rationed. Water cannot. FEMA and the American Red Cross say food may be rationed safely, except for children and pregnant women.1 Healthy people can survive on half their usual food intake for an extended period, and without any food for many days.12 That guidance covers healthy people. For anyone with diabetes, kidney disease or another diet-sensitive condition, read Special Diets before you change what they eat. Worked example: a family of 4 Two adults and two children have 120 person-days of food. Everyone eats full portions: 4 person-days used a day. 120 ÷ 4 = 30 days. Adults eat half, children eat full: 0.5 + 0.5 + 1 + 1 = 3 a day. 120 ÷ 3 = 40 days. Halving adult portions bought this family 10 days. It did not make any food. Use those days to start growing and collecting it. Food stretches when healthy adults eat half; children and pregnant women stay on full portions.1 Water is planned at 1 gallon per person per day,3 with at least 2 quarts for drinking.1 Do Cut healthy adults' portions first Keep children and pregnant women on full portions Write portions down so everyone sees them Recount every 7 days and adjust Don't Ration water Cut food for children or pregnant women Guess at stock levels Let one person control food in secret Children are not rationedFEMA and Red Cross guidance excludes children from food rationing.1 For babies on formula, see Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out. Pregnant women are not rationedThe same guidance excludes pregnant women from food rationing.1 For breastfeeding mothers, see Breastfeeding. Dogs are on the sheet tooCount dog food in days like everything else. If it runs out inside 30 days, read Feeding Dogs Without Kibble now. The 30-year viewRationing stretches a store. It never refills one. Every number on the inventory sheet reaches zero unless a system replaces it.

Give every job a person and every person a job. A shared routine means fewer decisions when everyone is tired. In a household of 2, each person takes 2 or 3 roles. Write them down anyway. Swap the hardest jobs each week. Household roles for the first 30 days RoleDaily jobsGood fit Water leadCollect, treat and log waterStrong teen or adult Sanitation leadToilet, handwashing, laundryEveryone, on rotation Food and inventory leadPortions, weekly count, recordsA careful counter; can be done seated Care leadBabies, children, elders, the sick, dogsA calm, patient person Watch and neighbors leadLocks, watch rota, neighbor contactSomeone known locally Example daily routine WhenJobs Wake-upHeadcount. Check babies, elders, the sick and dogs. Read the water log. MorningCollect and treat water. Clean and restock the toilet. MiddayMain meal. Rest. AfternoonRepairs, garden work, lessons for children. Before darkLamps ready, doors locked, tomorrow's jobs on the wall. NightWatch rota. Quiet hours. Hold a 20-minute family meeting on the same day each week. Recount, rotate jobs, and pick next week's main job from the 30-day map. For sleep and shift plans, see Stress, Sleep & Routines. If anyone in your house has ADHD, give them roles with a clear daily checklist and a visible result. See Surviving With ADHD. Jobs for childrenGive children small daily jobs and a fixed bedtime. A job they can finish is part of the routine too. See Survival Skills Kids Can Learn by Age. Roles for eldersMany key jobs can be done sitting down: record keeper, inventory counter, teacher, night radio listener. Give elders a named role on the wall. Practice a no-power weekendWhile help still exists, live by the routine table for one weekend without using grid power. Write down every problem, then fix it before you need to.

s.h: 🌡️ Week 2: One warm room or one cool room
s.x: Pick one room and live in it. One room is easier to keep warm or cool than a whole house, and easier to watch. Heat for warmth competes with fuel for cooking and boiling water. Use the fuel "days left" from your inventory before you choose a method. Choose the roomUse Staying Warm Without Heat or Staying Cool Without Air Conditioning to pick it. Move sleeping thereBabies, elders and sick people get the best spots. Check fuel days leftTake the number from the wall sheet. Keep enough fuel to treat water. Read the carbon monoxide chapterDo this before any flame or engine is used indoors or near the house. Check people twice a dayMorning and evening, check babies, elders, the sick and dogs. See Hypothermia, Frostbite & Heat Stroke for warning signs. Read this before you burn anything indoorsHeaters, stoves, lamps, grills and generators all burn fuel. Before you use any of them for heat, light or cooking, read Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer. Who to watch most closelySee What Kills People First for the groups at highest risk from heat and cold, and check them first every day.

Your nearest neighbors are your first backup. They are close enough to help today, and you are close enough to help them. Security in the first month is mostly quiet habits: locks, a watch rota, not showing what you have, and knowing who lives around you. Details are in Home Security & Deterrence and Keeping a Low Profile. Visit in daylight, in pairsStart with the two or three nearest homes. Share names and needsWho has babies, elders, medical devices or dogs. Swap skillsList who can do first aid, repairs, gardening and child care. See Organizing Neighbors. Set a weekly meetingSame place, same day, same time. Agree on a help signalA sound, a flag or a runner, so anyone can call for help without power. Do Lock doors and gates at dusk Keep supplies out of sight from doors and windows Keep a written night-watch rota Talk problems down. See De-escalation Don't Tell people outside your group how much you have Post about your supplies online Confront strangers alone Take from homes or stores without permission. That is theft. See Scavenging vs Looting Women and girls in the planMake sure women and girls have a say in where the toilet, water point and sleeping spaces go. Use a buddy for night trips and night watch. Dogs on the rotaA dog that barks at strangers is an early alarm. Keep it fed, vaccinated and under control around neighbors. See Rabies & Diseases Animals Give Humans.

Start long-term systems while stores still cover you. In the worked example, food lasted 40 days with adults on half portions. Anything you plant needs to be growing well before that day. Seeds planted in week 4 do not feed you in week 4. Check each crop's days to harvest on the seed packet, and plan for the gap. Match each store that runs out to a system that replaces it Store that runs outSystem to startRead Stored waterRoof rain catchmentRainwater Harvesting Stored foodGarden beds and staple cropsSurvival Gardening Seed packetsCount, sort and save seedSeed Saving Toilet suppliesComposting toiletComposting Toilets FertilizerCompostSoil & Compost Do the third inventoryAround day 28, recount everything. Sort by days leftPut the lowest numbers at the top of the list. Match each item to a systemUse the table above. Some items have no replacement yet: note them. Give each system an ownerWrite a name and a start date next to it. Write the month-2 planPut it on the wall. Then read Year 1 to Year 30. The 30-year viewThe habits from these 30 days carry on for decades: a daily water log, a weekly count, a toilet owner and a weekly meeting. What changes is where the supplies come from. For how each stored item ages, see What Fails When. Download and print while the internet worksThe FEMA and Red Cross brochure Food and Water in an Emergency (PDF), the CDC page How to Create an Emergency Water Supply, and the review Epidemics after Natural Disasters. Keep paper copies with this book.

Print this chapter and tape a blank inventory sheet (Item, On hand, Used per day, Days left) to a wall Buy a clipboard, notebook, pencils and a permanent marker Label every water container with its volume in liters and gallons Work out your household's 30-day water need at 3.8 L (1 gal) per person per day Choose your backup toilet method and where it will go Set up a handwashing station that works without tap water Find every family member's vaccination record Write a roles list with a name next to each role Introduce yourself to your two nearest neighbors Check your seed stock and note each crop's days to harvest Practice one no-power weekend using the routine table

Should you ration water?No. Drink what you need today and find more for tomorrow. How little food can healthy adults live on for an extended period?About half their usual intake. Never cut food for children or pregnant women. How much water do you plan per person per day?At least 3.8 L (1 gallon) stored, with at least 2 quarts (1.9 L) for drinking. Very hot weather can double the need. What drives outbreaks after disasters?Displacement most of all, plus crowding, water and sanitation, underlying health, vaccination coverage and access to health care. How soon after bad water can cholera start?Within a few hours to 5 days, usually 2 to 3 days. Hepatitis A takes 15 to 50 days. How many people per shared toilet?Plan 1 per 20 people (or 1 per household). Never more than 50 in the first phase. What is the days-left formula?Amount on hand ÷ amount used per day. Do dead bodies cause epidemics?No. A 2007 review found no evidence that they do.

t: Building Your Group: Size, Roles & Skills

s.x: One household cannot cover every job for years. The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) plans 20 liters (about 5 gallons) of water per person per day for household use and hygiene, so a family of 5 must move about 100 kg (220 lb) of water every day.1 Write a skills inventory on paper. Map who can do medical, food, repair, child care, security and teaching work, then train to fill the gaps. Stop the Bleed alone has trained more than 5 million people.2 Give every job a lead and a named backup. Fire-safety planners already do this for anyone who needs help to escape.3 Plan around the most vulnerable first. Older adults and young children are most at risk from extreme heat and cold.4 After Hurricane Maria, the poor and the elderly had the highest risk of death.5 Put every dog in the plan. Temporary public shelters may not allow animals.6 11 mountil all of Puerto Rico had power again after Hurricane Maria7 20 Lwater per person per day for household use and hygiene (UNHCR)1 26%of US adults with disabilities had nowhere to go if they evacuated (2024)8 4.6 M+US Medicare users who rely on powered equipment, dialysis, oxygen or home health9

s.h: 🏚️ Why one household struggles alone Year 1
s.x: Long outages last months, not days. After Hurricane Maria hit in 2017, it took about 11 months before power was restored to the whole of Puerto Rico.7 The people with the least suffered the most. A George Washington University study, commissioned by Puerto Rico's governor, counted 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018. The poor and the elderly were at the highest risk.5 A household has a fixed number of hands. Every hour spent hauling water is an hour not spent cooking, nursing, teaching or keeping watch. The daily workload, in numbers Water is the heaviest daily job. UNHCR plans for 20 liters (about 5 gallons) per person per day for household use and personal hygiene.1 One liter of water weighs 1 kilogram (2.2 lb). For a family of 5, that is 100 liters (26 gallons), or 100 kg (220 lb), every single day. Over a year it adds up to 36,500 liters (about 9,600 gallons). Food is the second big job. The 2010 US Dietary Guidelines estimate that adult women need about 1,600–2,400 kilocalories (kcal) a day and adult men about 2,000–3,000, depending on age and activity.10 Two adults eating 2,000 kcal each need about 1.46 million kcal a year. Then add cooking, firewood, washing, toilets, gardening, night watch, child care and nursing the sick. Each of those jobs takes hours every day. A bigger group shares them out. Arithmetic from UNHCR's planning figure of 20 liters (about 5 gallons) per person per day for household use and hygiene.1 A group of 25 must move half a metric ton (1,100 lb) of water a day. Most households have no plan yetIn a June 2024 survey by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), only 46% of US adults without a disability and 48% of adults with a disability had an emergency plan.8 The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) 2023 national survey found that 37% of adults made a plan in the past year, down from 41% in 2022.11 So more than half of US adults had no emergency plan in 2024. Do not assume your neighbors have supplies or skills. Ask. How to start that conversation is in Organizing Neighbors: Mutual Aid & Watch. The 30-year viewOver 30 years, every person in your group changes role. Babies become workers. Strong adults become elders who need care. Review your group plan every year, the same way Ready.gov tells you to re-think your emergency kit every year.12

s.h: 📋 The skills inventory: who can do what
s.x: Write down every person's skills, honestly. A paper inventory shows you the gaps before an emergency does. Use six areas: medical, food, mechanical, child care, security and teaching. For each person, mark one of three levels: can lead, can back up, or is learning. List every personInclude babies, elders, guests and dogs. Everyone has needs. Most people also have skills. Ask, then watchAsk each adult what they can do. Then watch them do it once: dress a wound, fix a leak, cook a meal for ten. Fill the gridOne row per person, one column per skill area. Mark lead, backup or learning in each box. Circle the gapsA column with no lead is your top training priority. A column with only one name means one illness can stop that job. Train to fill themBook classes while instructors and hospitals still exist. Start with the table below. Review every yearPeople age, move away and learn new things. Redo the grid on the same date each year.12 Example grid. Medical has a backup and a learner but no lead, so it is the first training priority. Security has a lead but no backup, so one illness stops the night watch. The six skill areas and where to start Skill areaWhat it coversTrain first inRead more MedicalFirst aid, bleeding, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), nursing the sickStop the Bleed, CPR and first aidStopping Severe Bleeding FoodStorage, cooking without power, food safety, growingFood safety without a fridgeLong-Term Food Storage MechanicalGenerators, tools, water systems, repairsGenerator and carbon monoxide safetyCarbon Monoxide Child careFeeding, safety, illness signs, playInfant and child CPRSick Baby & Child: Danger Signs SecurityWatch rota, locks, calm talkDe-escalationHome Security TeachingReading, math, practical skillsTeaching your own skills to othersTeaching Kids 🩺 Medical: the skill everyone needs some of Bleeding control is a course anyone can take. The Stop the Bleed course teaches direct pressure, wound packing and tourniquets. The American College of Surgeons counts more than 5 million people trained.2 Children 12 and older can learn CPR, according to the American Heart Association's 2025 guidelines, published on October 22, 2025.13 Train your teenagers, not just the adults. Everyone acts only within their training. The Red Cross first aid steps say to give care based on what you find, within your training.14 Your grid tells the group who that is

Every job gets a lead and a named backup. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) home fire escape advice assigns a helper to each person who needs help getting out, plus a backup in case the helper is not home.3 Use the same idea for every job in your group. The backup steps in when the lead is sick, injured, asleep or away. Write both names on the rota so nobody has to guess. Rotate the hardest jobs Swap heavy and light jobs on a set day each week. Water hauling, night watch, nursing and small-child care are the hardest. Nobody should be stuck with one of them for months. Example rota: each week, every adult moves one job clockwise. Nobody hauls water or stands night watch for weeks on end, and everyone learns every job. Match the job to the body. Pregnant women, elders and people getting over an illness can lead planning, teaching, record keeping and inventory while others carry loads. One 8-hour night watch (10 p.m. to 6 a.m.) shared by adults: simple arithmetic Adults on the rotaHours each, every nightOr: shift length if each stands every other night 24 hours8 hours 42 hours4 hours 81 hour2 hours Group size buys sleep. With 2 adults, each gives up 4 hours of every night. With 8 adults, each gives 1. Sleep and shift plans are in Stress, Sleep & Routines. Do Write the rota on paper where everyone sees it Name a backup for every job Rotate the hard jobs on a set day each week Pair each learner with a lead Hold a short meeting every week Don't Let one person be the only medic or mechanic Leave the same person on night watch for weeks Give child care to someone who is also on watch Hand out jobs by habit instead of by skill Keep the plan only in one person's head The person who never stopsWatch for the lead who skips meals, sleep and their turn off. Take them off the rota for a day and let the backup run the job. Signs that someone is not coping are in Mental Health: Grief, Trauma & Suicide Prevention. Different brains, different rolesGive each person roles with a clear checklist and a result they can see. How to match roles to people with ADHD or autism is in Surviving With ADHD, Autism & Different Brains.

s.h: 👵 Elders, disabled people, children and dogs come first
s.x: Build the plan around the people who cannot fend for themselves. Ready.gov warns that older adults and young children are vulnerable to extreme temperatures, and tells you to check on neighbors during an outage.4 Elderly and disabled people Disabled adults face bigger barriers to leaving. In the June 2024 CDC survey, 26% of adults with disabilities said they had nowhere to go, against 15% of adults without. 20% named the cost of evacuating, against 14%.8 They had also lived through more disasters: 80% of adults with disabilities had experienced a natural disaster, against 70% without.8 Millions depend on power to stay well. More than 3 million US Medicare beneficiaries have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment, and more than 4.6 million when dialysis, oxygen and home health services are included.9 Name a lead carer and a backup for each person who needs help.3 Make meeting places reachable with a wheelchair or walker. FEMA's family plan says to make them accessible for people with disabilities.17 List every powered device, medicine and supply each person uses, and how long it lasts without power. Ready.gov tells you to plan for medical devices that need power.4 Elders hold skills tooPut elders' skills in the inventory, not just their needs. Teaching, mending, cooking, record keeping and minding children are jobs that need no heavy lifting. Care details are in Caring for Elderly & Disabled People. Babies and children Children are not small adults in the planFEMA and the Red Cross say healthy people can survive on half their usual food for an extended period, but food should not be rationed for children and pregnant women.18Name one adult responsible for each child in any emergency, plus a backup. Reunion plans are in The Family Emergency Plan. Children grow into helpers. Teenagers 12 and older can learn CPR.13 Age-by-age jobs are in Survival Skills Kids Can Learn by Age. Women and girlsStore extra water for pregnant women: the CDC names them among those who need more.19 Do not ration a pregnant woman's food.18Make sure women and girls help decide where toilets, water points and sleeping areas go. Use a buddy for night trips. See Personal Safety for Women & Girls. Dogs and other pets Ready.gov says to include pets in your family emergency plan and to have your vet microchip them.20 Do not count on a public shelter for your dog. The FDA warns that

s.h: 👥 How big should your group be? Do the math
s.x: This book does not give a magic number. Every extra person adds hands and adds needs. Do your own arithmetic with official planning figures. Three figures set the floor for any group: Water: 20 liters (about 5 gallons) per person per day for household use and hygiene.1 The CDC says to store at least 1 gallon (3.8 liters) per person per day for emergencies.19 Toilets: UNHCR's target is 1 latrine per 20 people, or 1 per household. No latrine should serve more than 50 people in the first phase of an emergency.22 First aid: The Red Cross lists kit contents sized for a family of four.23 What a group needs, by size (arithmetic from UNHCR and Red Cross figures; round up) PeopleWater a day at 20 L eachLatrines at 1 per 20Family-size first aid kits (1 per 4) 480 L (21 gal)11 12240 L (63 gal)13 25500 L (132 gal)27 501,000 L (264 gal)313 Bigger groups need more structure. More people means more decisions to make and more chances to disagree. Rules, decision methods and dispute resolution are in Group Rules, Decisions & Resolving Disputes. Separate households can still work as one group. Each family keeps its own home and stores, and the households share skills, tools and night watch. Write the group's numbers on one pageHead count, babies, elders, pregnant women, dogs, daily water, daily calories, latrines and first aid kits. Recount every month. The full food math is in Calories & Nutrition.

s.h: 🤝 Forming the group and practicing together First 30 days
s.x: Start small and start now. A group is easier to build while phones, shops and classes still work. Start with who you knowFamily first, then your nearest neighbors, then friends who have skills you lack. Talk about needs firstEach household lists its people, health needs, medicines, pets and supplies. Fill the skills grid togetherAgree on a lead and a backup for every job. Write the gaps down. Write simple agreementsWho decides what, how work and food are shared, and how disputes are settled. Put them on paper. Practice togetherThe Red Cross advises practicing your plan at least twice a year.24 NFPA advises fire drills twice a year, once by day and once at night.3 Review every yearUpdate the grid, the rota and the numbers. Replace expired supplies.12 Run a 24-hour no-power weekendPick a weekend. Use only stored water and food, run the rota and stand a night watch. Write down every problem, then fix one each week. Get these for the group A paper notebook for the skills grid, rota and head count One family-size first aid kit per 4 people, checked for expiry dates23 Battery-powered CO alarms, replaced every 5 years16 Places in a Stop the Bleed, CPR or first aid class for at least two adults Download and print while the internet worksFEMA's Family Emergency Communication Plan, the Red Cross Family Disaster Plan Template and FEMA's Pet Preparedness Toolkit (all PDFs). Keep paper copies with this book.

s.h: ⏳ How the group changes over 30 years Long haul
s.x: Your group ages one year every year. Plan the roles for the people you will have, not only the people you have today. Year 0Babies and toddlers need full-time care. Older adults and young children are most at risk from heat and cold.4 Year 1Every lead has a trained backup. Every hard job rotates. The skills grid has no empty columns. Year 10A child who was 2 at the start is now 12: old enough to learn CPR under the 2025 guidelines.13 Teenagers become backups. Year 20Today's 50-year-olds are 70. Move them from heavy work to teaching, records and child minding. Year 30Children born after the outage are adults and leads. Skills must be taught, not just stored on paper. How to pass skills on is in Passing On Skills to the Next Generation. Which trades to rebuild first is in Rebuilding Local Trades & Economy.

Draw a skills grid on paper for everyone in your home: medical, food, mechanical, child care, security, teaching Circle every skill with no lead, or with only one person Book a Stop the Bleed, CPR or first aid class for at least two adults Sign up children 12 and older for a CPR class Name a lead and a backup for every job, every child, every elder and every dog List every powered medical device and medicine each person needs Ask your two nearest neighbors what skills they have Find out which shelters near you accept pets Write the group's numbers on one page: people, water, latrines, first aid kits Run a 24-hour no-power weekend and put a yearly review date on the calendar

How much water per person per day does UNHCR plan for household use?20 liters (about 5 gallons). For 5 people that is 100 kg (220 lb) to move every day. What are the six skill areas?Medical, food, mechanical, child care, security and teaching. Who gets a lead and a backup?Every job, every child, every elder and every dog. How many people per latrine?Aim for 1 per 20 people (or 1 per household). Never more than 50 in the first phase. At what age can children learn CPR?12 and older (AHA 2025 guidelines). Whose food should never be rationed?Children and pregnant women (FEMA and Red Cross). An 8-hour night watch with 4 adults?2 hours each per night, or 4 hours each every other night.

Pick one out-of-area contact. Local phone lines tend to overload after an emergency, so everyone reports to the same faraway person.4 Choose four meeting places: inside the home, in the neighborhood, outside the neighborhood and out of town.5 Text, don't call. Texts may get through when calls do not.7 Put the plan on paper. Give every person a wallet card with the numbers and meeting places.8 Practice twice a year, once in daylight and once at night.9 Name a helper and a backup for every baby, older adult and person with a disability, and put your pets in the plan.911 <50%of US adults had an emergency plan (CDC survey, June 2024)1 5,192children reported missing after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita (2005)2 2× a yearhow often to practice your escape plan9 1–2 minmay be all the time you get to escape a home fire9

s.h: 🗺️ Why a written family plan matters First 72 h
s.x: A family plan answers five questions before you need them. Where do we meet? Who do we tell? Who gets the kids? Who helps the people who need help? What happens to the dog? In a crisis there is no time to discuss these. A written plan means every person already knows their job. Most adults do not have one. In a June 2024 CDC survey, only 46% of adults without a disability and 48% of adults with a disability had an emergency plan.1 This chapter builds your plan in order: the out-of-area contact, meeting places, school and work, the people and pets who need help, drills, and a fill-in template at the end. Two decisions live in other chapters. Whether to shelter or leave is in Stay or Go?. What each person carries is in Go-Bags for Every Family Member. The 30-year view: build two layersOfficial family plans lean on phones and texting. Keep that layer, because it is fast while networks work.Then add a no-phone layer: fixed meeting places, set check-in times and paper notes. That layer still works when there is no power to charge anything. It is covered below in "When phones are down".

s.h: 📞 The out-of-area contact and the paper contact list
s.x: Choose one person who lives outside your area to be your family's message center. The American Red Cross advises this because local phone lines tend to be overloaded after an emergency.4 FEMA and Ready.gov give the same rule: pick someone outside town, because they may be easier to reach in a disaster.56 Everyone reports to the same person. Then one message to that person tells you where everyone is, and you do not have to reach five phones one by one. Each person contacts the same out-of-area person, who passes news to the rest. Local lines tend to overload after an emergency, so a distant contact may be easier to reach.46 Set up your out-of-area contact Ask a calm person far awayChoose a friend or relative who lives outside your area. The Red Cross calls this your out-of-area contact.4 Ask them, and get a clear yes. Pick a backup in a different regionIf your main contact lives in the same disaster zone as you on the day, you still have a second person to reach. Agree on a short message formatWho, where, condition, next move. Example: "Ana OK. At spot 3. Kids with me." Write both numbers on paperPut them on a wallet card for every person, including in each child's backpack.8 Test itHave every person text the contact once. Fix any wrong number the same day. Text first, keep calls short Do Text for anything that is not a life-threatening emergency57 Keep calls brief and give only vital information7 Limit non-emergency calls to save your phone battery7 Call 911 first for a life-threatening emergency7 Don't Redial at once if a call fails; wait 10 seconds first7 Make non-emergency calls that tie up the network7 Count on texting 911; it only works in some places7 If something happens, we will just call each other. Calls can fail even when the equipment works, because network congestion blocks them. The FCC advises texting instead, because texts may get through when calls do not.7 FEMA says the same.5 The paper contact list Write every important number on paper. A contact list inside a dead phone cannot help you. List the out-of-area contact and backup, close neighbors, each school or daycare, each workplace, your doctor or clinic, your vet, and the local animal shelter. Use the official wallet cardFEMA's family communication plan comes as a fillable, wallet-sized card.8 Fill one in for every person. Put copies in each go-bag, each car and each child's school bag.

s.h: 📍 Four meeting places, near to far
s.x: Pick safe, familiar places where your family can go for protection or to reunite. FEMA's plan uses four levels: indoors, in your neighborhood, outside your neighborhood and out of town.5 The Red Cross gives the reason for the two closest ones. One spot right outside the home is for a sudden emergency like a fire. A second spot is for when you cannot return home.4 FEMA's family communication plan uses indoor, neighborhood, out-of-neighborhood and out-of-town meeting places. FEMA's examples: an inner room for storms; a big tree, mailbox or neighbor's house; a library, community center, house of worship or family friend's home; and a relative's or friend's home out of town.5 What each meeting place is for SpotUse it whenGood examples 1. Inside homeHigh winds or a storm: you must shelter indoors5A small, windowless inner room on the lowest floor5 2. Just outsideA sudden emergency like a fire4A big tree, the mailbox or a neighbor's house5 3. Out of neighborhoodYou cannot get home4Library, community center, house of worship, friend's home5 4. Out of townYou cannot get home or to spot 3, or your area is told to evacuate5A relative's or friend's home in another town5 Every spot must work for every person. FEMA says to make sure meeting places are accessible for household members with disabilities.5 Check steps, slopes, distance and whether there is shelter from rain and sun. Every spot must work for your animals too. FEMA says to think about animal-friendly locations.5 Temporary public shelters may not allow animals, so line up pet-friendly options ahead of time.13 Measure the route to spots 3 and 4 on a paper map and write the distance in both kilometers and miles. See Map & Compass Navigation. Give each spot a backupA library can flood. A friend's house can burn. For spots 3 and 4, write a second choice next to the first, and agree that whoever arrives first leaves a dated note if they have to move on.

Disasters do not wait until everyone is home. Your plan must cover the hours when children are at school, adults are at work and someone is on the road. The Red Cross says to know the evacuation sites at work and at school or day care.4 It also tells commuters to make a plan for how the family will stay in contact if separated.10 Separation is a documented riskAfter Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005, 5,192 children were reported missing. Officials called it the largest child-recovery effort in US history, and it took more than six months.2 The last child was reunited in March 2006.3 Make the school and daycare plan Ask for the school's emergency planAsk where children go if the building is evacuated, and how the school contacts parents. Update the pickup listAsk who the school will release your child to. Add at least two trusted adults besides the parents, and keep it current. Teach your child the pickup namesName the adults on the school's list out loud with your child. Teach them to go only with those people. Put a card in every backpackParents' numbers, the out-of-area contact and the meeting places, on a wallet card.8 Teach the plan at the child's levelReady.gov has a family plan page written for kids.6 Practice it together. Work and commuting Know your workplace evacuation site.4 Then decide now who leaves work to collect the children and who goes home to the animals and older relatives. Write down a walking route home from work in case roads or transit stop. Keep walking shoes, water and a paper map at work, as part of your work go-bag. Babies and young childrenAssign one adult to each baby, plus a backup in case that adult is away. NFPA gives this advice for infants in home escape plans.9 Do the same for every child too young to get out alone.On the plan, write each child's feeding needs, formula type, medicines and allergies. Keep a current photo of each child with the wallet card.

s.h: 🔀 When phones are down: the no-phone plan
s.x: If the network is down, your plan must work on foot and on paper. That means fixed places, fixed times and written notes. Fixed check-in times. Example: "If we cannot reach each other, go to spot 3. Be there at 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. every day." Dated notes. Anyone who leaves home or a meeting spot leaves a note: date, time, names, where they went. One direction. Always move outward through the spots in order: 1, 2, 3, 4. Then searchers know where to look next. Move outward through the meeting places in order. The near spots cover a sudden emergency like a fire; the far spots cover times when you cannot go home.45 For ways to pass messages without phones, see Radios: Ham, GMRS, CB & Listening. Women and girlsPlan routes so that no woman or girl has to walk alone to a far meeting place, especially at night. Pair people up in the plan.If someone is pregnant, add her due date, her clinic and her prenatal records to the plan. See Personal Safety for Women & Girls. Keeping the plan alive for decadesChildren grow up, people move and pets change. Review the whole plan at each twice-yearly drill, the same schedule NFPA gives for escape plan practice.9Write in pencil so it is easy to update. Keep copies in sealed plastic bags, and give one to your out-of-area contact.

s.h: 🧑‍🦽 Babies, older adults, disabilities and pets
s.x: More adults with disabilities have lived through a disaster. In the CDC's June 2024 survey, 80% of adults with disabilities had lived through at least one natural disaster, compared with 70% of adults without disabilities.1 They also face more barriers to leaving. 26% said they had nowhere to go, compared with 15% of adults without disabilities. 20% named the cost of evacuating, compared with 14%.1 The CDC says accessible planning and communication may help close these gaps.1 That starts with your family plan. Older adults and people with disabilitiesName a helper and a backup for each person who needs help to move. NFPA says to plan for anyone with a disability and assign a backup in case the main helper is not home.9List their medicines, devices (wheelchair, walker, hearing aids, glasses) and exactly how to move them. Check that every meeting place is accessible to them.5 See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People. Dogs and other petsPets belong in the family plan. Ready.gov says to include them and to have your vet microchip each pet.11 If a lost pet is taken to a vet clinic or shelter, staff can scan it for the microchip number.13Find pet-friendly places to stay before an emergency, because public shelters may not take animals.1213 Check the microchip registry has your current phone number. See Dogs in a Long Emergency. Practice twice a year. NFPA says to practice your home fire escape plan twice a year.9 The Red Cross plan also says to practice evacuating your home twice a year.4 Drill in daylight and at night. For young children, NFPA suggests telling them about a drill before bed, because the goal is practice, not fear.9 Week 1Write the plan, fill in wallet cards and choose all four meeting places. Month 1Daytime drill: use both exits from each room, then text the out-of-area contact.9 Walk the routes to spots 3 and 4 with the children and write down the time and distance. Month 6Night drill, then review and update the whole plan.9 Month 12Daytime drill again. Keep going: one day drill and one night drill every year.9 Each new school year or jobUpdate school, daycare and work details and the pickup list. Run a home drill Tell young children firstExplain what will happen. For a night drill, tell them before bed.9 Start the drillPress the smoke alarm test button so everyone learns the sound. Use the second way outEvery room needs two ways out. Never go back insideOnce you are out, stay out. Do not go back into a burning home for any reason.9 A fire can leave you as little as 1 or 2 minutes to escape once the smoke alarm sounds.9 Tell the fire department who is missing, including pets. Firefighters have the equipment to do rescues.9 Teach this rule to every child. In an emergency you can always text 911. Text-to-911 is only available in some locations. Always try to call 911 first.7 For a bigger household or group, give each adult a written role. See Building Your Group: Size, Roles & Skills.
