t: Stay or Go? Sheltering in Place vs Evacuating

s.x: Follow official orders first. Leave when your zone is told to evacuate. Get inside at once when you are told to shelter in place.76 Run from water. Hide from bad air. Storm surge is the greatest threat to life on the coast. In a radiation emergency: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned.34 Leave early, or the road itself can kill. In the 2005 Hurricane Rita evacuation, over 100 of at least 119 storm deaths were linked to the evacuation.2 Keep at least half a tank of fuel at all times. Fill it up when an evacuation looks likely.1 Staying has its own killers. After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, portable generators poisoned at least 78 people with carbon monoxide (CO) and killed 10.5 3.7 Mpeople left the Texas coast before Hurricane Rita in 20052 100+of at least 119 Rita deaths were linked to the evacuation2 49%of US hurricane deaths (1963–2012) came from storm surge9 ½ tankof fuel to keep in your car at all times1

s.h: 🧭 The official rule: plan for both, then follow orders
s.x: Plan for staying and for leaving, before anything happens. An earlier Ready.gov page (archived 2008) called stay-or-go the first important decision in an emergency, and told you to plan for both.8 Stay inside when the outside is the danger. Officials recommend sheltering in place when there is little time to react and being outside would be more dangerous.6 Leave when the hazard will reach your home. For hurricanes, a National Hurricane Center (NHC) official put it simply: "We evacuate from the water, not the wind, and we have evacuation zones."7 Orders come first If officials order you to shelter in place, act immediately.6 Do not finish chores or go outside to look. If you are told to evacuate, follow the recommended routes. Do not take shortcuts. They may be blocked.1 Leave early enough that severe weather cannot trap you. Plan now how you will leave and where you will go.1 Find your zone todayHurricane evacuations are ordered by zone.7 Look up the zones for your home, work and school while the internet still works. Write them on your paper plan. See The Family Emergency Plan. The 30-year viewIf no official orders reach you, use the same tests officials use: get away from rising water, and get inside when the air outside is the danger.36A safe, stocked home with water, food and a garden is a strong reason to stay. See Preparing Your Home for a Long Outage.

s.h: 🌊 When leaving is the right call
s.x: In hurricanes, water kills more people than wind. The NHC says storm surge and large waves pose the greatest threat to life and property along the coast.3 An NHC study of US storms from 1963 to 2012 found that 49% of deaths, nearly half, were blamed on storm-surge flooding.9 Inland, flooding is the major threat from tropical storms.3 See Floods. An NHC study blamed 49% of US hurricane and tropical storm deaths from 1963 to 2012 on storm surge.9 Surge is the greatest threat to life on the coast.3 Which hazards usually mean stay, and which mean go HazardUsual moveWhere to be Storm surge on the coastGo when your zone is ordered out7Outside the surge zone3 Radiation releaseStay: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned4Basement or middle of the building4 Chemical cloud (plume)Stay if told to shelter in place6Interior room above ground, sealed1011 Any danger with little warningStay when outside is more dangerous6Indoors For other hazards, see Wildfire & Smoke, Nuclear & Radiation Emergencies and Chemical Spills & Industrial Accidents. Hurricane wind is the main killer, so a strong house is enough. Storm surge is the greatest threat to life on the coast.3 It caused 49% of US hurricane and tropical storm deaths from 1963 to 2012.9

s.h: 🏠 When staying is the right call: shelter in place
s.x: Shelter in place means you stay inside, in the safest room, until officials say it is safe to go out.4 It is the right move when being outside is more dangerous than being inside.6 Chemicals: go up. Radiation: go down or to the middle. Ready.gov guidance sends you above ground for a chemical release, but below ground for a radiological one.104 Radiation: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned Get inside nowThis is the first of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) three rules: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned.4 Go to the basement or the middleGet to the middle of the building or a basement, away from doors and windows.4 Shut out the outside airClose and lock windows and doors. Turn off fans, air conditioners and forced-air heaters that pull in outside air.4 Stay tunedListen for updated instructions from officials.4 Without grid power, that means a battery or hand-crank radio. Stay until officials say it is safeSheltering usually lasts at least 24 hours.13 Keep everyone inside, pets included.12 Chemical cloud: an interior room above ground, sealed Bring everyone in, pets tooPets should not go outside during a chemical emergency.12 Shut out the outside airClose and lock windows and outside doors. Close the fireplace damper. Turn off fans, heating and air conditioning.12 Go to an interior room above groundTake everyone into an interior room with no or few windows and shut the door.12 For a chemical cloud, shelter above ground, not in the basement.10 Seal the roomSeal windows, doors and air vents with plastic sheeting and duct tape.11 Ready.gov cites studies showing that sealing a room with common materials makes it safer against a chemical plume.10 Listen and waitKeep the radio on. Leave the room only when officials say the air outside is safe. Radiation: basement or middle, away from windows.4 Chemicals: an interior room above ground, sealed.1011 Storm surge: leave the zone.3 Dogs and pets come inside with youPets should not go outside during a chemical or radiation emergency. Bring them into the shelter room.12 Keep a leash, a water bowl and waste bags in that room. See Dogs in a Long Emergency. No generator near your shelter roomAfter Katrina and Rita, most generator CO poisonings involved generators placed outside but near homes.5 Outside is not enough. See Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer. Shelter-in-place kitPlastic sheeting and duct ta

s.h: 🚗 What really happened on the road: Hurricane Rita, 2005
s.x: In September 2005, nearly 3.7 million people left the Texas coast in the days before Hurricane Rita made landfall.2 A 2018 review calls it the largest emergency evacuation in US history.2 The evacuation killed more people than the storm did. Over 100 of the at least 119 deaths attributed to Rita were linked to the evacuation itself, about 107 by that count.2 Heat in stuck cars was a major killer. At least 10% of evacuation deaths were linked to hyperthermia (dangerous overheating) in vehicles.2 Medical examiners suspected overheating or a worsened chronic illness in about another 50% of evacuation deaths.2 A bus carrying nursing-home residents caught fire in the evacuation traffic. About two dozen people died.2 Plans can be fixed. Texas revised its evacuation plans after Rita and used the changes successfully in later storms.2 Three lessons for your own plan Leave early. Go early enough that severe weather cannot trap you.1 Long waits in traffic were where Rita evacuees overheated.2 Pack for a long, hot wait. Carry drinking water and a way to stay cool for every person and animal in the car. Overheating in vehicles was linked to at least 10% of evacuation deaths.2 Plan transport for frail people first. People with chronic illness were among those who died on the road.2 Arrange their ride and supplies before anyone else's. No car? Arrange a ride now. Ready.gov says to make arrangements with family, friends or your local government.1 Deaths attributed to Hurricane Rita, from a 2018 review of the evacuation.2 Bars are drawn to scale. Older, sick and disabled peopleRita's deaths show the danger: overheating and worsened chronic illness in vehicles, and a burning bus full of nursing-home residents.2If someone in your home is frail, uses medical equipment or cannot cope with heat, plan to leave early, before roads fill.1 See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People. Babies and children in the carOverheating in vehicles was a recorded cause of Rita evacuation deaths.2 Pack water, feeds and diapers for a long delay, not just the planned drive time. Never leave a child alone in a car. See The Baby & Toddler Prep Kit.

s.h: ⚖️ Risks of leaving vs risks of staying
s.x: Neither choice is free of risk. Compare the documented dangers for your hazard, your home and your people. Then pick the smaller danger. Documented risks on each side If you goIf you stay Heat in stalled traffic: at least 10% of Rita evacuation deaths2Storm surge: 49% of US hurricane deaths, 1963–20129 Vehicle fire: the Rita nursing-home bus2Carbon monoxide: 10 generator deaths in Alabama and Texas after Katrina and Rita5 Blocked shortcuts, washed-out roads, downed power lines and flooded roads1Inland flooding from tropical storms3 Being outdoors during a radiation or chemical release, when inside is safer46Being trapped by severe weather if you leave too late1 Leaving is always the safe choice. In the Hurricane Rita evacuation, the evacuation itself was linked to over 100 of at least 119 deaths.2 Leave when your zone is ordered out, and leave early.1 A generator outside the house cannot hurt anyone inside. After Katrina and Rita, most generator CO poisonings involved generators placed outside but near homes. At least 78 people were poisoned and 10 died.5 Do Leave early when your zone is ordered out Follow the recommended routes Keep half a tank of fuel, always Get inside fast for radiation or chemicals Follow official instructions on a battery radio Don't Take shortcuts that may be blocked Wait until severe weather traps you Run a generator near the house Go outside to look during a release Drive into flooded areas Each rule above comes from Ready.gov, the CDC or Ready Illinois guidance.1456

s.h: ⛽ If you go: fuel, timing and routes

Ready.gov advises this to reduce congestion and delay.1 Know your range before you need it. Multiply the fuel in the tank by your car's fuel economy. s.h: 📍 Where to go: relatives, shelters, rural or urban
s.x: Decide where you will go before you need to. Ready.gov tells you to plan where you will go if you are told to evacuate.1 Pick several destinations in different directions. Ready.gov advises this so you still have options in an emergency.1 Your options, in planning order Friends or relatives outside the hazard zone. Agree now, in writing, that you can come. Say how many people and animals. Public shelters opened by officials. Listen to official instructions for which shelters are open. Temporary public shelters may not allow animals, so plan where your dog will stay.14 Any safe place you can reach on half a tank, by your own range math above.1 Rural or urban? What the evidence supports We found no reliable study that ranks rural or urban places as safer in a long outage. So this book makes no such claim. Instead, test any destination against facts you can check yourself: Is it outside storm-surge and flood zones?3 Can you reach it on the fuel you will have?1 Does it have water you can make safe? See Finding Water When the Taps Stop. Do people there know you and expect you? Can your baby, your oldest relative and your dog cope with the trip? Women and girlsBefore you arrive, ask how sleeping areas and toilets work at your destination or shelter. Travel and use facilities in pairs. Pack menstrual supplies and any prescribed medicines in each go-bag. See Personal Safety for Women & Girls. Leaving for goodIn a multi-year outage, leaving can mean leaving your stores, water system and garden behind. Weigh that against a hazard that will reach the house, such as storm surge.3

Pack one bag per person, sized to their body. Keep a child's pack at or under 10% of body weight. Even fit soldiers are advised to stay at or under 30%.89 Each bag covers 3 days away from home. The Red Cross evacuation supply is 1 gallon (3.8 liters) of water per person per day, plus easy food, for 3 days.2 Babies, elders and dogs need their own supplies. Formula and diapers; medicines, glasses and hearing-aid batteries; collar, leash, ID, food and a bowl.12 Copies of documents and cash go in a waterproof packet. ID, insurance, proof of address, birth certificates and a medication list.12 Check every bag at least once a year. Replace expired items and refit bags as children grow.1 3 daysof supplies in an evacuation bag2 3.8 L(1 gallon) of water per person per day2 ≤10%of a child's body weight in a backpack8 ≤30%of body weight: the recommended ceiling for soldiers9

s.h: 🎒 What a go-bag is for First 72 h
s.x: A go-bag is the bag you grab when you must leave home fast. Fire, flood, a chemical leak or a damaged house can all force you out in minutes. The American Red Cross says every household should pack one.3 It is not your home supply. The Red Cross uses two sizes: a 3-day supply to take when you evacuate and a 2-week supply to keep at home.2 Your long-term stores stay at home. See Storing Water and Long-Term Food Storage. Ready.gov says to keep supplies at home, at work and in the car.1 At work, be ready to shelter for at least 24 hours, and keep comfortable walking shoes with your supplies.1 Ready.gov also says to store items in airtight plastic bags and keep the whole kit in one or two easy-to-carry containers.1 For a family on foot, that means one backpack for each person who can carry one. Whether to leave at all is a separate decision. It is covered in Stay or Go? A go-bag should hold everything you need to survive. Official lists size it for 3 days of evacuation. The 2-week supply stays at home.2 Carrying heavy loads causes injuries: foot blisters, stress fractures and back strains are among the most common.10 DoPack one bag per person who can carry oneKeep bags in one known spot near the exitWeigh every bag on a bathroom scalePut the heavy shared gear on the strongest adults Don'tPack one giant family bag that only one person can liftHide bags where only one person knows to lookGuess the weightBorrow from the bags for daily use and forget to refill

s.h: 🧾 The adult bag: what the official lists include
s.x: Ready.gov and the American Red Cross publish the two most-used kit lists. Their core items overlap. The table merges them so you can pack from one list.12 Adult go-bag core items (Ready.gov and American Red Cross) NeedWhat to packSource Water1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day; 3 days for evacuationRed Cross2 FoodNon-perishable, easy-to-prepare food; manual can openerRed Cross, Ready.gov21 Light and newsFlashlight; battery or hand-crank radio (NOAA Weather Radio in the US); extra batteriesReady.gov, Red Cross12 First aidFirst aid kit; 7-day supply of medicines and medical itemsRed Cross2 Signal and airWhistle to signal for help; dust mask to help filter contaminated airReady.gov1 ShelterPlastic sheeting, scissors and duct tape; emergency blanketReady.gov, Red Cross12 HygieneMoist towelettes, garbage bags and plastic ties; soap and hand sanitizerReady.gov1 ToolsMulti-purpose tool; wrench or pliers to turn off utilitiesRed Cross, Ready.gov21 Phone and mapsCell phone with chargers and a backup battery; local mapsReady.gov1 Clothes and sleepComplete change of clothes for your climate; sturdy shoes; sleeping bag or warm blanketReady.gov1 Papers and moneyCopies of key documents; family and emergency contacts; cashRed Cross, Ready.gov21 ExtrasSpare car and house keys; matches in a waterproof container; rain gear; work glovesRed Cross, Ready.gov21 The first aid kit, light, radio and navigation each have their own chapter. See Building a Long-Term Medical Kit, Radios and Map & Compass Navigation. Water is the heavy part One liter of water weighs 1 kg (2.2 lb). So 1 US gallon (3.8 L) weighs about 3.8 kg (8.3 lb). The Red Cross 3-day evacuation supply is 3 gallons (11.4 L) per person.2 That is 11.4 kg (25 lb) of water for one person, before food, clothes or anything else. For a 60 kg (132 lb) adult, that water alone is 19% of body weight. Compare that with the limits in the next section. Split the water loadReady.gov says to keep a kit in the car too.1 If you leave by vehicle, the extra water rides there. On foot, carry what you can and pack a way to treat water you find. See Disinfecting Water and Water Filters. Women and girlsReady.gov lists feminine supplies and personal hygiene items in the basic kit.1 Pack at least 3 days of products for every girl and woman who menstruates, plus spares and a few sealable bags for used products.Reusable options are in Periods With

Weigh every bag, then compare it with the carrier's body weight. Most research on carrying loads comes from soldiers. It gives clear ceilings you can use. Adults A U.S. Army report gives the Infantry School's recommended limits: a fighting load of 22 kg (48 lb), about 30% of body weight, and an approach-march load of 33 kg (72 lb), about 45%.11 A 2018 study in Military Medicine notes that loads of 30% of body mass or less are recommended to avoid drops in performance.9 It tested soldiers on a 10 km (6.2 mi) mixed-terrain course carrying 30% and 45% of body mass.9 It found that standard equations underestimate the energy cost of carrying loads over rough ground.9 A pack that feels fine on a flat road costs more on trails, mud or rubble. These numbers come from trained, fit soldiers. Treat 30% as a ceiling for healthy adults, not a target. Children The National Safety Council (NSC) says a child's backpack should weigh no more than 5–10% of the child's body weight.8 KidsHealth, from the Nemours children's health system, gives a wider range of 10–20%. Its example: an 80 lb (36 kg) child should carry no more than 8–16 lb (3.6–7.3 kg).7 For a long walk, use the lower number. Arithmetic from the cited limits: children at 10% of body weight (NSC) and adults at the 30% ceiling used for soldiers.89 Water: 3 gallons (11.4 L) for one person for 3 days (Red Cross).2 Pack weight at 10%, 20% and 30% of body weight (arithmetic) Body weight10%20%30% 20 kg (44 lb)2 kg (4.4 lb)4 kg (8.8 lb)6 kg (13 lb) 35 kg (77 lb)3.5 kg (7.7 lb)7 kg (15 lb)10.5 kg (23 lb) 50 kg (110 lb)5 kg (11 lb)10 kg (22 lb)15 kg (33 lb) 60 kg (132 lb)6 kg (13 lb)12 kg (26 lb)18 kg (40 lb) 80 kg (176 lb)8 kg (18 lb)16 kg (35 lb)24 kg (53 lb) Children use the 10% column. The 20% column is the top of the KidsHealth range.7 The 30% column is the soldiers' ceiling.9 What too much weight does A 2004 review of soldier load carriage lists the common injuries: foot blisters, stress fractures, back strains, metatarsalgia (pain in the ball of the foot), rucksack palsy (numbness or weakness from strap pressure on nerves) and knee pain.10 The same review says loads are easier to carry when they are lighter, better distributed and carried in better-designed equipment.10 Narrow straps cause numbnessTight, narrow straps that dig into the shoulders can cause tingling, numbness and weakness in the arms and hands.7 Choose

A child who walks well can carry a small, light bag of their own. It holds personal items. Adults carry the water and heavy gear. Ready.gov lists books, games, puzzles or other activities for children.1 The Red Cross adds games and activities, plus family and emergency contact information.2 A contact card with parents' names, phone numbers and an out-of-area contact A complete change of clothes and sturdy shoes1 A whistle to signal for help1 A small flashlight, a water bottle and a few snacks One comfort item and one small game or book Fit rules Use two wide shoulder straps. Bags slung over one shoulder, across the chest, or with only one strap do not spread the weight as well.7 The pack should rest evenly in the middle of the back and should not sag down to the buttocks.7 Lighten or adjust the pack if a child struggles to put it on or take it off, has back pain, or leans forward to carry it.7 Fit rules and warning signs from KidsHealth (Nemours); weight limit from the National Safety Council.78 Children grow out of their bagsClothes, shoes and safe pack weight all change as a child grows. Ready.gov says to re-think your needs every year and update the kit as your family changes.1 Re-weigh the child and the bag at every check.Skills children can learn by age are in Survival Skills Kids Can Learn by Age.

s.h: 👶 The baby's bag (carried by an adult)
s.x: A baby cannot carry anything, so the baby's supplies add to an adult's load. If you can, have one adult carry the baby and another carry the baby's bag. Ready.gov lists infant formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream.1 The Red Cross lists bottles, formula, baby food and diapers.2 3 days of formula or baby food, plus bottles and a way to clean them 3 days of diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream Spare clothes and a warm layer A sling or soft carrier, so your hands stay free The baby's medicines, a thermometer and a copy of the vaccination record Count the baby in the carrier's load. Weigh yourself holding the baby and wearing the bag, then compare the difference with your 30% ceiling.9 Full lists and safe feedingQuantities for 2 weeks, 3 months and 1 year are in The Baby & Toddler Prep Kit. Safe formula preparation without power is in Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

Pack the small medical items people forget. The Red Cross lists hearing aids with extra batteries, glasses, contact lenses, syringes and a cane.2 Ready.gov adds prescription eyeglasses, contact lens solution, prescription medicines, and non-prescription medicines such as pain relievers, anti-diarrhea medicine, antacids or laxatives.1 How many days of medicine? The current Red Cross survival kit list says a 7-day supply of medications and medical items.2 Its power outage checklist says the same.5 Another Red Cross emergency supply checklist says a 1-month supply.6 Ask the doctor or pharmacist how to build an emergency supply. See Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies. Pack a written medication list with medical information. The Red Cross lists it among the documents to copy.2 If they cannot carry the bagWeigh the bag while they wear it. Watch for the same warning signs used for children: struggling to put it on or off, back pain, or leaning forward.7 If you see them, move the weight to someone else.Mobility aids, oxygen and dementia care are covered in Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

Your dog needs its own supplies. The Red Cross lists pet supplies: collar, leash, ID, food, carrier and bowl.2 Ready.gov adds pet food and extra water for your pet.1 Pack current photos of you with your pet.3 If you are separated, a photo helps you show that the dog is yours. Collar with ID tag, plus a spare leash 3 days of food in an airtight bag Water and a collapsible bowl Any medicines your dog takes Copies of vaccination and medical records Waste bags The dog's food and water add to an adult's load. Weigh them into someone's budget. More on dogsFood and water needs by dog size are in Dogs in a Long Emergency and Feeding Dogs Without Kibble. A dog first aid list is in Dog First Aid.

Pack copies of documents, sealed against water. The Red Cross lists copies of these: medication list and medical information, proof of address, deed or lease, passports, birth certificates and insurance policies.2 Ready.gov lists copies of insurance policies, identification and bank account records, saved electronically or in a waterproof, portable container.1 FEMA's financial first aid kit The US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and Operation HOPE publish the Emergency Financial First Aid Kit (EFFAK) for free.12 It has sections for household information, professional advisors and health care providers, and a checklist of legal documents and financial statements.12 Its checklist includes items such as military ID and discharge papers (DD 214). If a document is missing, it says to contact the company or agency for a copy.13 Ready.gov's financial preparedness page links the kit and its forms.14 GatherUse the EFFAK checklist to find each document.13 Ask the agency for copies of anything missing. CopyPhotocopy each document. Add the family contact list and a current photo of each pet with you.3 SealPut the copies in airtight plastic bags or a waterproof container.1 SplitGive a packet to each adult bag, so one lost bag does not lose everything. Back upReady.gov mentions saving records electronically.1 Keep paper as well, because phones need charging. Cash Both official lists include cash. Ready.gov lists cash or traveler's checks; the Red Cross lists extra cash.12 Pack small billsReady.gov warns that ATMs and card machines may not work in a power outage.15 Small bills mean you do not depend on anyone having change. Split the cash between adult bags. The 30-year view: papersDeeds, birth records and identity papers matter for decades, long after phones fail. See Preserving Knowledge & Records for paper and ink that last.

A bag only works if what is inside still works. Ready.gov's maintenance advice is short:1 Keep canned food in a cool, dry place Store boxed food in tightly closed plastic or metal containers Replace expired items as needed Re-think your needs every year and update the kit as your family's needs change Make sure every family member knows where the kits are kept.1 Ready.gov: replace expired items and re-think your needs every year.1 Re-weigh children against the 10% limit at each check.8 TodayStart with what you already have, including a backpack or duffel bag.4 ThenAdd a few useful items at a time, as your budget allows.4 Each checkReplace expired items.1 Write the earliest expiry date on a tag on the outside. Every yearRe-think everyone's needs and update the bags.1 After any useRefill the bag before you put it away. Growth spurtRe-weigh the child and the bag against the 10% limit.8 The 30-year view: bags without storesWhen stores are gone, you cannot buy replacements. Eat bag food at home before it expires and refill from your home stores. Choose bag items that do not expire, such as tools, whistles, cups and clothing.The bag's job stays the same for decades: 3 days away from home. What changes is the family: children grow, elders need more help, and dogs age. Download and print while the internet works Ready.gov: Build a Kit American Red Cross: What Do You Need in a Survival Kit FEMA: Emergency Financial First Aid Kit (large print) KidsHealth: Backpack Safety Printable lists for every kit are in Master Checklists.

Pick one backpack per person who can carry one, using bags you already own Pack 3 days of water, food, a flashlight, a radio and a first aid kit in each adult bag Add 7 days of each person's medicines, plus glasses and hearing-aid batteries Pack the baby bag: formula or food, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream Pack the dog bag: collar with ID, leash, food, water, bowl and a photo of you together Copy key documents, seal them in waterproof bags and add small bills Put a contact card and a whistle in every child's bag Weigh every bag: children 10% of body weight or less, adults well under 30% Store all bags together near the exit and show everyone where they are Set a yearly date to unpack, check and refit every bag

How many days does a go-bag cover?3 days for evacuation. The 2-week supply stays at home (Red Cross). How much water per person per day?1 gallon (3.8 L). Three days weighs about 11.4 kg (25 lb). How heavy can a child's pack be?10% of body weight or less (NSC). A 20 kg child carries 2 kg. What is the adult ceiling?30% of body weight, the figure recommended for trained soldiers. How many days of medicine?At least 7 days (Red Cross). Another Red Cross checklist says 1 month. Originals or copies of documents?Copies, sealed in airtight or waterproof bags. How often do you check the bags?At least every year, and replace expired items.

t: How Much Water You Really Need

s.x: Store at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day. That is the CDC and Ready.gov (FEMA) minimum. Keep at least 3 days, and 2 weeks if you can.12 In very hot weather, plan for double. Official guidance says heat can double water needs.2 Store extra for pregnant and breastfeeding women, children, sick people and pets. The CDC names pregnant women, sick people and pets; extension guidance adds children and nursing mothers.16 One gallon is a floor, not a full day. The humanitarian Sphere standard is 15 L (4 gallons) per person per day for drinking, cooking and hygiene.3 Thirty years cannot come out of storage. At 1 gallon a day, a family of 4 uses 1,460 gallons (5,527 L) a year. You need a source that refills.1 3.8 L(1 gallon) per person per day: the CDC home minimum1 14 daysof stored water: the CDC goal if you can manage it1 ×2how much water needs can rise in very hot temperatures2 15 Lper person per day: the Sphere humanitarian minimum3

s.h: 📏 The official numbers, side by side
s.x: Agencies give different numbers because they answer different questions. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Ready.gov tell households what to store at home for a short emergency.1 Sphere sets minimum standards for humanitarian aid after a disaster.4 Know both. The home number tells you what to store. The humanitarian number tells you what a household uses once drinking, cooking and washing all count. Home storage: CDC and FEMA First 72 h Store at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) of water per person per day. The CDC says to keep at least a 3-day supply, and a 2-week supply if possible.1 Ready.gov, the FEMA preparedness site, gives the same figure of 1 gallon per person per day.2 The CDC says this water covers drinking, cooking and brushing teeth.1 Notice the words "at least". Both agencies present the gallon as a minimum, and both say hot climates need more.12 Disaster relief: Sphere and UNHCR First 30 days The Sphere standard is 15 L (about 4 gallons) per person per day for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene (Sphere Handbook, 2011 edition).3 That is almost 4 times the CDC home minimum. Sphere training material says 7.5 L (2 gallons) per person per day may be appropriate only for a short time, in the acute phase of a drought.4 It also says a minimum is never a maximum.4 UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, plans for 20 L (5.3 gallons) per person per day for domestic needs and personal hygiene in refugee settings.5 Home storage minimums sit far below what aid agencies supply for longer stays. "Very hot weather" is the CDC gallon doubled, as Ready.gov warns.12345 Official daily water figures, per person Who says itPer dayWhat it is for CDC, Ready.gov (FEMA)At least 3.8 L (1 gal)Home emergency stock: drinking, cooking, brushing teeth Ready.gov (FEMA)Up to doubleVery hot weather Sphere, short term only7.5 L (2 gal)Acute phase of a drought, for a short time Sphere minimum15 L (4 gal)Drinking, cooking and personal hygiene UNHCR20 L (5.3 gal)Domestic needs and hygiene in refugee settings Sources for each row: CDC and Ready.gov12, Sphere34, UNHCR.5

Sphere splits basic daily water into three uses: drinking (including water in food), basic hygiene and basic cooking.3 Seeing the split shows why one gallon runs out fast. Basic survival water needs per person per day (Sphere) UseLitersUS gallonsDepends on Drinking and food2.5–3 L0.7–0.8 galClimate and the person's body Basic hygiene2–6 L0.5–1.6 galSocial and cultural norms Basic cooking3–6 L0.8–1.6 galType of food and local norms Total7.5–15 L2–4 gal Figures from the Sphere water supply standard.3 Gallon values are conversions (1 US gallon = 3.785 L). What is left of a gallon after drinkingSphere puts drinking and food water at 2.5–3 L per person per day.3 Take that out of a 3.8 L gallon and only 0.8–1.3 L (about 1 quart) is left for cooking and washing. Sphere's own range for those two uses is 5–12 L (1.3–3.2 gal).3 Same scale for all three bars. After drinking, a gallon leaves little for cooking or washing.13 When water is short, drinking comes first. Sphere calls drinking and food water "survival needs", while hygiene and cooking are "basic" needs.3 Do not plan for hygiene water to be zero for long. Clean hands and safe toilets are covered in Handwashing & Personal Hygiene.

The 1 gallon minimum is not enough for everyone. The CDC says to store more for pregnant women, people who are sick, pets, and anyone living in a hot climate.1 University of Florida (UF/IFAS) Extension guidance adds children and nursing mothers to the list.6 Heat, hard work and exercise In very hot temperatures, water needs can double.2 Ready.gov also says people in warm climates may need more water.2 FEMA and the Red Cross say a normally active person needs to drink at least 2 quarts (1.9 L) a day.7 They add that needs vary with age, physical condition, activity, diet and climate.7 Hauling water, cutting wood and long walks are more than normal activity. Plan extra drinking water for whoever does that work. For a family of 4, that turns a 2-week store of 56 gallons (212 L) into 112 gallons (424 L).12 Heat exhaustion and heat stroke are in Hypothermia, Frostbite & Heat Stroke. Pregnant and breastfeeding womenThe CDC lists pregnant women among the people to store extra water for.1 UF/IFAS Extension guidance adds nursing mothers.6Give her a personal bottle with liter marks. Then everyone can see how much she has had, and nobody has to ask. Babies and childrenCount every child as a full person in your plan. UF/IFAS Extension guidance says homes with children should store more, not less.6A baby on powdered formula needs safe water for every bottle. The CDC says to use bottled water for formula until tap water is declared safe.9 Add it to the plan, and see Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out. Dehydration warning signs in babies are in Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs. Sick and older relativesThe CDC says to store more for people who are sick.1 UF/IFAS Extension guidance says the same.6Put any relative with a long-term illness in the "needs more" group. Keep a filled cup within their reach, and refill it on a schedule. Dogs, cats and other petsThe CDC lists pets as a reason to store more water than the people's minimum.1 Ready.gov says a pet's emergency kit needs a water bowl and several days' supply of water.10 Your dog's needs are real numbers you can measure, so measure them now.Fill the bowl from a measuring jug. Each time you top it up, write down how much you added. Average 3 days. Do it again in the hottest month. Dog dehydration and heatstroke are in Dog First Aid. DoCount babies, children and older relatives as full peoplePlan double for very hot weatherA

s.x: Work out one number and write it on your water store. Follow the steps, then check them with the calculator. Count everyoneAdults, children, babies and older relatives. Add anyone who may shelter with you. Write pets on a separate line. Multiply by 1 gallon (3.8 L)That is the minimum per person per day.1 Adjust for heatIf your summers are very hot, double the number for those months.2 Add for higher-need peoplePregnant or breastfeeding women, children and anyone sick get extra.16 Add your petsUse the daily amount you measured for each animal.1 Multiply by days3 days at least. 14 days if you can.1 Write it downMark the total on your containers and in the margin of this page. Use the same steps in the calculator above.126 The weight of water One liter of water weighs 1 kg; one US gallon weighs about 3.8 kg (8.3 lb).11 Two weeks of minimum water for a family of 4 is 212 L, so it weighs about 212 kg (467 lb). That fits in eleven 20 L (5.3 gal) jerrycans, or one 55-gallon (208 L) drum plus a little more. Container choice, placement and weight are in Storing Water for Months & Years. Store in sizes you can liftA full 20 L jerrycan weighs 20 kg (44 lb).11 A full 55-gallon drum holds 208 L, so it weighs over 200 kg (450 lb): far too heavy to carry. Keep some water in small containers so a child or an older adult can pour a drink.

Drinking water is a survival need, not a comfort. Sphere lists 2.5–3 L a day for drinking and food under "survival needs".3 Sphere also says that amount depends on the climate and the individual's body.3 That is why heat matters so much: very hot weather can double needs.2 Warning signs: the WHO scale The World Health Organization (WHO) sorts dehydration into three levels: none, some and severe. It uses these signs to check people with diarrhea.8 WHO signs of dehydration (two or more signs place a person in a level) LevelSigns SevereVery sleepy (lethargic) or unconscious; sunken eyes; cannot drink or drinks poorly; pinched skin goes back very slowly (2 seconds or more) SomeRestless or irritable; sunken eyes; drinks eagerly, thirsty NoneNot enough signs for "some" or "severe" Signs from the WHO diarrheal disease fact sheet (2024).8 Severe dehydration is an emergencyIf anyone shows two or more severe signs, get medical care at once. Children are at high risk: WHO lists diarrheal disease as the third leading cause of death in children aged 1 to 59 months.8 Treatment and more warning signs This book prints the treatment, and the signs for babies, dogs and heat illness, in these chapters: Adults and children, by severity, with the oral rehydration solution (ORS) recipe: Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration Babies and young children: Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs Dogs: Dog First Aid Heat exhaustion and heat stroke: Hypothermia, Frostbite & Heat Stroke Why this page prints no "days without water" numberThis book prints only numbers it can check against an official or peer-reviewed source. A reliable figure for how long people survive with no water at all could not be confirmed for this edition, so none is given here.Plan so that nobody in your household ever goes a day without drinking. That is the whole point of the numbers above. A short-term minimum is fine to live on for months. Sphere says 7.5 L per person per day may be appropriate only for a short time in an acute drought, and that a minimum is never a maximum.4 Its standard for drinking, cooking and hygiene is 15 L.3 One gallon a day covers everything a person needs. The CDC calls 1 gallon a minimum and says to store more for pregnant women, sick people, pets and hot climates.1 Sphere's drinking figure alone is 2.5–3 L, leaving little of the gallon for anything else.3

s.h: ⏳ The 30-year math: why storage alone cannot last
s.x: A year of minimum water for one person is 365 gallons (1,382 L). That is 1 gallon a day for 365 days.1 Stored water is a bridge. It carries you from the first hour until a source that refills is working. Real outages have lasted far longer than 2 weeks. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, a survey of 3,299 households in Puerto Rico found they went an average of 68 days without water service (New England Journal of Medicine, 2018).12 That is almost 5 times the CDC 2-week goal.1 Same scale for all bars. Puerto Rico figure: average days without water service after Hurricane Maria, from a household survey.112 Day 33 gallons (11 L) per person. The CDC minimum stock.1 Day 1414 gallons (53 L) per person. The CDC goal if you can store it.1 Year 1365 gallons (1,382 L) per person. A family of 4 needs 1,460 gallons (5,527 L), about 27 drums of 55 gallons. Year 1 at Sphere levelA family of 4 at 15 L each uses 21,900 L (5,785 gal), about 105 drums.3 Year 3010,950 gallons (41,450 L) per person at the minimum. A family of 4 needs 43,800 gallons (about 165,800 L). The 30-year viewNo household can store 30 years of water. The plan is a renewable source plus treatment, with stored water as the buffer for droughts, freezes and breakdowns.Start with Rainwater Harvesting and Finding Water When the Taps Stop. Treat every new source using Disinfecting Water. Size your source with the same math. If your household needs 840 L (222 gal) every 2 weeks at the Sphere level, your source and tanks must deliver at least that, every 2 weeks, all year.3 Then add a margin for the hot season, when needs can double.2

s.h: 📓 Track it, plan it, never guess
s.x: A written water log tells you how many days you have left. Write it down so nobody has to remember it or guess. Never ration drinking waterFEMA and the Red Cross say: never ration water. Drink the amount you need today, and look for more for tomorrow.7 The log is there to warn you early, not to cut what people drink. The rule is one division: liters left ÷ (people × liters per person per day) = days left. Example: 56 gallons (212 L) for 4 people at 1 gallon each per day lasts 14 days.1 Daily water log (copy onto paper) DateLiters at startLiters usedLiters leftDays left Day 12121519712 Day 21971618111 Day 3181 The example assumes 4 people at the CDC minimum, about 15 L (4 gal) a day for the household, so 197 ÷ 15.2 = 12.96, rounded down to 12.1 Round "days left" down, never up. Do a 24-hour water audit nowWhile the taps still work, live for one day only on water you pour from marked containers. Write down every liter you use for drinking, cooking, washing and cleaning.Compare your total with 3.8 L and 15 L per person.13 Your real number is the one to store and to plan your source around. Mark your containersWrite the volume in large numbers on each one, plus the fill date. Give each person a marked bottleFill it each morning. You can see at a glance who is drinking too little. Drink first, then cook, then washSphere calls drinking water a survival need.3 Cooking and hygiene come next. Log every eveningMeasure what is left and update "days left". Act at 7 days leftStart collecting and treating water from another source before you run out. Get these before you need themA 1 L (1 quart) measuring jugA marker pen and tape for labelsOne marked bottle per personEnough containers for your 14-day number (see Storing Water) Save these official pages while the internet worksCDC: How to Create an Emergency Water SupplyReady.gov: WaterSphere: Water supply standard 1, access and water quantityPrint them or save them as PDF files next to this book.

Count everyone in your household, including babies, older relatives and pets Store at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day for 3 days Build up to 14 gallons (53 L) per person for 2 weeks If your summers are very hot, plan double for those months Add extra for anyone pregnant, breastfeeding, sick, and for children Measure each pet's daily drinking for 3 days and add it to the total Do a 24-hour water audit and write down your real daily use Mark every container with its volume and fill date Print the tables in this chapter and tape them near your water Start planning a refilling source: rainwater, a well or a safe local supply

What is the CDC minimum water per person per day?At least 1 gallon (3.8 L). Store 3 days at least, 2 weeks if you can. What happens to water needs in very hot weather?They can double. What is the Sphere minimum per person per day?15 L (about 4 gallons) for drinking, cooking and hygiene. How much of that is for drinking and food?2.5–3 L, depending on climate and the person's body. Who needs extra water stored?Pregnant and breastfeeding women, children, sick people and pets. Two weeks of minimum water for a family of 4?56 gallons (212 L), weighing about 212 kg (467 lb). A year of minimum water for a family of 4?1,460 gallons (5,527 L). Storage is a bridge; you need a source that refills. Should you ration drinking water?No. Drink what you need today and look for more for tomorrow (FEMA and Red Cross).

Use only food-grade containers. Never reuse bottles that held bleach, pesticides, milk or juice.12 Label every container "drinking water" with the date. Replace water you bottled yourself every 6 months.1 Store it cool, dark and away from fuel. The CDC says 10–21°C (50–70°F), out of sunlight, away from gasoline and pesticides.1 Your house already holds water. A home water heater holds 30–80 gallons (114–303 L). The toilet tank (never the bowl) is a last resort, disinfected first.34 Bathtub water is for flushing and washing, not drinking. A filled tub is also a drowning risk for small children.56 A full 208 L (55-gallon) drum weighs about 208 kg (458 lb). Put it where it will stay before you fill it.7 6 moreplace water you stored yourself1 458 lbweight of a full 208 L (55 gal) drum7 30–80 gal(114–303 L) of water inside a home water heater3 53 daysAsheville, NC, went without drinkable tap water after Hurricane Helene in 20248

s.h: 🚰 Why stored water comes first First 72 h
s.x: When the taps stop, stored water is what you drink while you find and treat more. The CDC calls unopened, commercially bottled water the safest and most reliable water in an emergency.1 Long outages happen. After Hurricane Helene, Asheville, North Carolina, did not lift its boil water notice for all customers until November 18, 2024.9 Local public radio called it a 53-day water crisis.8 The CDC minimum is 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day. Store at least 3 days, and a 2-week supply if you can.1 Store more in hot climates, and for pregnant women and people who are sick.1 Do the math onceAt 1 gallon per person per day, a family of 4 needs 56 gallons (212 L) for 2 weeks.1 That is about one 208 L (55-gallon) drum. For heat, babies, nursing mothers and dogs, see How Much Water You Really Need. 2-week supply at the CDC minimum of 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day PeopleWaterWeightExample containers 228 gal (106 L)106 kg (233 lb)Six 19 L (5 gal) jugs 456 gal (212 L)212 kg (466 lb)One 208 L drum + one jug 684 gal (318 L)318 kg (700 lb)Two 208 L drums Amounts use the CDC daily minimum.1 Weights use 1 kg per liter and about 8.3 lb per gallon.7 Add more for dogs, heat and illness.  Stored water is a bridge, not a forever supply. Over years you will refill from rain, wells and other sources. See Rainwater Harvesting, Wells & Hand Pumps and Finding Water When the Taps Stop.

Use containers made for food or water. The CDC says FDA-approved, food-grade water storage containers are best.1 Look for the number 2 inside the recycling triangle. Utah's emergency management agency calls food-grade high-density polyethylene (HDPE #2) containers your best choice.10 If you reuse bottles, Ready.gov says to choose 2-liter soft drink bottles (PETE #1), not milk or juice jugs.2 Which containers can hold drinking water? ContainerUse it?Why Sealed store-bought bottled waterYes, bestSafest, most reliable emergency water1 Food-grade HDPE #2 jugs and blue drumsYesThe recommended long-term choice10 2 L soft drink bottles (PETE #1)Yes, after cleaningReady.gov's choice for reused bottles; sanitize first2 Milk and fruit juice jugsNoProtein and sugar residue stay inside and bacteria grow2 Anything that held bleach, pesticides or other chemicalsNeverThe CDC says do not use them1 GlassAvoidNebraska Extension says use plastic, not glass, if water may freeze12 Food-grade HDPE #2 containers and clean 2-liter soft drink bottles (PETE #1) are accepted. Anything that held milk, juice or toxic chemicals is not.1021 A well-rinsed milk jug is fine for drinking water. Ready.gov says milk protein and fruit sugar cannot be fully removed from these jugs, so bacteria can grow.2 Utah's guidance adds that milk jugs break down quickly and turn brittle.10 Never reuse a chemical bottleThe CDC says containers that held toxic chemicals, such as bleach or pesticides, must not be used for drinking water.1 If you do not know what a container once held, do not use it. 55-gallon (208 L) drum facts Food-grade HDPE #2 only. Look for the 2 in the recycling triangle.10 Place it before you fill it. Full, it weighs about 208 kg (458 lb).7 Keep it out of the sun. Barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart within 5 years.22 Raise it off concrete or dirt on a pallet or boards.1322 Draw water with a pump or siphon, never a cup or a hand.23 Get this before you need it Food-grade HDPE #2 jugs or drums, in sizes your family can lift A drum pump or siphon hose, and a bung wrench for drum caps Plain, unscented liquid chlorine bleach A waterproof marker and labels Wood pallets or boards to keep containers off concrete

Sanitize every container before its first fill. This is the CDC method. It needs only soap, water and plain unscented bleach.1 Wash and rinseWash the container with soap. Rinse it completely with water.1 Mix the sanitizerStir 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of unscented liquid chlorine bleach (5–9% sodium hypochlorite) into 1 quart (about 1 liter) of water.1 Coat every surfacePour it into the container, cap it and shake well so the solution touches all inside surfaces.1 Wait, then emptyWait at least 30 seconds, then pour the solution out. Let the container air-dry, or rinse it with clean, safe water.1 Fill with safe waterFill it with clean, safe water and screw the cap on tightly.1 Label itWrite "drinking water" and the date on the container.1 Know where your fill water comes from. Ready.gov says tap water from a utility that treats it with chlorine needs nothing added. Water from a well or other untreated source needs bleach.2 Utah State University Extension says water from wells, rivers or rainwater must be treated before you store it.13 To treat clear water with bleach, the EPA dose is 8 drops of 6% bleach, or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach, per gallon (3.8 L).14 Double the dose if the water is cloudy, colored or very cold.14 Stir, then wait 30 minutes before anyone drinks it. The water should smell slightly of chlorine. If it does not, EPA says to repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes.14 For a full 208 L (55-gallon) drum of clear, untreated water, scale up EPA's 8-gallon dose of 2/3 teaspoon. That is about 4½ teaspoons (23 mL) of 6% bleach, or about 3½ teaspoons (17 mL) of 8.25% bleach.14 Double it for cloudy water.14  Plain, unscented bleach onlyThe EPA says not to use scented or color-safe bleach, or bleach with added cleaners.14 Its method uses bleach stored at room temperature for less than a year.14 For more on fresh bleach, tablets and pool shock, see Disinfecting Water. Bleach cannot fix chemical pollutionThe CDC warns that water polluted with harmful chemicals or toxins cannot be made safe by boiling, disinfecting or filtering.15 Never store water from a source that may hold fuel or chemicals. See Chemical Contamination.

Replace water you bottled yourself every 6 months. The CDC and Ready.gov both give this interval.111 For store-bought water, go by the date on the bottle. That is the CDC's household rule.1 Its planning guide for hospitals adds that commercial "sell by" dates mainly help stores rotate stock. They do not mean the water has gone bad.16 Water you disinfect and bottle yourself does not keep forever. The same CDC guide says to check it from time to time for leftover (residual) chlorine and to treat it again if needed.16 Day 0Sanitize, fill and treat if needed. Label "drinking water" with the date.1 Month 6Replace the water.1 Use the old water for flushing, washing or the garden. Check each empty container for cracks and leaks. Month 12Rotate again. Buy a fresh bottle of bleach at the same time: EPA's method uses bleach less than a year old.14 Use the oldest store-bought water first. Every rotationWrite the next due date on a calendar on paper, not only on your phone. A label that answers every questionWrite four lines on each container: DRINKING WATER, the fill date, the source (city tap, or well treated with how many drops of bleach), and the replace-by date. The CDC asks for "drinking water" and the date at minimum.1 Label each container with its date, keep it cool and dark, and replace self-filled water every 6 months.111 Start rationing your stored water on day one. FEMA, the Red Cross and county emergency managers say never ration drinking water unless authorities order it.2017 Drink the amount you need today and try to find more for tomorrow.20

s.h: 🏠 Hidden water already in your house First 72 h
s.x: Protect the water in your pipes first. If the public supply may be contaminated, find your home's incoming water valve and close it.17 That keeps dirty water out of your pipes and water heater. The Red Cross lists the hot-water tank, the pipes and ice cubes as safe water inside the home.18 The CDC also lists the water heater tank, and melted ice cubes made with water that was not contaminated.19 Hidden household water: the water heater, the pipes, ice and, as a last resort, the toilet tank. Bathtub water is for washing and flushing only.42035 The water heater: 30–80 gallons A home water heater can hold 30–80 gallons (114–303 L).3 The CDC means the tank that supplies your taps, not a home heating system.19 Turn off the power or gasSwitch off the electricity or gas that heats the tank.420 Let it coolWait for the tank to cool before you open anything.4 Close the cold-water inletTurn off the water intake valve at the tank.20 Let air inTurn on a hot-water faucet in the house so the tank can drain.20 Drain into a clean containerPut a clean container under the drain valve at the bottom of the tank, then open the valve.4 Refill before you restartRefill the tank before you turn the power or gas back on.20 If the gas was shut off, a professional needs to turn it back on.20 Power off, then waitFEMA's order is power off, let the tank cool, then open the drain.4 Keep children away from the drain valve while the water is still hot. Find your valves todayFind your main water valve and the water heater drain valve now, in daylight. Tag the main valve so anyone can find it in the dark. If you live in an earthquake zone, see Earthquakes for strapping the water heater. Water in the pipes Close the main valveStop outside water from flowing in.17 Open the highest tapTurn on the faucet on the highest floor to let air into the pipes. A small amount of water will trickle out.20 Drain the lowest tapCollect the water from the lowest faucet in the house.20 The toilet: tank maybe, bowl never Never use water from the toilet bowl. FEMA and the Red Cross both rule it out.418 The tank behind the toilet is different. FEMA's current guidance lists it only if the water is clear and has no chemical cleaners, such as colored tablets, and says to disinfect it before use.4 The older FEMA and Red Cross booklet says not to use flush tank water at all.1820 Use tank water for flushing and washing fir

Fill the bathtub before a storm, but do not drink it. The National Weather Service says to fill bathtubs and large containers in case tap water stops. Use bathtub water for cleaning and flushing only.5 Clean the tub and test that the plug holds before the storm. Scoop the water out with a bucket when you need it. For flushing without running water, see Toilets Without Water. A full bathtub is a drinking water reserve. The National Weather Service says bathtub water is for cleaning and flushing only: do not drink it.5 Keep drinking water in sanitized, food-grade containers.1 A filled tub or bucket can drown a toddlerFrom 2006 to 2010, CPSC counted 434 drowning deaths of children under 5 at home. 82% were under age 2, and 81% of the incidents involved bathtubs or bath products.6Drowning can happen quickly and in very shallow water. Never leave a tub, bucket or any container of water unattended. Keep bathroom doors closed and use toilet-lid locks.21 See Keeping Kids Safe.

s.h: 📍 Where to keep it: heat, light, fumes and weight
s.x: Pick a cool, dark spot away from fuel and chemicals. The CDC says 10–21°C (50–70°F), out of direct sunlight, and away from toxic substances such as gasoline or pesticides.1 Fumes can pass through plastic. Nebraska Extension warns that vapors from gasoline, kerosene and pesticides can penetrate plastic containers.12 Do not keep water next to the fuel cans in the garage. Light ruins containers and feeds algae. Be Ready Utah says sunlight, and even artificial light, makes containers brittle or leaky. Blue 208 L (55-gallon) barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart within 5 years.22 Sunlight also lets algae grow in stored water.22 Raise containers off bare concrete or dirt. Utah State University Extension says plastic absorbs odors there, which changes the taste.13 Be Ready Utah adds that air flow underneath limits moisture and mold.22 Good spots An inside closet or under a bed, away from outside walls A cool, dark ground floor, on a pallet122 Several places in the house, so one leak or break does not take it all Bad spots Next to gasoline, kerosene or pesticides12 In direct sun, such as a porch or window122 On bare concrete or dirt13 On a shelf that is not built for the weight12 Weight: choose the spot before you fill Water weighs 1 kg per liter, or about 8.3 lb per gallon.7 So a full 208 L (55-gallon) drum weighs about 208 kg (458 lb). Once it is full, you will not move it. Nebraska Extension says shelves must be sturdy and stable, because water weighs over 8 pounds per gallon.12 Put drums at ground level on a pallet, where a pump or siphon can reach them. Do not dip cups or hands into stored water. CDC guidance on safe storage says hands, cups and dippers carry germs into open containers.23 Pump or siphon water from a drum into a smaller container that has a lid and a tap.23 Full-container weights worked out from USGS figures (1 kg per liter; about 8.3 lb per gallon). Bar length is to scale.7 Carry less, store closerA full 19 L (5-gallon) jug weighs about 19 kg (42 lb).7 If someone in your home cannot lift that, keep small jugs with a tap where they sleep, and refill them from the big containers. See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

Leave 5–8 cm (2–3 inches) of air at the top of any container that might freeze. Water expands as it freezes and can burst a full container.12 Use freezer-safe plastic, not glass, for water that may freeze.12 If your storage spot freezes in winter, leave the headspace or move the water into the heated part of the house. Pipes freeze too. See Preparing Your Home for a Long Outage and Winter Storms & Extreme Cold. Hot climates: store more, store lowerIn the tropics, 10–21°C (50–70°F) may be impossible to reach. The CDC says to store more water in hot climates.1 Use the coolest, darkest room you have, away from sunny walls and tin roofs.

Every stored container is temporary. Sun-exposed barrels can start to fall apart within 5 years.22 Plan to replace containers, not only the water in them. For daily drinking water over years, use a safe-storage container. CDC guidance describes one with a small opening and a lid, plus a tap or narrow spout, so no hands or cups go inside.23 Open buckets and pots let hands, cups and dippers carry fecal germs into treated water.23 Build the refill loopIn year 1, stored water carries you until rain catchment, a well or a treated stream supply is working. Then stored water becomes your buffer for dry spells and broken pumps. See Water Filters & SODIS, Build a Biosand Filter and Pottery & Making Containers. Keep sealed water for the babyFor powdered formula, the CDC says use bottled water until officials say tap water is safe. With no bottled water, boil water for 1 minute (3 minutes above 2,000 m or 6,500 ft) and let it cool.15For babies under 2 months, premature babies or babies with weak immune systems, do not let the boiled water cool below 70°C (158°F) before you mix in the powder. That heat kills Cronobacter germs.15 Then cool the bottle to body temperature, and test a few drops on your wrist before feeding.15 See Feeding Babies. Count the dogsReady.gov's pet kit includes a water bowl and several days' supply of water.24 Store dog water in the same food-grade containers and add it to your totals. See Dogs in a Long Emergency. Pregnancy and periodsThe CDC says to store extra water for pregnant women.1 Keep a small covered container in the bathroom for washing during periods. See Periods Without Stores. Download these while the internet works CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply FEMA: Emergency water sources in your home National Weather Service: Hurricane safety checklist (PDF)

Buy food-grade HDPE #2 containers in sizes your family can lift Throw out any milk, juice or chemical bottles you planned to use for water Sanitize containers: 1 teaspoon (5 mL) unscented bleach per quart (1 L) of water Fill, cap and label each container "drinking water" with today's date Store them cool, dark, off bare concrete and away from fuel and pesticides Put a 6-month rotation date on a paper calendar Find and tag your main water valve and water heater drain valve Put lids on every bucket and keep bathroom doors closed around toddlers Set aside a sealed case of commercial bottled water for baby formula Print this chapter and the CDC water storage page

How often do you replace water you bottled yourself?Every 6 months. For store-bought water, follow the date on the bottle. Which plastic is best for storing water?Food-grade HDPE #2. Clean 2-liter soft drink bottles (PETE #1) also work. Can you reuse a milk jug?No. Residue stays inside, bacteria grow, and the plastic turns brittle. How much water is in a home water heater?30–80 gallons (114–303 L). Power off and let it cool before draining. Toilet bowl or toilet tank?Never the bowl. The tank only if clear and chemical-free, as a last resort, and disinfected first. Can you drink bathtub water?No. Use it for flushing and washing. What does a full 55-gallon drum weigh?About 208 kg (458 lb). Place it before you fill it. How much headspace if water might freeze?5–8 cm (2–3 inches) of air at the top.

t: Finding Water When the Taps Stop

s.x: Use your stored, bottled water first. FEMA calls bottled water the safest and most reliable option after a disaster.2 Look inside before you look outside. The water heater tank, ice made from clean water and the toilet tank (never the bowl) are usable.2 Treat every outdoor source. CDC lists rain, streams, rivers, ponds, lakes and springs as sources you must make safe before drinking.1 Never drink floodwater, seawater or urine. Floodwater can carry sewage and chemicals, and your body cannot clear the salt in seawater.58 Boiling does not remove fuel or chemicals. If a source may hold fuel or toxic chemicals, do not use it.1 Pool and spa water is for washing and cleaning only. CDC says not to drink it.1 4 typesof outdoor source on CDC's list: rain, moving water, ponds and lakes, springs. All need treatment.1 3hidden indoor sources FEMA names: water heater, ice, toilet tank2 3.5%of seawater's weight is dissolved salt9 0.8–5 ppmchlorine range in Canadian pool rules: set for swimmers, not for drinking10

s.h: 🧭 Where to get water, in the right order
s.x: When the taps stop, work from the safest source outward. Stored water first, then hidden water inside the building, then outdoor water that you treat. FEMA's advice is plain: use bottled water first when you have it, because it is the safest and most reliable option.2 Building that store is covered in Storing Water for Months & Years, and how much you need is in How Much Water You Really Need. No official body publishes one safety ranking of rain, springs, wells, streams and ponds. CDC's rule is simpler: every outdoor source needs treatment before anyone drinks it.1 The table below puts every common source in one place. It runs from your first choice to the water you must never drink. Water sources, from first choice to never (FEMA, CDC, EPA) SourceWhat official guidance saysBefore you drink Stored bottled waterSafest and most reliable option2Use first Water heater tankUsable if it is part of the drinking water system, not the heating system2Use Melted iceUsable if made with water that was not contaminated2Use Toilet tank (not bowl)Only if clear and free of toilet cleaners2Disinfect RainOn CDC's list of outdoor sources1Treat Natural springsOn CDC's list of outdoor sources1Treat Private wellsCan be contaminated during floods1Treat; test and disinfect after a flood7 Streams, rivers, ponds, lakesMay hold livestock waste, sewage and chemicals1Treat; reject if chemicals are possible Pools and spasHygiene and cleaning only1Do not drink Floodwater, seawater, urine, radiators, waterbeds, toilet bowlsUnsafe to drink358Never drink The outdoor rows (rain to ponds) are not ranked against each other by any official source. Treat all of them the same way. Ask the questions in order. CDC lists rain, moving water, ponds, lakes and springs as treatable sources, warns against water with fuel or toxic chemicals, and limits pool water to hygiene.1

s.h: 🏠 Hidden water inside your home or building
s.x: Before you walk anywhere, check the building you are in. FEMA names three indoor sources you can use when the taps stop.2 Water heater tank. Use it only if it is part of your drinking water system, not your home heating system.2 Melted ice. Safe if the ice was made with water that was not contaminated.2 Toilet tank (the box behind the seat). Only if the water is clear and no toilet cleaner has been added, and disinfect it first.2 An older FEMA and Red Cross booklet ruled out toilet tanks completely.3 FEMA's current guidance allows clear, cleaner-free tank water once it is disinfected.2 When in doubt, treat it. How to drain a water heater safely is covered step by step in Storing Water. Do it once now, while you can still call a plumber if something goes wrong. FEMA lists the water heater, clean ice and a clear toilet tank as usable, and says not to use radiator, boiler, waterbed or pool water for drinking.23 Getting water out of a toilet tank Lift the tank lid and lookCheck for colored water, a cleaner tablet or a clip-on cleaner. If any toilet cleaner is in there, do not drink it.2 Use it only if it is clearFEMA allows tank water only when it is clear.2 Scoop it, do not flush itLadle it into a clean container. Flushing sends it to the bowl, and bowl water is never drinking water.3 Disinfect itBoil or treat it before anyone drinks it.2 See Disinfecting Water. Do use (indoors) Water heater tank on the drinking water line Ice made from clean water Clear toilet tank water, after disinfecting Pool or spa water for washing and cleaning Don't drink Toilet bowl water Radiator or hot water boiler water Waterbed water Pool or spa water Heating systems and waterbeds are not drinking waterFEMA's emergency food and water guide says not to use water from radiators, waterbeds, toilet bowls, or swimming pools and spas for drinking.3 FEMA's older shelter guide gives the reason for waterbeds: fungicides added to the water, or chemicals in the vinyl, can make it unsafe.4 Remove toilet cleaner tablets nowAn in-tank cleaner tablet turns a usable tank into one you cannot drink from.2 Take tablets out today and flush a few times, so every tank in the house stays a backup supply.

s.h: 🌧️ Outdoor sources: rain, springs, wells, streams and ponds
s.x: CDC lists four kinds of outdoor water you can make safe: rainwater; streams, rivers and other moving water; ponds and lakes; and natural springs.1 All four must be treated to kill germs before anyone drinks them.1 No outdoor source gets a free pass, however clean it looks. Rain Rain is on CDC's list of outdoor sources, and it still needs treatment.1 Roof catchment, gutters, first-flush diverters and tank math are in Rainwater Harvesting. Springs Natural springs are on the same list, with the same rule: treat the water before drinking.1 Wells Well water can be contaminated during floods.1 EPA says private wells need to be tested and disinfected after floodwaters recede.7 Well types, hand pumps and shock chlorination are in Wells & Hand Pumps Without Electricity. Streams, rivers, ponds and lakes CDC warns that rivers, streams and lakes may be contaminated with livestock waste, human sewage, chemicals and other contaminants.1 Treatment kills germs, but boiling does not remove chemical pollutants.1 That makes choosing the source your first filter. See Chemical Contamination for what filters can and cannot remove. Look upstream firstNote farms and animal pens, sewage pipes and septic systems, and factories, fuel stores or dumps. These match the livestock waste, sewage and chemicals CDC warns about.1 Reject chemical waterIf the water may hold fuel or toxic chemicals, walk away. Boiling will not remove them.1 Collect in a clean containerUse a container that has only held food or water. Keep the cap and the rim clean. Clear cloudy waterSettle and strain cloudy water before you treat it. Methods are in Water Filters & SODIS. Treat every literBoil or disinfect it to kill germs.1 Doses and times are in Disinfecting Water. Store and label itPour it into a clean, covered container. Write "TREATED" and the date on it so nobody mixes it up with raw water. Clear, fast-running stream water is clean enough to drink as it is. CDC lists streams and rivers among sources that must be treated, and warns they may carry livestock waste, human sewage and chemicals.1 How fast the water moves does not change that rule. Women and girls: fetch water togetherGo to water in pairs or groups, in daylight, with an agreed route and return time. Never send a girl alone to a distant source. Safe paths, lighting and latrine design are in Personal Safety for Women & Girls. Older and disabled peopl

s.h: 🗺️ Map every water source near you, now
s.x: The best time to find water is before you need it. A paper map of nearby sources lets anyone in the family find water when you are sick, away or asleep. Draw it on paper, so it works without a charged phone. See Maps & Compass for reading and marking maps. Get a paper mapA local street or topographic map, or a hand-drawn sketch. Mark your home in the center. Walk a circle around homeMark every stream, river, pond, lake and spring. Add wells, rain barrels, large clean roofs and public taps. Note what is upstreamMark farms, sewage pipes and fuel or chemical sites near each source.1 Note who owns itAsk the owner now for permission to draw water in an emergency. Taking without permission can be a crime. See Scavenging: the Law & Ethics. Note the route and the carryWrite the distance and how long the walk took with a full container. Pick the flattest route. Recheck after every floodFloods can contaminate wells, and floodwater can reach streams and lakes.15 Mark flooded sources as "test before use". Practice the carry this weekFill a 19 L (5 gal) container, carry it 100 m (110 yd) and time yourself. Then try it with a cart. You will learn which containers, handles and routes work for your family before it matters. Get these before you need them Food-grade water containers with handles and tight caps, in sizes each person can carry A wagon, garden cart or wheelbarrow A funnel and clean cotton cloths for straining A bucket with 10 m (33 ft) of rope, for reaching water from banks and open wells A waterproof paper map, pencils and labels Treatment supplies from Disinfecting Water What this chapter leaves out, and whyThis edition gives no methods or yield figures for finding water by plant or animal signs, dew collection, solar stills or plant bags. We could not verify published figures for this printing, and this book does not print unverified numbers.Plan your supply around stored water, rain and treated surface water. Official guidance covers all three.12

s.h: 🏊 Pools, spas and other urban water
s.x: CDC says pool and spa water can be used for personal hygiene and cleaning, but not for drinking.1 FEMA's emergency guide also lists pools and spas among the sources not to drink from.3 Pool chemistry is set for swimmers. Canadian pool rules keep free chlorine between 0.8 and 5.0 parts per million (ppm), a level judged not harmful to bathers who swallow some water.10 That is a swimming standard, not a drinking-water standard. Pool water is already chlorinated, so it is safe to drink. CDC limits pool and spa water to hygiene and cleaning.1 Pool chlorine levels are set for swimmers who swallow a little, not for daily drinking.10 Good uses for pool water Washing hands and bodies Cleaning floors, tools and surfaces Laundry (see Laundry Without Machines) Every bucket of pool water you use for cleaning is a bucket of treated drinking water you save. Tanks in apartment and office buildings If your building has water tanks, find out now what each tank is for. Ask the building manager whether it is on the drinking water line, the heating system or the fire system. Water from heating systems, such as radiators and hot water boilers, is not drinking water.3 A water heater tank on the drinking water line is.2 Neighbors' pools and tanksAsk before you take. Agree now, in writing if you can, who may use a pool or tank in an emergency and for what. Shared rules prevent fights later. See Community & Mutual Aid.

s.h: 🌊 Floodwater: water everywhere, none to drink
s.x: Never drink floodwater. CDC says it can contain sewage, and eating or drinking anything contaminated by it can cause diarrheal disease such as E. coli or Salmonella infection.5 Floods also move containers of chemicals away from where they were stored.5 So floodwater can hold germs and chemicals at once, and boiling does not remove chemical pollutants.1 Touching floodwater is a smaller risk than swallowing it. CDC says skin contact alone does not pose a serious health risk; eating or drinking anything contaminated with floodwater is what causes disease.6 Floods poison wells and streams tooWell water can be contaminated during floods.1 EPA says private wells must be tested and disinfected after floodwaters recede.7 CDC also warns against bathing in rivers, streams or lakes contaminated by floodwater.5 If you must work in or near floodwater Cover upWear rubber boots, rubber gloves and goggles.5 Keep it out of your mouthDo not eat, drink or smoke with floodwater on your hands. Swallowing it is the main risk.6 Do not bathe in itNot in floodwater, and not in rivers, streams or lakes it has reached.5 Wash clothes hotWash clothes that touched floodwater or sewage in hot water and detergent before wearing them again.5 Check for advisoriesAsk your water utility or health department whether a boil water advisory is in force.7 Babies and childrenCDC says toys that were in floodwater must be disinfected before children play with them.5 Keep children out of floodwater and away from cleanup work.Mix infant formula only with your best water: stored bottled water first.2 See Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out. DogsFloodwater can carry sewage and chemicals.5 Keep dogs out of it where you can, and give them the same treated water you drink. If a dog wades through floodwater, rinse its paws and coat with clean water before it licks itself. See Dog Health. For the full picture of flood hazards, see Floods. For the diseases floodwater spreads, see Waterborne Diseases.

Some water makes you worse off than drinking nothing. Learn these by heart and teach them to every child old enough to understand. Seawater Seawater is toxic to humans. USGS explains that your body cannot get rid of the salt: the kidneys cannot get enough fresh water to dilute it, and the body fails.8 About 3.5% of seawater's weight is dissolved salt.9 For every cup of seawater you drink, you would need at least the same amount of fresh water for your kidneys to flush that salt out.9 Seawater is about 3.5% salt, and each cup needs at least a cup of fresh water to flush the salt out, so it never adds usable water.89 Urine Do not drink urine. It carries salts and waste products your body has just removed. Drinking it hands that load back to your kidneys, which need more water to clear it again.11 Urine is also not sterile. It can contain bacteria, even in healthy people.11 Drinking your own urine stretches your water supply in an emergency. Urine returns salt and waste to a body that is already short of water, so the kidneys need extra water to remove it again.11 Water with fuel or chemicals in it CDC says do not use water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals. Boiling will not remove chemical pollutants.1 Find another source. If you boil water long enough, any water becomes safe. Boiling does not remove chemical pollutants such as fuel.1 Choose a different source when chemicals are possible. Heating systems, waterbeds and toilet bowls FEMA lists radiators, waterbeds, toilet bowls, and pools and spas as water not to use for drinking.3 Waterbed water can hold fungicides or chemicals from the vinyl.4 The 30-year viewStored water is a bridge, not a supply. Any supply that lasts decades has to come from rain, springs, wells or surface water, and CDC says all of those need treatment.1Use year 1 to build lasting systems: rain catchment, a hand-pumped well if you can, and a biosand filter. Keep your source map up to date every year.
