Which water do you use first?Stored bottled water. FEMA calls it the safest and most reliable option. Name 3 hidden water sources at home.Water heater tank, ice made from clean water, and the toilet tank (not the bowl). Which outdoor sources need treatment?All of them: rain, streams, rivers, ponds, lakes and springs. Can you drink pool or spa water?No. Use it for hygiene and cleaning only. Why can't you drink seawater?Your body cannot clear the salt. Each cup needs at least a cup of fresh water to flush it out. Does boiling fix water with fuel in it?No. Boiling does not remove chemicals. Find another source. What must you do to a private well after a flood?Test it and disinfect it before you use it.

t: Disinfecting Water: Boiling, Bleach, Iodine & Tablets

s.x: Boil clear water at a rolling boil for 1 minute. Above 2,000 m (6,500 ft), boil for 3 minutes. Boiling kills bacteria, viruses and parasites.1 Cannot boil? Use regular, unscented bleach. 8 drops of 6% or 6 drops of 8.25% per 3.8 liters (1 gallon). Double it for cloudy or very cold water, then wait 30 minutes.2 Bleach and iodine do not kill Cryptosporidium. Boiling does. Chlorine dioxide does too, but it needs hours.34 Boiling and disinfection do not make water with fuel or toxic chemicals safe. If you suspect them, find another source.1 No iodine for pregnant women or people with thyroid problems. CDC does not recommend it for them.3 Bleach weakens with age. EPA's method uses bleach stored less than a year. For the long haul, learn the pool shock method.2 1 minat a rolling boil kills germs in clear water1 8 dropsof 6% bleach per gallon (3.8 L) of clear water2 30 minwait after adding bleach before you drink2 Hourschlorine dioxide needs to kill Cryptosporidium4

Safe bottled water comes first. If you have none, EPA ranks boiling ahead of bleach. Bleach is the backup when you cannot boil.2 Boiling is the best way to kill germs, including viruses, bacteria and parasites.1 CDC notes that, except for boiling, few water treatment methods are 100% effective against all germs.3 Use the four steps below every time you treat water. Step 1 matters most, because no disinfectant fixes chemical pollution. Quick picks You have fuel: boil. It is the most reliable method.1 No fuel, clear water: unscented bleach, then wait 30 minutes.2 No fuel, unknown source or a sick person at home: chlorine dioxide tablets for the full label time, because they also kill Cryptosporidium.4 Cloudy water: clear it first, and double the bleach dose.2 Possible fuel or chemicals: do not treat it. Find another source.1 Check for chemicals, clear the water, kill the germs, then store it covered. Boiling kills all the main germ types. Chlorine dioxide kills most, including Cryptosporidium, but slowly. Bleach does not kill Cryptosporidium.134 Disinfection methods at a glance (CDC, EPA) MethodHowKills Crypto?Watch out BoilingRolling boil 1 min (3 min above 2,000 m)YesNeeds fuel; leaves chemicals in Bleach8 drops of 6% per gallon, wait 30 minNoUnscented only; replace yearly IodineFollow the labelNoNot in pregnancy or thyroid disease Chlorine dioxideFollow the label; hours for CryptoYes, slowlyKeep sealed from air and light Pool shockMake stock, dilute 1 to 100NoStrong chemical; label the stock Sources for the table: boiling1, bleach2, iodine and chlorine against Cryptosporidium3, chlorine dioxide14 and pool shock7. This chapter is about killing germs. To remove dirt and parasites, see Water Filters & SODIS. To clean water for years, see Build a Biosand Filter.

s.h: 🔥 Boiling: the most reliable method First 72 h
s.x: A rolling boil for 1 minute makes clear water safe from germs. Above 6,500 ft (about 2,000 m), boil it for 3 minutes.1 The full minute is already a safety margin. CDC asks for a whole minute to allow for people misjudging when water is really boiling.5 Clear cloudy water firstLet it settle and draw off the clear water, or pour it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter.1 Bring it to a rolling boilA rolling boil means big bubbles that keep breaking the surface even when you stir. Hold the boil for 1 minuteHold it for 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft). Use the timer below.1 Cool it with the lid onDo not add ice unless the ice was made from safe water. Store it clean and coveredPour it into clean, sanitized containers with tight covers.1 See Storing Water.  Know your altitude before an emergency. Below 6,500 ft (about 2,000 m), boil for 1 minute; above it, boil for 3 minutes.1 You must boil water for 10 or 20 minutes to make it safe. CDC says 1 minute at a rolling boil, or 3 minutes above 6,500 ft.1 Boiling kills germs quickly, and the full minute already adds a safety margin.5 Extra minutes only burn fuel you will need later. Flat taste? Pour the cooled water back and forth between two clean containers a few times.1 Boiling does not remove chemicalsWater polluted with fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfection.1Use a different source. See Chemical Contamination. Save fuel for waterBoiling depends on fuel. Keep a pot with a lid and a fuel reserve that is only for water. See Cooking Without Power for stoves that run on wood and charcoal.

s.h: 🧴 Bleach: the right bottle, the right drops
s.x: Use regular, unscented chlorine bleach whose label says it is for disinfection and sanitizing.2 Do not use scented, color-safe or "with cleaner" bleach. EPA rules those out for drinking water.2 Read the strength on the label. EPA's table is for bleach with 6% or 8.25% sodium hypochlorite.2 Use fresh bleach. EPA's method calls for bleach that has been stored at room temperature for less than one year.2 That limit assumes room temperature, so keep bottles in a cool, dark place and date each one. Unscented household bleach per volume of clear water (EPA) Water6% bleach8.25% bleach 1 quart or 1 liter2 drops2 drops 1 gallon (3.8 L)8 drops6 drops 2 gallons (7.6 L)16 drops12 drops (⅛ tsp) Cloudy, colored or very coldDouble itDouble it EPA gives these doses for clear water and says to double them for cloudy, colored or very cold water.2 For bigger containers, multiply the 1-gallon dose, or use the calculator. Bleach of another strengthEPA's table covers 6% and 8.25% bleach only.2 If your label shows another percentage, do the arithmetic from EPA's 6% dose: drops per gallon = 48 ÷ your %, rounded up.For example, 5.25% bleach needs 10 drops per gallon and 4% bleach needs 12. The same formula gives EPA's 6 drops for 8.25%. Double it for cloudy, colored or very cold water.2  Clear the waterIf it is cloudy, murky or colored, let it settle or pour it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter.2 Count the dropsUse a clean dropper and the table above. Keep that dropper only for bleach. Stir and wait 30 minutesDo not drink it, cook with it or give it to pets during the wait.2 Smell itIt should smell slightly of chlorine. If not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes.2 Fix a strong tasteLet it stand open to the air for a few hours, or pour it from one clean container to another several times.2 Minute 0Add the drops and stir. Minute 30Smell test. s.h: 🦠 Cryptosporidium: the germ bleach cannot kill
s.x: Bleach and iodine kill most harmful bacteria and viruses. They are less effective against the tougher parasites Cryptosporidium and Giardia.1 Against Cryptosporidium ("Crypto"), iodine and chlorine are not effective. That is CDC's rating in its water treatment guide.3 Boiling kills it. So does chlorine dioxide, if you follow the maker's instructions.1 Chlorine dioxide is more potent than the same dose of chlorine and kills most waterborne germs, including Cryptosporidium.4 Boiling kills all germ types. Bleach and iodine kill most bacteria and viruses, are less effective on Giardia, and do not kill Cryptosporidium. Chlorine dioxide kills most germs, including Crypto, but Crypto takes hours.134 Layer your methods A filter with pores of 1 micron or smaller, plus chlorine dioxide, has a "very high" rating against Cryptosporidium in CDC's guide.3 Filter first, then disinfect. CDC says to add a disinfectant after filtering to kill viruses and any remaining bacteria.13 Filter types and pore sizes are in Water Filters & SODIS. Only boiling comes close to 100%CDC states that, except for boiling, few water treatment methods are 100% effective at removing all germs.3 When someone in your home is very young, very old or sick, boil when you can. Symptoms of Crypto, Giardia and other water germs are in Waterborne Diseases.

Iodine: short-term only Iodine does not reliably kill Cryptosporidium, and it works less well in cloudy water.4 Follow the manufacturer's instructions for the dose and the waiting time.3 Who should not use iodineCDC does not recommend iodine-treated water for:Pregnant womenPeople with thyroid problemsPeople with a known iodine hypersensitivityAnyone using it continuously for more than a few weeks at a time3 Pregnant? Skip iodineCDC does not recommend iodine-treated water during pregnancy.3 Boil water instead, or use bleach or chlorine dioxide tablets.Write "NOT FOR PREGNANCY" on the iodine bottle so no one forgets. Thyroid disease or iodine allergyCDC does not recommend iodine-treated water for people with thyroid problems or a known iodine hypersensitivity.3 Ask about thyroid conditions before you hand out iodine water. Chlorine dioxide: slow but thorough Chlorine dioxide kills most waterborne germs, including Cryptosporidium.4 The catch is time. Tablets and drops need several hours of contact time. They also leave no lasting disinfectant in the water.4 Why the label wait mattersIn a 2014 lab study of chlorine dioxide tablets, killing Cryptosporidium took hours, not minutes, and weaker doses took longer.6Lab results are not a field promise. Always use the wait time on your product label. Protect the tablets. Chlorine dioxide is volatile and breaks down in sunlight. Do not expose tablets to air, and use any mixed solution quickly.4 Read the labelFind the water volume per tablet and the wait time. Some labels give a longer time for Cryptosporidium. Clear the water firstSettle it, then pour it through a clean cloth.1 Add the tabletUse the exact volume on the label. Open one blister at a time. Wait the full timeIf you do not know the source, use the longest time on the label. Crypto needs hours.4 Keep it coveredTreated water has no lasting protection, so store it clean and closed.4

s.h: 🏊 Pool shock: EPA's long-term chlorine source Long haul
s.x: Granular calcium hypochlorite is dry chlorine. EPA's emergency disinfection guidance, as archived in 2013, uses it in two steps: make a strong stock solution, then dilute it into the water you drink.7 The method is written for high-test granular calcium hypochlorite with about 70% available chlorine.7 If the label lists a different active ingredient, this method does not apply. EPA's two-step method: 1 heaping teaspoon in 2 gallons makes a stock of about 500 mg/L; add 1 part stock to 100 parts water.7 Work outside, away from kids and dogsUse a measuring spoon and bucket that you keep only for chlorine. Make the stockDissolve 1 heaping teaspoon (about ¼ oz, 7 g) in 2 gallons (7.6 L) of water. This gives about 500 mg/L of chlorine.7 Label the stockWrite "CHLORINE STOCK: DO NOT DRINK" and the date on the container. Dilute 1 part to 100Add 1 part stock to 100 parts clear water. That is roughly 1 pint (16 oz) of stock per 12.5 gallons (47 L).7 Air out a strong smellIf the chlorine smell is too strong, pour the water back and forth between clean containers.7 Stock to add at 1 part per 100 (arithmetic from EPA's ratio) Water to treatStock to add 1 liter (about 1 quart)10 mL (about 2 tsp) 1 gallon (3.8 L)38 mL (1.3 fl oz) 20 liters (5.3 gallons)200 mL (6.8 fl oz) 12.5 gallons (47 L)1 pint (about 470 mL) The stock is not drinking waterThe stock is about 500 mg/L of chlorine, 100 times stronger than the water you drink after dilution.7 Keep it labeled, capped and locked away.Never mix pool chemicals with other cleaners, and keep the granules dry and sealed. If someone swallows the stock, see Poisoning. Pool shock still misses CryptoCalcium hypochlorite is chlorine. CDC rates chlorine as not effective against Cryptosporidium.3 Boil, or use chlorine dioxide, when Crypto is a concern.

Babies and childrenLock up bleach, tablets and pool shock where children cannot reach them.Keep children away from pots of boiling water. Let water cool on a back burner with the lid on.For mixing formula and feeding bottles, follow Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.Teach older children the 30-minute rule: no drinking from a bucket that is still "waiting". Dogs and petsGive your dog the same treated water your family drinks, in a bowl you wash daily.Never leave stock solution or a dosing bucket where a dog can drink from it. Dog water diseases are covered in Dog Health. Older and disabled peopleA full pot of boiling water is heavy. Let it cool, then ladle it out instead of lifting it.Counting drops is hard with poor eyesight. Pre-mark a measuring spoon, or have one person do all dosing.Check thyroid conditions before using iodine.3

Plan for each method running outBleach: EPA's method uses bleach under a year old.2 Stored bleach is a first-year tool, not a 30-year one.Iodine: CDC does not recommend continuous use for more than a few weeks at a time.3Chlorine dioxide: Tablets must stay sealed from air and light.4Boiling: Works for decades if you have fuel.1 The arithmetic for one household Say your household drinks and cooks with 15 liters (4 gallons) a day. That is about 5,500 liters (1,460 gallons) a year. Your real daily need depends on climate, work and family size. Bleach: at 12 drops (⅛ teaspoon) of 8.25% bleach per 2 gallons, 1,460 gallons takes about 91 teaspoons.2 That is about 450 mL (15 fl oz) of fresh bleach a year, for clear water. Pool shock: 1 heaping teaspoon makes 2 gallons of stock, which treats 200 gallons at 1 to 100.7 So 1,460 gallons needs about 7 heaping teaspoons (about 50 g, 1.8 oz) a year. This is dosing arithmetic only. It is not a promise of shelf life. Store granules dry, sealed and dated, and check the label. Use more than one barrierClear water first, then kill germs. Over the years, pair a biosand filter or a certified filter with boiling or chlorine.3 Keep a simple water log Write down every batch: the date, the container, the method and the dose. When someone gets sick, a log shows which water they drank. Add a line when you open a new bleach bottle or tablet pack. That tells you when the bleach passes one year.2 Practice this nowDose 1 gallon of tap water with bleach. Count the drops, wait 30 minutes and learn the faint chlorine smell.2Time a 1-minute rolling boil on your emergency stove and note how much fuel it uses.Look up your home's altitude and write "1 min" or "3 min" on your pot lid.1 Get these before you need themRegular, unscented bleach with the strength on the label (date every bottle)A glass or plastic dropper and a measuring spoon set used only for chemicalsChlorine dioxide tablets, kept sealedA large pot with a lid, and fuel set aside for waterGranular calcium hypochlorite labeled about 70%, stored dry and lockedCoffee filters or clean cotton cloth for clearing water Print or download these official pages now CDC: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency EPA: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water CDC guide: what each treatment method removes CDC Yellow Book 2026: Water Disinfection for Travelers

Start oral rehydration solution (ORS) right away. Most people with cholera can be treated with ORS.4 See Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration. Cholera can kill within hours. Watch for milky "rice-water" diarrhea, vomiting and leg cramps.46 Chlorine alone does not stop Cryptosporidium. It survives 3.5–10.6 days in properly chlorinated water.13 Boiling kills it.19 Toilets, treated water and clean hands save lives. Unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene were linked to at least 1.4 million deaths in 2019.3 Count back from the first symptom. Cholera starts within hours to 5 days; hepatitis A takes 15–50 days. s.h: 🦠 Why these diseases matter so much
s.x: Diarrhea is one of the top killers of young children. Diarrheal disease is the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months.1 Each year it kills about 443,832 children under 5 and another 50,851 children aged 5 to 9.1 There are nearly 1.7 billion cases of childhood diarrheal disease every year.1 Water is a main route. The World Health Organization (WHO) says contaminated drinking water can spread diarrhea, cholera, dysentery, typhoid and polio.2 It causes about 505,000 diarrheal deaths each year.2 A 2023 WHO report added up the cost of unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH). In 2019, safe WASH could have prevented at least 1.4 million deaths.3 More than 1 million of those deaths were from diarrhea.3 WHO's 2023 estimate for 2019. Bars are drawn to scale. Hand hygiene alone was linked to about 384,000 diarrheal deaths.3 Children pay the highest priceAmong children under 5, unsafe WASH caused 395,000 deaths in 2019.3 Diarrhea caused 273,000 of them.3 The 30-year viewIn a grid-down life, your household does the work of the water plant, the sewer and the first clinic, for decades. This chapter is the "why". Disinfecting Water, Toilets Without Water and Handwashing & Personal Hygiene are the "how".

s.h: 🔍 Know the diseases: signs and timing
s.x: Learn the first signs and how long each germ takes to show. Use the table as a quick guide. The details follow below it. Five waterborne diseases at a glance (CDC) DiseaseGermFirst signsStarts after CholeraBacteriumWatery "rice-water" diarrhea, vomiting, leg crampsA few hours to 5 days (usually 2–3)6 CryptosporidiumParasiteDiarrhea2–10 days (average 7)12 GiardiaParasiteDiarrhea, gas, greasy floating stools, cramps1–2 weeks11 TyphoidBacteriumFever, headache, stomach problems6–30 days10 Hepatitis AVirusTiredness, nausea, dark urine, yellow skin or eyes15–50 days (average 28)16 Cholera Cholera can kill within hours. WHO calls it a severe diarrheal disease that can kill within hours if it is not treated.4 You catch it by drinking or eating something that contains cholera bacteria. Symptoms usually start 2–3 days later, but can start within a few hours or as late as 5 days.6 Early signs are watery diarrhea, vomiting, leg cramps and restlessness. The diarrhea often looks milky white and is called "rice-water stool".6 About 1 in 10 people get severe symptoms. Untreated severe dehydration can lead to kidney failure, shock, coma and death.6 Cholera: act in hours, not daysIf someone has large amounts of watery diarrhea, start ORS immediately and get them to any working clinic. With early and proper treatment, even people with severe cholera can survive.6 Typhoid fever Typhoid spreads through sewage. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says it spreads through food, drinks and water contaminated by sewage, and through food rinsed in contaminated water.9 Symptoms usually appear 6–30 days after infection.10 They include fever, headache and stomach problems such as constipation or diarrhea.910 Feeling better does not mean the danger is over. CDC says people can keep carrying and spreading the bacteria after their symptoms go away.9 Dysentery (bloody diarrhea) Dysentery is diarrhea with blood in it. WHO calls acute bloody diarrhea dysentery.1 It lists dysentery among the diseases that contaminated drinking water spreads.2 Blood in the stool is a reason to get professional care. See when diarrhea becomes an emergency in Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration. E. coli E. coli is a leading cause of serious diarrhea. WHO names rotavirus and Escherichia coli (E. coli) as the two most common causes of moderate-to-severe diarrhea in low-income countries.1 It

s.h: ⏱️ Water or food? Use the clock
s.x: The same germs travel by water, food and hands. The true source is always someone's stool. CDC lists food, drinks and water contaminated by sewage as typhoid routes.9 For hepatitis A it lists close contact and contaminated food or water.16 So the useful question is: which water, which food, which hands? The incubation period, the time from swallowing a germ to the first symptom, tells you when the exposure happened. Incubation ranges drawn to scale. Short gaps point to the last few days; long gaps point weeks back.610111216 Do the arithmetic. If a child's first hepatitis A symptoms start on day 60, the exposure was between day 10 and day 45 (60 minus 50, and 60 minus 15).16 If cholera-like diarrhea starts on day 60, look at what people drank and ate from day 55 to day 60.6 Look-back windows: if symptoms started today, search this far back Suspected diseaseLook backMost likely CholeraA few hours to 5 days62–3 days ago6 Cryptosporidium2–10 days12About 7 days ago12 Giardia1–2 weeks111–2 weeks ago Typhoid6–30 days10Anywhere in that window Hepatitis A15–50 days16About 4 weeks (28 days) ago16 Long windows mean a wide search. For typhoid and hepatitis A, the source can be a meal or a water run from weeks ago, so a written log matters more than memory. Write it downFor every sick person, note the day and hour of the first symptom, and what the symptoms are. Match the diseaseUse the table above to find the most likely germ. Count backSubtract the incubation range from the first-symptom day. That gives the exposure window. List shared sourcesEvery water source, drink, shared dish and food handler in that window. Compare sick and wellThe source the sick people shared and the well people did not is your lead suspect. Cut it offStop using it. Treat all drinking and rinse water. See Epidemics: Quarantine, Isolation & Infection Control for caring for the sick safely. Clues: water, food or hands? Water: the sick people all drank from one source, even if they ate different meals. Food: the sick people all ate one dish, whatever they drank. See Food Safety Without a Refrigerator. Hands and close contact: cases follow one another inside a household. Hepatitis A spreads from person to person.16 No germ pattern fits: think about fuel, pesticides or other chemicals. See Chemical Contamination.

s.h: 🚰 Break the chain: toilets, water, hands, food
s.x: Every disease in this chapter starts in someone's stool. Typhoid travels through sewage,9 and hepatitis A moves from stool to mouth.16 Block each route and the germ cannot reach a mouth. Germs in stool reach the mouth through water, hands and food. A toilet blocks all three routes at the start.916 Hands matter as much as water. WHO linked about 384,000 diarrheal deaths in 2019 to poor hand hygiene alone.3 It linked another 356,000 deaths from respiratory infections to poor hand hygiene.3 The four barriers Toilet: keep stool far from water and food. See Toilets Without Water for distances from wells. Treat water: every drop for drinking, brushing teeth, mixing baby formula and rinsing food. See Disinfecting Water. Wash hands: after the toilet and diaper changes, and before touching food. See Handwashing & Personal Hygiene. Food: rinse it in treated water only. CDC lists food rinsed in contaminated water as a typhoid route.9 Chlorinated water is safe from every germ. Cryptosporidium survives 3.5–10.6 days in water held at 1–3 mg/L of free chlorine.13 Chlorine still kills most bacteria and viruses; for Crypto, boil or use a 1-micron filter.19 Do Drink, cook and brush teeth with treated water only Rinse fruit and vegetables in treated water9 Wash hands after the toilet, diapers and caring for the sick Keep the toilet away from wells and streams Start ORS at the first watery stool Don't Rely on bleach alone for Cryptosporidium13 Let anyone with diarrhea cook for others Let someone who had typhoid cook for others without a clinician's advice9 Use one dipper for both raw and treated water Guess with antibiotics

Replace lost fluid first. That is what keeps people alive. WHO says most people with cholera have mild or moderate diarrhea and can be treated with ORS.4 CDC adds that with early, proper treatment, even people with severe cholera can survive.6 Start at the first watery stools. WHO defines diarrhea as 3 or more loose or liquid stools in a day.1 For children with diarrhea, WHO and UNICEF recommend low-osmolarity ORS plus zinc supplements.18 Zinc shortens an episode of diarrhea by 25%.1 Take the zinc dose from a clinician or the package label. The full method and home recipe are in Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration. Start ORS right awayGive small sips often. Use sachets, or the recipe in the ORS chapter.18 Keep feedingBabies keep breastfeeding. Children keep eating their normal food.18 Check for dehydrationFast heartbeat, dry mouth, skin that is slow to flatten after a pinch.6 Protect everyone elseOne carer, one toilet or bucket for the sick person, handwashing after every contact, and no cooking for others. Get professional care for danger signsUse the table in the next section. Go early, not late. Caring for a sick person without spreading it The carer is the person most exposed. Hepatitis A spreads by close contact,16 and typhoid can spread even after the patient feels better.9 Set up the sickroom before you need it. One carer where possible, who washes hands after every contact, every bucket and every diaper. One toilet or lidded bucket for the sick person, emptied into the latrine, never near water. Separate cup, plate and towel, washed apart from the family's. Soiled bedding and clothes handled with gloves and washed away from the water source. No food preparation by the sick person or, ideally, by the carer. Disinfectant strengths for surfaces and laundry are in Epidemics: Quarantine, Isolation & Infection Control. Day-to-day nursing is in Nursing the Sick at Home.  Cholera is a death sentence without a hospital. Most cholera patients can be treated with ORS.4 Early treatment is what matters; even severe cases can survive with it.6 Do not guess with antibioticsNever give leftover, fish or animal antibiotics. ORS comes first; antibiotics are a clinician's decision. Read the facts in Infections, Sepsis & Antibiotic Facts and get a clinician's advice wherever one exists.

Move fast when fluid loss is heavy. Cholera can kill within hours.4 Other diseases are slower, but still need professional care. s.h: 👪 Protect the people most at risk
s.x: The same germ hits some people much harder. Plan your best water, your ORS and your fastest trip to care around them. Babies and young childrenDiarrhea kills about 443,832 children under 5 every year.1 In 2019, unsafe WASH caused 273,000 diarrheal deaths in this age group.3Wash hands after every diaper change: 70% of young children with hepatitis A show no symptoms.16 Mix formula only with safe water (see Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out). Elderly people and weak immune systemsIn people with weak immune systems, Crypto can cause diarrhea for weeks to months and life-threatening wasting.14 Even nitazoxanide, a drug used for Crypto, has not been shown to work in these patients.15Giardia can also last beyond 6 weeks in them.11 Give them boiled water, because boiling kills Crypto,19 and watch them closely for dehydration. Pregnant womenIf you are pregnant and get heavy diarrhea, vomiting, fever or yellow eyes, get professional care as early as you can. Keep drinking ORS meanwhile, and see Pregnancy Care Without a Hospital. DogsYour dog shares your floor, your hands and often your water. Give dogs clean water, keep them out of the latrine and away from the drinking-water source, and bury or bag their feces away from water. See Rabies & Diseases Animals Give Humans.

s.h: ⏳ The long haul: outbreaks keep coming
s.x: Cholera is not a disease of the past. In 2024, 60 countries reported 560,823 cholera cases and 6,028 deaths to WHO.8 Cholera deaths rose for the second year in a row: 2024 deaths were about 50% higher than in 2023.7 By WHO's September 2025 report, 31 countries had reported outbreaks that year.7 Keep a sickness log for 30 yearsA paper notebook beats memory. Record each case: name, date of first symptom, symptoms, and what the person drank and ate. It turns the arithmetic above into a real early warning. See Public Health for a Small Community. Vaccinate while clinics still existCDC recommends typhoid vaccination for travelers to high-risk areas.9 Hepatitis A is a vaccine-preventable disease covered in CDC's vaccine reference, the Pink Book.16 Ask a clinician now which vaccines fit your family. Get these before you need them ORS sachets, low-osmolarity formula18 Zinc for children, to use as a clinician or label directs18 A water filter with an absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller, which removes Cryptosporidium, plus spare parts19 Fuel set aside only for boiling drinking water A thermometer, gloves and a notebook for the sickness log A lidded bucket set aside for a sick person Read and save while the internet works CDC: Signs and Symptoms of Cholera CDC: Symptoms of Giardia Infection WHO: Cholera fact sheet CDC: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

Buy ORS sachets for every person in the household Print the danger-signs table and the incubation chart and put them by your water station Add a second water treatment that handles Cryptosporidium: boiling, or a 1-micron filter (see Water Filters) Set up handwashing next to the toilet and next to the kitchen Choose a toilet spot away from your well, stream or water tank Label one container "drinking water only" with its own clean dipper Start a sickness log notebook with columns for name, first symptom, symptoms, water and food Ask a clinician about hepatitis A and typhoid vaccines Teach every adult the signs of dehydration

How soon can cholera cause symptoms?Within a few hours to 5 days; usually 2–3 days. What do cholera stools look like?Milky white, watery "rice-water" stools. What is the first treatment for watery diarrhea?Oral rehydration solution (ORS), started right away. Does chlorine kill Cryptosporidium?Not reliably. It survives 3.5–10.6 days at 1–3 mg/L free chlorine. Boil the water instead. Hepatitis A incubation?15–50 days, average 28. Classic Giardia signs?Gas, cramps, smelly greasy floating stools, 1–2 weeks after exposure. Deaths linked to unsafe WASH in 2019?At least 1.4 million, over 1 million of them from diarrhea.

t: Calories & Nutrition: How Much Food Keeps You Alive

s.x: Plan 2,100 kcal per person per day. It is the minimum planning figure that food aid uses for general rations (the Sphere standard).1 Hard work needs more. Adult men need about 2,000–3,000 kcal a day and adult women about 1,600–2,400, depending on age and activity.4 Get 10–12% of calories from protein and about 17% from fat. That is the Sphere split for a 2,100 kcal ration.2 Adult protein floor: 0.8 g per kg of body weight a day. The 2025–2030 US Dietary Guidelines now advise 1.2–1.6 g/kg.97 Pregnant and breastfeeding women need more protein: 71 g a day in the US reference tables.10 2,100kcal per person per day: the emergency planning minimum1 766,500kcal per person per year at 2,100 a day (2,100 × 365)1 0.8 g/kgadult protein RDA per day, nearly unchanged since 19419 71 gprotein a day in pregnancy and breastfeeding (US tables)10

s.h: 🔢 The planning number: 2,100 kcal a day First 30 days
s.x: Start every food plan at 2,100 kilocalories (kcal) per person per day. In this book, "calories" means kilocalories. The Food Security Cluster, which coordinates humanitarian food aid, calls 2,100 kcal the minimum planning figure for general rations and asks partners to align with Sphere.1 Its 2025 emergency guidelines call it the Sphere standard and ask all groups to harmonize around it.2 A 2002 National Academies report on emergency relief food also used 2,100 kcal per day as its planning basis.5 It is a floor for planning, not a perfect fit for each body. The guidance says to adjust the requirements to the context.1 WFP and UNHCR guidance calls 2,100 kcal the initial reference value for the early stage of an emergency, when people have no other food.3 Calories needed at 2,100 kcal per person per day (simple multiplication) Period1 personFamily of 4Family of 6 1 day2,1008,40012,600 1 week14,70058,80088,200 30 days63,000252,000378,000 1 year766,5003,066,0004,599,000 30 years22,995,00091,980,000137,970,000 Every number in the table is 2,100 × people × days.1 Use it to see the scale of the job before you buy anything. One average, many bodies2,100 kcal is a planning average for a whole group. Adult needs alone run from 1,600 to 3,000 kcal a day, depending on sex, age and activity.4 Plan the group total first, then check each person. The 30-year viewOne person eating 2,100 kcal a day for 30 years needs about 23 million kcal (22,995,000).1 Plan stored food as the bridge while you build food production. Read Feeding a Family Forever: The Land Math.

s.h: 👪 Real needs: sex, age and workload
s.x: Adult women need about 1,600–2,400 kcal a day. Adult men need about 2,000–3,000 kcal a day.4 Where a person falls in that range depends on age and how physically active they are.4 The US Dietary Guidelines give estimates by age, sex and three activity levels: sedentary, moderately active and active.6 In the 2015–2020 edition this table is Appendix 2, "Estimated Calorie Needs per Day, by Age, Sex, and Physical Activity Level".14 The estimates are rounded to the nearest 200 kcal. One person's real needs may be higher or lower than the average in the table.6 Adult calorie ranges (US Dietary Guidelines) compared with the 2,100 kcal plan Whokcal per dayGap at the active end Adult women1,600–2,400Up to 300 kcal short Adult men2,000–3,000Up to 900 kcal short The gaps are simple subtraction: 2,400 − 2,100 = 300, and 3,000 − 2,100 = 900.4 Averages can hide a hungry workerA household that averages 2,100 kcal a day can still leave its most active man up to 900 kcal short every day.4 Set a target for each person, not just for the group. Without power, many chores are done by hand: hauling water, cutting wood, washing clothes, digging. Put anyone who does them every day at the active end of their range when you plan. List everyoneWrite each person's name, age, sex and body weight on one page. Pick an activity levelMark each person sedentary, moderately active or active.6 Be honest about the work they do now, not last year. Look up the estimateFind their age, sex and activity level in the printed calorie table.13 Add the household upTotal the daily targets. Compare the total with 2,100 × the number of people. Plan with the bigger numberUse whichever total is higher for buying and storing. Recheck every seasonRedo the list when work, ages, pregnancies or body weights change. Print these while the internet worksDownload or print the full tables so you can plan offline: Merck Manuals: Estimated calories needed by age, sex and activity level Dietary Guidelines 2015–2020 (archived), Appendix 2 calorie table Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030 (PDF) Food Security Cluster Handbook: Food Assistance

s.h: 🥩 Protein: the floor and the new target
s.x: Adults need at least 0.8 g of protein per kg of body weight per day. This US recommended dietary allowance (RDA) has changed very little since the RDA idea began in 1941.9 The number comes from nitrogen balance studies. They gave an estimated average requirement (EAR) of 0.66 g/kg and an RDA of 0.83 g/kg, which was rounded down to 0.8.9 The same 0.8 g/kg RDA applies to every adult age group from 19 to over 70.12 The 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans raise the target to 1.2–1.6 g/kg a day, adjusted to each person's calorie needs.78 That is 50–100% more than the old RDA (1.2 ÷ 0.8 = 1.5; 1.6 ÷ 0.8 = 2). The new guidelines appeared in January 2026.11 Harvard's Nutrition Source points out that protein needs vary a lot between people, that the National Academies set wider ranges, and that needs are best set with a health professional.11 Daily protein for adults by body weight (body weight × g/kg) Body weightRDA 0.8 g/kg2025–2030 DGA 1.2–1.6 g/kg 50 kg (110 lb)40 g60–80 g 60 kg (132 lb)48 g72–96 g 70 kg (154 lb)56 g84–112 g 80 kg (176 lb)64 g96–128 g 90 kg (198 lb)72 g108–144 g The new guidelines base protein on body weight because protein needs vary with age, body size and physical activity.7 The g/kg figures come from the RDA and the new guidelines.97 This table is for adults only. Do not use it for babies or children. Bar heights are 70 kg multiplied by the estimated average requirement (0.66 g/kg), the RDA (0.8 g/kg) and the 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines range (1.2–1.6 g/kg).97 Protein foods named in the 2025–2030 guidelines: eggs, poultry, seafood and red meat, plus beans, lentils, nuts and soy.7 The guidelines say to put a high-protein food in every meal.8 For which of these keep for years, read Long-Term Food Storage. Use kilograms for protein mathDivide pounds by 2.2 to get kilograms. A 154 lb adult is 70 kg, so the RDA is 70 × 0.8 = 56 g a day.9

s.h: 🧈 Fat, carbohydrate and the Sphere split
s.x: Sphere puts 10–12% of a ration's energy from protein and 17% from fat.2 The Food Security Cluster calls these the minimum nutritional requirements for planning general rations.1 In a 2,100 kcal day, that is 210–252 kcal from protein and 357 kcal from fat.2 The remaining 1,491–1,533 kcal (71–73%) come from carbohydrate foods. Sphere sets protein at 10–12% and fat at 17% of a 2,100 kcal ration; the kcal values are those percentages of 2,100.2 Calories and protein are not the whole dietThis chapter covers energy and protein. Vitamins and minerals need their own plan. Read Deficiency Diseases: Scurvy, Pellagra, Beriberi & More before you finish your food list.

s.h: 🧮 From people to kilograms: label math
s.x: Turn your calorie total into kilograms of food with the label on each package. A calorie plan only helps once you know how many kilograms (or pounds) of each food to store. Start from 2,100 kcal per person per day, or from each person's own target if it is higher.14 Read the labelFind the energy per serving (Calories or kcal) and the serving size in grams. Work out kcal per kgkcal per serving ÷ grams per serving × 1,000. Choose the food's shareDecide what part of your calories this food will supply, for example one third. Work out the kilogramsTotal kcal × share ÷ kcal per kg. Multiply by 2.2 for pounds. Round up and write it downWrite the target on your inventory sheet and on the storage bin. Worked example with a made-up label (not a real product) StepWorkingResult Label160 kcal per 45 g serving160 ÷ 45 × 1,000 kcal per kg3,556 kcal in each kg3,556 Family of 4, 1 year4 × 2,100 × 3653,066,000 kcal Food gives one third3,066,000 ÷ 31,022,000 kcal Kilograms needed1,022,000 ÷ 3,556 = 287.4Round up: 288 kg (635 lb) The 2,100 kcal starting figure is the planning minimum from the Food Security Cluster.1 Swap in your own household total if it is higher. How many days will your food last? Days of food = total kcal you have stored ÷ your household's kcal per day. Count every food, using the kcal per kg from its label. Example: a family of 4 at 2,100 kcal each needs 8,400 kcal a day.1 If the inventory adds up to 500,000 kcal, that is 500,000 ÷ 8,400 = 59.5, so 59 full days. Day 1List everyone with age, sex, weight and activity level. Set each person's calorie and protein target. Week 1Do the label math (kcal per kg) for every stored food. Write it on each container. Month 1Add up total kcal on hand. Divide by the household's daily total to get days of food. Every seasonReweigh people, update targets for work and pregnancy, and redo the days-of-food count.  The calculator multiplies people × days × kcal per person per day. Change the kcal box to match your household's own targets. Practice the label math this weekPick three foods you already store. Work out kcal per kg for each and write it on the container with a marker. Next time you shop, you can compare foods by kcal per kg and price. See Prepping on a Budget. s.h: 🤰 Who needs extra: pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and elders
s.x: Pregnant and breastfeeding women need more protein than other adults. The US reference tables set 71 g a day in pregnancy and in breastfeeding, for ages 19–30 and 31–50.10 Those tables base adult protein on 0.8 g per kg of a reference body weight.10 An AHRQ research protocol lists pregnancy and lactation at 1.1–1.3 g/kg a day, above the adult 0.8 g/kg.12 For a 60 kg (132 lb) woman, 0.8 g/kg is 48 g. The 71 g figure is 23 g more each day.10 These protein reference values were published in 2005. AHRQ notes they had not been updated for nearly two decades.12 Plan her extra share firstWhen food is short, set aside the extra protein for pregnant and breastfeeding women before you split the rest of the household's food. Read Pregnancy Care Without a Hospital and Breastfeeding: The Survival Superpower. Babies are not small adultsDo not plan a baby's food from the adult numbers in this chapter. Read Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out and the First Foods chapter. For children, use the age rows in the printed calorie table.13 Older adults: protein does not shrink with ageThe adult protein RDA stays at 0.8 g/kg from age 19 to over 70.12 Calorie needs change with age and activity, so check each older person's row in the table.4 For diabetes, kidney disease and other special needs, read the Special Diets chapter. Dogs need their own planThe human calorie and protein numbers in this chapter do not apply to dogs. Plan their food separately with Feeding Dogs Without Kibble.

s.h: 📋 Share food fairly and keep records
s.x: Write down each person's daily target and weigh what they actually get. A plan on paper does nothing if portions are guessed. Weigh people on the same scale, at the same time of day, about once a month. Write it in the food log next to their target. A falling weight tells you to recheck their share and their workload. Do Set a calorie and protein target for each person Plan active workers at the top of their range Set aside extra protein for pregnant and breastfeeding women first Weigh portions with a scale Keep a dated food log and inventory Re-plan when the work or the season changes Don't Give everyone the same portion by habit Plan below 2,100 kcal a head without a reason Use adult tables for babies or dogs Guess food stocks by eye Forget to count yourself in the plan Everyone needs 2,000 calories a day. Adult estimates run from about 1,600 to 3,000 kcal a day, by sex, age and activity.4 Any one person may need more or less than the table average.6 2,100 kcal a day is enough for anyone. 2,100 kcal is a minimum planning figure that aid planners adjust to the context.1 Active adult men can need up to 3,000 kcal.4 Protein advice is settled and never changes. The 0.8 g/kg RDA held almost unchanged from 1941, but the 2025–2030 US guidelines now advise 1.2–1.6 g/kg.97 Harvard notes that individual needs vary widely.11 Make it a routinePick one day a week to update the food log and inventory. Assign it to one person as a job, and rotate the job each month.

Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut. A closed fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours. A full freezer holds about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.12 Perishables above 4°C (40°F) for 2 hours or more go in the trash. That means meat, poultry, fish, eggs and leftovers. Above 32°C (90°F) the limit is 1 hour.1513 Eat in this order: fridge food first, then freezer food, then non-perishable pantry food.7 Within the fridge, perishables go before the foods the USDA chart lets you keep.3 Never taste food to check it. When in doubt, throw it out.2 Get medical help for danger signs: bloody diarrhea, diarrhea with a fever over 38.9°C (102°F), vomiting that stops you keeping liquids down, dehydration, or diarrhea longer than 3 days.11 4 ha closed fridge keeps food safe without power2 48 ha full freezer holds, door shut (24 h if half full)1 2 hmost time perishables may sit above 4°C (40°F)1 20 minbacteria can double in the danger zone4

s.h: ⏱️ The countdown starts when the power stops First 72 h
s.x: A closed refrigerator keeps food safe for up to 4 hours. After 4 hours without power, throw out refrigerated meat, fish, eggs, milk and leftovers.2 A full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours if the door stays shut. A half-full freezer holds for about 24 hours.12 These times come from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). They only hold if the doors stay closed.1 The fridge runs out of safe time 12 times faster than a full freezer. Times assume closed doors.12 Keep an appliance thermometer in both the fridge and the freezer. Safe readings are 4°C (40°F) or colder in the fridge and −18°C (0°F) or colder in the freezer.12 The first 30 minutes of an outage Write down the timePut it on the fridge door. Your 4-hour fridge clock and 24 to 48-hour freezer clock start now.2 Keep both doors shutOpen them only to read the thermometer or move food out. The safe times assume closed doors.113Tape a list of what is in the freezer to its door, so no one opens it to look.7 Read both thermometersWrite down the readings. The fridge should be 4°C (40°F) or colder and the freezer −18°C (0°F) or colder.2 Pack the freezer tightGroup frozen food together. Food packed close stays cold longer.1 Get coolers and ice readyIf the outage may last more than 4 hours, plan to move fridge perishables into a cooler with ice.1 Two numbers, two different clocks4 hours is how long a closed fridge stays cold enough. 2 hours is how long a perishable food may sit above 4°C (40°F).1No thermometer? Use the 4-hour rule.2 Have a thermometer? Use the 2-hour rule on what it reads.3 Freeze water now, while you have powerFreeze containers of water and gel packs ahead of time. They keep the freezer, fridge or cooler cold after the power goes.1 Full jugs also fill empty freezer space, and a full freezer holds twice as long as a half-full one.1

s.h: 🌡️ The danger zone and the 2-hour rule
s.x: Bacteria grow fastest between 4°C and 60°C (40°F and 140°F). USDA calls this range the "Danger Zone."4 In that range, bacteria can double in number in as little as 20 minutes.4 Keep hot food at 60°C (140°F) or hotter and cold food at 4°C (40°F) or colder.4 Food in between has a 2-hour limit, or 1 hour above 32°C (90°F).5 Never leave perishable food in the danger zone for more than 2 hours. If the air is above 32°C (90°F), the limit is 1 hour.56 Keep hot food at 60°C (140°F) or hotter, and cold food at 4°C (40°F) or colder. USDA lists chafing dishes, warming trays, slow cookers and ice as ways to do it.4 Why 2 hours matters: the math At the fastest rate, one doubling every 20 minutes, 2 hours is 6 doublings.4 That turns 1 germ into 64. 0 min1 germ on the food 20 min2 40 min4 1 hour8 (the hot-weather limit above 32°C / 90°F)5 80 min16 100 min32 2 hours64 (the normal limit: throw out perishables)1 Hot weather cuts your time in halfAbove 32°C (90°F), perishable food may sit out for only 1 hour, not 2.5 In a hot climate with no ice, plan every meal around this limit. Lost track of the time?If you do not know how long food has been out of the cold, you cannot apply the 2-hour rule. Follow the official fallback: when in doubt, throw it out.2

s.h: 🧊 Stretching the cold: coolers, block ice and dry ice
s.x: If the power will be off longer than 4 hours, move fridge perishables into a cooler with ice or frozen gel packs.1 Do it before the 4 hours run out. Keep the cooler at 4°C (40°F) or colder.6 Add ice as it melts to hold that temperature. Pack a cooler Pick the riskiest foods firstMeat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk and leftovers. These are the foods USDA says to discard after 2 hours above 4°C (40°F).1 Layer food with iceUse ice cubes, block ice or frozen gel packs.1 Put a thermometer insideThe target is 4°C (40°F) or colder.6 Keep the lid shutOpen it only to take food out or read the thermometer. Add ice as it meltsTop it up before the reading climbs above 4°C (40°F).6 Apply the 2-hour rulePerishables that sat above 4°C (40°F) for 2 hours or more go in the trash.1 Dry ice and block ice for longer outages About 23 kg (50 lb) of dry ice should hold a full 510-liter (18-cubic-foot) freezer for 2 days.1 USDA advises getting dry ice or block ice if the power will be out for a long time.1 Find out now where you can buy it locally. Dry ice burns skinNever touch dry ice with bare hands.16 Use thick gloves or a towel. Keep it where children and pets cannot reach it. Get these before you need them 2 appliance thermometers: one for the fridge, one for the freezer1 A third thermometer for the cooler At least one good cooler1 Gel packs and jugs to freeze water in1 Running a fridge on a generatorA generator can keep a fridge cold, but it brings its own dangers. Read Carbon Monoxide before you start one.

Eat the food that spoils fastest first. The American Red Cross order is: food from the refrigerator first, then food from the freezer, then non-perishable food.7 The official clocks explain why: about 4 hours for the fridge, 24 to 48 hours for the freezer.12 First: hours 0–4Fridge perishables: meat, poultry, fish, milk, eggs, leftovers, cut fruit and cooked pasta. Cook and eat them, or move them to a cooler with ice.23 Second: days 1–2Freezer food as it thaws. Food that still has ice crystals or is at 4°C (40°F) or colder can be refrozen or cooked.12 ThirdFridge foods the USDA chart lists as safe to keep even after 2 hours above 4°C (40°F): hard cheese, butter, whole fresh fruit, dried fruit, whole raw vegetables, bread, peanut butter and condiments.3 LastNon-perishable pantry food: cans, dry grains, beans and other long-life stores.7 See Long-Term Food Storage and Shelf-Life Tables. Cook only what you will eat at one mealWithout a working fridge, leftovers are on the 2-hour clock (1 hour above 32°C / 90°F).5 Cooking smaller amounts means less to throw away. For safe ways to cook without power, see Cooking Without Power. Babies and young childrenOpened baby formula is on the USDA discard list once it has been above 4°C (40°F) for more than 2 hours.3 Children under 5 are more likely to get seriously ill from food poisoning.11Worldwide, diarrheal disease is the third leading cause of death in children aged 1 to 59 months.15Give them the safest food first, and never the doubtful item. For feeding without power, see Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out. Dogs: do not feed them the trash pileThe USDA rules in this chapter are written for people, and no official rule here says thrown-out food is safe for dogs. Bag or bury discarded food so dogs cannot get it. See Feeding Dogs Without Kibble.

s.h: ✅ Keep or throw out: the USDA tables
s.x: Judge each food item separately. The official FoodSafety.gov power outage chart is built for exactly this.3 The chart's fridge rule applies to food that sat at 4°C (40°F) or above for more than 2 hours.3 When the power comes back (or at the 4-hour mark) Read the freezer thermometerAt 4°C (40°F) or below, the frozen food is safe and may be refrozen.2 Read the fridge thermometerNo thermometer? Count the hours. Past 4 hours, perishables go.2 Go item by itemUse the table below. Each food gets its own decision.3 Check smell, color, texture and warmthAnything that seems wrong or feels warm goes, even if the table says keep.3 Bag the discards securelyKeep them away from children and dogs. See Garbage & Waste Management. Check the full chart. If you still cannot tell, throw it out.2 Run every item through these three questions.13 The bottom rule overrides everything above it.3 Frozen food Thawed food can be refrozen if it still has ice crystals or is at 4°C (40°F) or colder.13 If the freezer thermometer reads 4°C (40°F) or below when power returns, the food is safe and may be refrozen.12 No thermometer in the freezer? Check each package on its own.1 Frozen meat, poultry, fish and other perishables that thawed and stayed above 4°C (40°F) for more than 2 hours go in the trash.3 Any food, any time Throw out any food with an unusual smell, color or texture, or that feels warm to the touch.313 Never taste food to decide if it is safe. When in doubt, throw it out.12 If it looks and smells fine, a small taste will tell you if it is safe. USDA and CDC both say never t

s.h: 🤢 Food poisoning: symptoms and danger signs
s.x: The common symptoms are diarrhea, stomach pain or cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever.11 Food poisoning is common even with working fridges. A CDC study published in 2025 estimated that major germs in food caused about 9.9 million illnesses in the US in 2019.12 What the US numbers show (CDC study, 2025)The same study estimated 53,300 hospital stays and 931 deaths from food eaten in the US in 2019.12 Norovirus alone caused about 5.5 million of the illnesses.12 Get medical help now for any of these Bloody diarrhea11 Diarrhea with a fever over 38.9°C (102°F)11 Vomiting so often that you cannot keep liquids down11 Signs of dehydration11 Diarrhea that lasts more than 3 days11 Botulism and home-canned food are covered in Home Canning Safely. Danger signs in babies are in Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs. Watch for dehydration Signs of dehydration include little or no urine, a very dry mouth and throat, and feeling dizzy when standing up.11 Replace lost fluid early. How to mix and give oral rehydration solution (ORS) is in Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration. Who gets sickest Some people are more likely to get food poisoning and to get seriously ill: adults 65 and older, children under 5, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems.11 Check people in these groups often for the danger signs above, and get help at the first one.11 Give them the safest food in the house. When someone gets sick Start fluids at onceDrink plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration.11 Use ORS if you have it.15 Check the danger signsBloody diarrhea, diarrhea with fever over 38.9°C (102°F), can't keep liquids down, dehydration, or diarrhea past 3 days means get help.11 Find and remove the suspect foodThrow out anything else from the same batch so no one else eats it. Keep the sick person out of the kitchenHave someone else cook. Wash hands after every bathroom trip and cleanup; see Handwashing & Personal Hygiene. PregnancyPregnant people are in a higher-risk group for food poisoning.11 CDC advises a pregnant person with fever and flu-like symptoms to talk to a doctor.11 See Pregnancy Care Without a Hospital. Older adultsAdults 65 and older are more likely to get seriously ill from food poisoning.11 Check them often for dehydration and the other danger signs, and get help at the first one.11

s.h: ⏳ No fridge for years: the daily rules Long haul
s.x: Without power, a fridge is just an insulated box. It keeps food safe for about 4 hours after the power goes, and no longer.2 After the first days, the 2-hour rule governs every meal you cook. Perishable food may sit in the danger zone for 2 hours at most, or 1 hour above 32°C (90°F).5 Three safe choices for any cooked food Eat it nowServe within 2 hours of cooking, or 1 hour in heat above 32°C (90°F).5 Keep it hotHold it at 60°C (140°F) or hotter, for example in a covered pot over low heat.4 Or throw it outWhen time is up and it is not hot, discard it.1 For the long haul, your food has to be safe at room temperature from the start. These chapters cover the methods: Ways to keep food without a refrigerator MethodWhere to learn it Dry goods in sealed containersLong-Term Food Storage Canning in jarsHome Canning Safely Drying, smoking, salting, fermentingDrying, Smoking, Salting & Fermenting Cool storage for roots and fruitRoot Cellars & Cold Storage The 30-year viewThe rules in this chapter do not expire. The danger zone, the 2-hour rule and "never taste to test" apply in year 30 exactly as on day 1.45What changes is your tools. Look after your thermometers, because they are the only way to know a temperature instead of guessing it. Run a cooler test this monthFill a cooler with ice and a thermometer, then note the reading every few hours. Record how long it stays at 4°C (40°F) or colder in your climate.6 Now you know your real number, not a guess. Label cooked food with the timeWrite the cooking time on the pot lid with chalk or tape. Then anyone can see when the 2-hour limit runs out.5

Put an appliance thermometer in the fridge and another in the freezer Freeze jugs of water and gel packs to fill empty freezer space Buy or find a cooler and a thermometer for it Print the FoodSafety.gov fridge and freezer charts and tape them inside a cupboard Write "Fridge 4 h / Freezer 48 h / Food 2 h" on a card on the fridge door Find out where to buy block ice or dry ice near you Stock shelf-stable food your family already eats Teach everyone, including children: never taste food to check it Put oral rehydration salts in your medical kit Run a cooler test and write down how many hours it held 4°C (40°F)

How long does a closed fridge keep food safe without power?About 4 hours. How long does a freezer hold with the door shut?About 48 hours if full, 24 hours if half full. What is the danger zone?4–60°C (40–140°F). Bacteria can double in as little as 20 minutes. How long can perishables sit in the danger zone?2 hours. Only 1 hour above 32°C (90°F). When can thawed food be refrozen?If it still has ice crystals or is at 4°C (40°F) or colder. Can you taste food to check it?No. When in doubt, throw it out. Which fridge foods can you keep after an outage?Hard cheese, butter, whole fruit, whole raw vegetables, bread, condiments. Five food poisoning danger signs?Bloody diarrhea, diarrhea with fever over 38.9°C (102°F), can't keep liquids down, dehydration, diarrhea over 3 days.

Cook outdoors only with camp stoves and charcoal grills, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows. That is the Ready.gov (FEMA) rule for power outages.1 Never use a gas stove or oven to heat your home. It is a carbon monoxide (CO) risk.13 Put a battery-powered CO alarm near every sleeping area. People who are asleep can die from CO before they feel any symptoms.2 Keep cooked food at 60°C (140°F) or hotter, or eat it within 2 hours. In heat above 32°C (90°F), the limit is 1 hour.45 Save fuel for drinking water. A rolling boil for 1 minute makes water safe from germs, or 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft).7 6 m(20 ft) from windows for camp stoves and charcoal grills1 60°C(140°F) or hotter keeps cooked food out of the danger zone4 1 minat a rolling boil makes water safe from germs7 3–6 Lof water per person per day just for cooking (Sphere)9

s.h: 🚫 Rule one: every flame cooks outside First 72 h
s.x: Every cooking fire makes carbon monoxide (CO). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists stoves, lanterns, grills, fireplaces and gas ranges among the things that make it whenever fuel burns.2 You cannot see or smell CO. It builds up in enclosed or partly enclosed spaces and poisons the people and animals who breathe it.2 Camp stoves and charcoal grills go outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1 A garage, carport, tent or camper is an enclosed or partly enclosed space, not "outdoors".23 If your gas range still works, use it for cooking only, then turn it off. Never use a gas stove or oven to heat the home.13 Where each way of cooking is allowed CookerSafe placeNever Camp stove (propane, butane, liquid fuel)Outdoors, 6 m (20 ft) from windows1Inside a home, garage, tent or camper Charcoal grillOutdoors, 6 m (20 ft) from windows1Inside, even "just to finish cooking" Gas range or ovenCooking only, then offHeating the home1 Wood fire or rocket stoveOutdoors, away from the houseAn open fire indoors Solar cookerA sunny spot outdoorsLeaving food in it after the sun goes Outside but close is not enoughAfter Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005, portable generators poisoned at least 78 people in Alabama and Texas and killed 10. Most of those generators were outside, but near the home.21Stoves and grills make CO too.2 Keep the full 6 m (20 ft) from windows,1 and set up so the smoke blows away from the house. Know the warning signs CO poisoning causes headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion.3 CDC notes that people often describe these as "flu-like".2 If anyone feels this way while a stove, grill or fire is burning nearby, get everyone into fresh air first. Then get medical help.3 Fit CO alarms with battery backup,1 and replace each alarm every 5 years.2 The full story is in Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer. Pick the spotOpen air, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1 Keep it away from doors and vents too. Check the windSet up so smoke blows away from the house and from where people sit. Clear the groundBare soil, gravel or paving. Nothing that can burn underneath or hanging overhead. Mark a no-go zoneLay a rope or a ring of stones around the cooker. Children and dogs stay outside it. Keep fire tools within reachA metal lid that fits your pan, a bucket of sand or soil, and a flashlight. Never leave it

s.h: 🔥 Your cooking options, side by side
s.x: You have five main ways to cook without the grid. Three of them burn fuel and make CO. A solar cooker and a retained-heat box burn nothing themselves, because CO comes from burning fuel.2 Camp stove (propane, butane or liquid fuel) Best for: boiling water and quick meals in the first days and weeks. Rule: outdoors only, 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1 Limit: its fuel comes from stores. Fuel pumps are among the systems FEMA lists as hit by power outages (2025).13 Charcoal grill Same rule as the camp stove: outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1 Never bring it indoors to keep warm or to finish cooking. Once bought charcoal runs out, you can make your own from wood. See Charcoal, Lime, Ash & Useful Low-Tech Materials. Wood fire and rocket stove Wood is a cooking fuel you can gather locally, year after year. A rocket stove is a small stove with an insulated, L-shaped burn chamber that you feed with sticks. Wood smoke still carries CO: CDC lists fireplaces and stoves among CO sources.2 Cook on wood outdoors. For indoor wood stoves and chimneys, read Heating With Wood. To light fires for decades, read Fire Starting Methods That Last Decades. Solar cooker No fuel, no flame, no CO.2 It cooks only while the sun shines on it. Retained-heat box ("haybox") You boil the pot on a stove, then let insulation finish the cooking. No flame goes in the box. The safety rules are in the no-flame section below. DoCook in the open air, 6 m (20 ft) from windows1Keep a lid on every potUse the sun on sunny daysFinish long dishes in an insulated boxKeep a battery CO alarm by every bed2 Don'tUse a grill or camp stove in a home, garage, tent or camperHeat the house with a gas stove or oven1Leave a fire aloneLet kids or dogs inside the no-go ring

s.h: ⛽ Fuel: count it, store it, stretch it
s.x: Stored fuel is all you can count on. FEMA lists fuel pumps, lighting and payment systems among the systems hit by power outages (2025).13 Outages can last months. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, surveyed households in Puerto Rico went an average of 84 days without power.14 Hurricane Helene in 2024 cut power to 5.9 million customers across 10 states.15 So measure how much fuel your family uses per day, while you still have a scale and time to practice. Weigh the fuelWeigh a full canister, bag of charcoal or bundle of dry wood on a kitchen scale. Write it down. Boil 1 liter (about 1 quart)Lid on. Time how long it takes to reach a rolling boil. Weigh againThe difference is your fuel per liter boiled. Cook a normal dayBreakfast, dinner and drinking water. Weigh the fuel before and after. Do the mathFuel stored ÷ fuel per day = days of cooking you have. Post the numberWrite "days of fuel left" on the fuel shelf and update it every week. Worked example (use your own numbers)These numbers are made up to show the math. Say your test shows one day uses 300 g (0.66 lb) of fuel, and you have 10 kg (22 lb) stored.10 kg ÷ 0.3 kg per day = about 33 days of cooking. Store fuel away from water and food Fuel vapors can pass through plastic. University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension warns that gasoline, kerosene and pesticide vapors can penetrate plastic water containers.16 Keep stored water, and anything you eat or drink from, well away from fuel. For storing and rotating liquid fuels, read Generators & Fuel Storage. Fuel handling habitsChange or refill fuel canisters only when every flame nearby is out.Close valves fully after each use.Store fuel where children cannot reach it.Keep matches and lighters in a closed metal tin. The 30-year viewBought fuel runs out first. Plan to move, step by step, to fuels you can renew: dry wood you cut and season, charcoal you make, and the sun.Every liter of fuel you save with a lid, a solar cooker or an insulated box is a liter you still have next winter.

s.h: 💧 Water first: the biggest fuel job
s.x: Boil drinking water at a rolling boil for 1 minute. Above 2,000 m (6,500 ft), boil it for 3 minutes.7 Longer is not needed. CDC's Yellow Book says boiling kills organisms quickly, and the full minute already adds a margin of safety.8 Every extra minute burns fuel you need later. Boiling does not remove fuel or chemicals.7 For other methods, read Disinfecting Water.  You must boil drinking water for 10 minutes or more. CDC says 1 minute at a rolling boil, or 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft).7 The full minute already includes a safety margin.8 Cooking needs water too Plan 3–6 L of water per person per day just for cooking. That is the Sphere humanitarian figure, on top of 2.5–3 L for drinking and food.9 The CDC home minimum of 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day covers drinking, cooking and brushing teeth.10 Sphere's cooking figure alone, 3–6 L, can use up that whole gallon.9 Cooking water for a family of 44 people × 3–6 L = 12–24 L (3.2–6.3 gal) a day, using the Sphere range.9Over 30 days that is 360–720 L (95–190 gal), just for cooking. Keep fuel for the baby's waterFor powdered formula, CDC says to use bottled water until officials say tap water is safe. With no bottled water, boil water for 1 minute (3 minutes above 2,000 m or 6,500 ft).11For babies under 2 months, premature babies or babies with weak immune systems, mix the formula with water that is still about 70°C (158°F).11 Cool the bottle before feeding. Set aside fuel that is only for this. See Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

s.h: 🌡️ Cook it safe: heat, time and leftovers
s.x: Bacteria grow fastest between 4°C and 60°C (40°F and 140°F). USDA calls this the "Danger Zone". In that range, bacteria can double in as little as 20 minutes.4 Keep hot food at 60°C (140°F) or hotter until you serve it.4 Cooked food left in the danger zone has 2 hours. If the air is above 32°C (90°F), it has 1 hour.5 After that, throw it out. Never taste food to check whether it is safe. When in doubt, throw it out.6 0 min: off the heatServe it now, or keep it at 60°C (140°F) or hotter.4 20 minIn the danger zone, bacteria can already have doubled.4 1 hourLimit in hot weather, above 32°C (90°F).5 2 hoursLimit in cooler weather. Throw out what is left.5 Leftover starches count too. FoodSafety.gov lists cooked pasta among foods to discard after more than 2 hours above 4°C (40°F) in a power outage.22 Cook one meal at a timeWithout a fridge, cook only what your household will eat at that meal. Write the time on the pot lid with chalk or tape, so anyone can see when the 2-hour limit runs out.5 For storing food without power, read Food Safety Without a Refrigerator. Get two food thermometersA thermometer shows whether food is still at 60°C (140°F) or hotter.4 Buy a dial or glass one that needs no battery, plus a spare. When food makes someone sick Get medical help for these signs: bloody diarrhea, fever over 38.9°C (102°F), frequent vomiting, signs of dehydration, or diarrhea that lasts more than 3 days.12 Some people get much sicker: adults 65 and older, children under 5, pregnant people and people with weak immune systems.12 For fluids, read Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration.

s.h: 📦 No-flame cooking: insulated boxes and the sun
s.x: Retained-heat ("haybox") cooking Bring the pot to a full boil on a safe outdoor stove, then put the lidded pot into a well-insulated box. The insulation holds the heat in, so you stop burning fuel to keep it simmering. The one rule: the food must stay at 60°C (140°F) or hotter. That is USDA's hot-holding temperature. Below it, bacteria grow fastest.4 Build the boxUse a box, basket or cooler. Line every side, the bottom and the top with thick insulation: blankets, pillows, a sleeping bag, straw or crumpled paper. Choose the potA pot with a tight lid and handles, that fits the hollow with insulation pressed all around it. Boil it hardBring the food to a full rolling boil on the outdoor stove. Stir so it is hot all the way through. Move it fastLid on, straight into the box, insulation over the top. Close every gap. Leave it closedDo not open it to peek. Every opening lets heat out. Check before eating60°C (140°F) or hotter: serve it.4 Cooler, and for under 2 hours: boil it again, then eat. Longer, or you do not know: throw it out.56 Hot food must stay at 60°C (140°F) or hotter.4 If it has cooled, the 2-hour danger-zone limit applies.5 Keep the box away from flamesBlankets, straw and paper burn. Take the pot off the stove before it goes into the box, and keep the box well away from the fire. Test your box with water nowBoil 2 L (about 2 quarts) of water, box it, and check it with a thermometer every hour. Write down how many hours it stays at 60°C (140°F) or hotter.4That is your box's safe time. Never leave food in it longer than that. Beans and grains in the boxAlways bring them to a full boil first. Do not leave them in the box overnight unless your water test shows the box holds 60°C (140°F) or hotter that long.4 Solar cookers A solar cooker burns nothing, so it makes no CO.2 It needs direct sun and a cook who checks the food. Set it up in full sun, outside the children's and dogs' play area. Use a dark pot with a lid. Turn the cooker to face the sun as it moves across the sky. Do not stare into the shiny reflector. Check the food with a thermometer before you eat it: 60°C (140°F) or hotter.4 If clouds come and the food cools, the 2-hour clock starts.5 Finish it on the stove.

s.h: 🫘 Beans, rice and grains on less fuel
s.x: Humanitarian food planning starts at 2,100 kcal per person per day.19 The 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines list beans and lentils among protein foods.20 Your fuel decides how often you can cook them. Use the habits below, then measure what works with your own stove and food. Six fuel-saving habits One pot, one fireCook beans, grain and vegetables together, or one after another on the same fire. Lid on, alwaysKeep the lid on from the moment the water goes in. Boil, then boxBring the pot to a full boil, then finish the long, slow part in a retained-heat box, using the safety checks above.4 Use only the water you needEvery extra liter heated is fuel wasted. Cooking water is already 3–6 L per person per day.9 Cook while the sun is outPut slow dishes in the solar cooker on clear days, and save stove fuel for water and bad weather. Cook only what you will eatLeftovers have 2 hours, or 1 hour above 32°C (90°F).5 Food you throw away is fuel thrown away. Run a soak test nowTake two equal cups of the same dried beans. Soak one in clean, treated water overnight; leave the other dry.Cook both on the same stove. Write down the minutes until soft and the fuel used for each. Now you know, for your beans and your stove, what soaking saves. Soak and cook with safe water. CDC counts cooking in the clean water you need each day.10 If you are unsure about a source, treat it first with the methods above. For growing and processing these crops, see Growing & Processing Grains and Beans. Every path ends with the same check: 60°C (140°F) or hotter,4 or eaten within 2 hours (1 hour above 32°C / 90°F).5 Stoves stay 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1

s.h: 👪 Children, elders, women and dogs at the cooking fire
s.x: The cooking spot puts flames, hot pots, fuel and CO in one place. Plan for each person who comes near it. Babies and childrenInfants are among those at higher risk from CO.2 Keep babies and young children indoors or well away from the cooker, never inside the no-go ring.Give older children safe jobs away from the flame: carrying water, washing vegetables, setting out bowls. Cook full portions for children; FEMA and the American Red Cross say food may be rationed except for children and pregnant women.17 See Survival Skills Kids Can Learn by Age and Burns. Elders and people with heart or lung diseaseOlder people and people with heart disease, anemia or breathing problems are at higher risk from CO.2 Seat them upwind and away from the smoke.Adults 65 and older are also more likely to get seriously ill from food poisoning.12 Serve them food hot, straight from the pot. PregnancyPregnant people are in a higher-risk group for food poisoning.12 Give them freshly cooked, hot food, not leftovers.Do not cut a pregnant woman's portion: FEMA and the Red Cross exclude pregnant women from food rationing.17 CDC also says to store extra water for pregnant women.10 DogsCO poisons animals as well as people.2 If the dog and people feel unwell at the same time while something is burning nearby, treat it as CO and get everyone into fresh air.3Keep dogs out of the no-go ring, tied or shut away while you cook. For feeding dogs from the family pot, read Feeding Dogs Without Kibble. If a fire gets away Plan two ways out of every room. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) says to practice the plan twice a year, during the day and at night.18 You may have only 1 to 2 minutes to escape once a home fire starts. Get out and never go back inside.18 Use flashlights, not candles, for light while you cook and clean up after dark.1 Download and print while the internet worksReady.gov's Power Outages page, CDC's Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics, and USDA's Danger Zone page. Keep paper copies with this book.

Buy a battery-powered CO alarm for every sleeping area and write the date on it Pick and mark your outdoor cooking spot, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows Buy a camp stove or grill, plus fuel, and store the fuel away from water containers Buy two food thermometers that need no batteries Do the stove fuel test and write "days of fuel left" on the fuel shelf Build a retained-heat box and test it with 2 L (2 quarts) of boiling water Set aside fuel that is only for drinking water and baby formula Stock several days of no-cook meals for rainy days Teach everyone the CO symptoms and the rule "fresh air first" Run the soak test on your dried beans Practice your fire escape plan, day and night Cook one full day of meals outdoors without power, as a drill

Where do camp stoves and charcoal grills go?Outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows. Can you heat the house with a gas stove or oven?Never. It is a carbon monoxide risk. Someone has a headache and dizziness near a burning stove. First move?Everyone into fresh air first, then medical help. How hot must food stay until it is served?60°C (140°F) or hotter. How long can cooked food sit out?2 hours, or 1 hour above 32°C (90°F). Then throw it out. How long do you boil drinking water?1 minute at a rolling boil. 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft). The haybox rule?Boil first, lid on, box closed, check 60°C (140°F) before serving. How much cooking water per person per day?3–6 L (Sphere), on top of drinking water.

Build three tiers, not one big box. A personal kit on each adult, a household kit at home and in the car, and a shared group store. The Red Cross says to keep a kit both at home and in the car.1 Start the household kit from the Red Cross family-of-four list. It includes 2 absorbent compress dressings, 25 adhesive bandages and 1 roll of cloth tape.1 Personal kits are for bleeding first. The US Army built its soldier kit around severe bleeding and airway problems, two leading causes of battlefield death, and added a second tourniquet.2 Use the WHO Essential Medicines List (2025) as a planning map, not a shopping list. It names 523 medicines for adults and 374 for children, and it is written for working health systems.34 Skills beat gear. More than 5 million people have taken Stop the Bleed training: direct pressure, wound packing and tourniquets.5 A kit is a living inventory. Check expiration dates and replace anything used or out of date.1 25adhesive bandages in the Red Cross family-of-four kit1 2tourniquets in the US Army IFAK II soldier kit2 523adult medicines on the WHO 2025 Essential Medicines List3 5M+people trained in Stop the Bleed worldwide5

One kit cannot do every job. A box at home does not help on the road. A pocket kit cannot treat a whole family for a month. So split your supplies into three tiers. Each tier copies an established model: the US Army's Improved First Aid Kit (IFAK) for personal kits, the American Red Cross family list for households, and the World Health Organization (WHO) essential medicines idea for the group store.614 Smallest and always carried at the top; biggest and shared at the bottom. Skills sit under every tier. The three tiers at a glance TierWhere it livesBuilt fromMain job 1. PersonalOn your body or beltArmy IFAK ideaStop severe bleeding fast 2. HouseholdHome and carRed Cross family listCuts, burns, sprains, fever 3. GroupOne locked, shared storeWHO essential medicines idea + a clinicianRestock tiers 1 and 2; long-term medicines Color-code the tiersUse a red pouch for bleeding gear, a clear box for the household kit and labeled tubs for the group store. A tired person can then grab the right thing in the dark.

The personal kit solves one problem: bleeding that can kill before help arrives. The US Army says severe bleeding and airway problems are two of the leading causes of death on the battlefield, and its kit targets both.2 In 2013 the Army introduced a redesigned kit, the IFAK II.6 The redesign drew on soldier feedback and added a second tourniquet.2 The Army names a second combat application tourniquet, a chest seal with a valve, an eye shield, a casualty card, a marker and a strap cutter among the IFAK II contents.62 The civilian version You are not a soldier, but the logic carries over: small, light, always on you, and focused on bleeding. Carry only items you have been trained to use. Put the tourniquet where both hands reach itAn outside pocket or belt pouch, not the bottom of a bag. Learn it first in a class. See Stopping Severe Bleeding. Add a pressure bandage and gauzeThese are for wounds a tourniquet cannot reach. Stop the Bleed teaches wound packing alongside tourniquets.5 Add glovesAt least 2 pairs. The Red Cross kit specifies nonlatex gloves.1 Add a few days of your own medicinesKeep them in labeled containers with a written list of names, doses and allergies. Add a card and a markerWrite what you did and the time. The Army kit carries a casualty card and marker for the same job.6 Make every kit the sameSame pouch, same layout, same place on every adult. Anyone can then find anything in the dark. DoCarry it on your bodyKeep the tourniquet reachable with either handTrain before you rely on the gearReplace anything you use the same day Don'tBury it in a backpackCarry gear you have never practiced withAdd "nice to have" items until it is too heavy to carry dailyShare one personal kit across the family A tourniquet is a skill, not a gadgetStop the Bleed courses teach tourniquets together with direct pressure and wound packing.5 Take the course before you trust the gear, and practice only the way your instructor shows you.

Start with the American Red Cross list. It is written for a family of four. The Red Cross says to keep one kit at home and one in the car.1 Copy the list exactly first.
