Add your family's extras after. The Red Cross also says to include personal items such as medicines and emergency phone numbers, or other items your health care provider suggests.1 Red Cross first aid kit for a family of four1 ItemAmount Absorbent compress dressings, 5 × 9 in (13 × 23 cm)2 Adhesive bandages, assorted sizes25 Adhesive cloth tape, 10 yd × 1 in (9 m × 2.5 cm)1 roll Antibiotic ointment packets, about 1 g each5 Antiseptic wipe packets5 Aspirin packets, 81 mg each2 Emergency blanket1 Breathing barrier with one-way valve1 Instant cold compress1 Nonlatex gloves, size large2 pairs Hydrocortisone ointment packets, about 1 g each2 Scissors1 Roller bandage, 3 in (7.5 cm) wide1 Roller bandage, 4 in (10 cm) wide1 Sterile gauze pads, 3 × 3 in (7.5 × 7.5 cm)5 Sterile gauze pads, 4 × 4 in (10 × 10 cm)5 Oral thermometer, non-mercury and nonglass1 Triangular bandages2 Tweezers1 First aid instruction booklet1 Only four items are medicines or antiseptics: antibiotic ointment, antiseptic wipes, hydrocortisone ointment and low-dose aspirin.1 Everything else is dressings, tools and protection. The aspirin in the kit is fine for anyone in pain. Never give aspirin to children.7 Do not give it to teenagers either unless a doctor says so. If you are allergic to aspirin, have a bleeding problem or take a blood thinner, do not take the kit aspirin unless a clinician tells you to. Read the warnings on the label first. Add these for your household Each person's prescription medicines and a written medicine list Children's versions of any OTC medicines you use, in their own pouch Menstrual supplies, including reusable ones Extra gloves, tape and gauze Elastic bandages and splint material A printed copy of this book's medical chapters Children get their own pouchNever give aspirin to children.7 WHO keeps a separate children's list, the EMLc, with 374 medicines in 2025.3Keep children's medicines apart from adult ones, write each child's weight on the pouch, and dose only as the label says. See The Baby & Toddler Prep Kit. Women and girlsPack menstrual products for every woman and girl, plus pain relief used only as the label directs. If anyone is pregnant or breastfeeding, read the warnings on every label firs

A group store is a small supply room, not a bigger first aid kit. It refills the personal and household kits, and it holds what one family cannot. The model is how health systems plan. WHO says essential medicines are meant to be available within functioning health systems at all times, in adequate amounts.4 A group store tries to keep that promise on a small scale. What goes in it Bulk consumables: multiples of every Red Cross item, especially gloves, gauze and tape Durable tools: tweezers, scissors, splints and spare thermometers (the Red Cross specifies non-mercury, nonglass)1 The medicine plan made with a doctor or pharmacist (next section) Printed references and the supply log Separate shelves for children's and dogs' supplies Do the arithmetic. The Red Cross list covers 4 people.1 For a group of 12, three lists give 75 adhesive bandages, 6 compress dressings, 30 gauze pads and 6 pairs of gloves. That is only a starting point. The quantities section shows how to scale it from your own use. Give the store one keeperName one person to run the log and a second person to check it. Every item that leaves gets written down: what, how many, for whom, and the date. The 30-year viewEven today, with power and pharmacies, WHO reports that availability and affordability of essential medicines remain problems in many countries.4 Over decades, plan for supplies running out: keep reusable tools, learn the skills, and stay connected to any clinic that still works.

WHO's Model List of Essential Medicines (EML) names the medicines a health system needs most. WHO defines essential medicines as those that satisfy the priority health-care needs of a population.4 WHO published the current edition on 5 September 2025: the 24th adult list and the 10th children's list (EMLc).3 Together they name 523 medicines for adults and 374 for children.38 The 2025 update added 20 medicines to the adult list and 15 to the children's list.3 The 2025 update by the numbers (WHO)3 MeasureNumber New medicines added to the adult list20 New medicines added to the children's list15 Listed medicines given new uses7 Total adult medicines523 Total children's medicines374 The 2025 update added key cancer treatments.3 It also added diabetes and obesity medicines in the GLP-1 class (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) and the dual-action medicine tirzepatide.3 Core and complementary lists The core list covers the minimum medicine needs of a basic health-care system. The complementary list covers priority diseases that need specialist diagnosis, monitoring or care.4 WHO chooses each medicine by public health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness.4 That is a good test for your own plan too: what problems are common in your group, and what is proven to help? The WHO list is a home stockpile list. Buy everything on it. It is written for health systems. Even the core list is the minimum for a basic health-care system, and complementary items need specialist diagnosis, monitoring or care.4 Use it as a map to discuss with a doctor or pharmacist. What "OTC" means Over-the-counter (OTC) medicines are sold without a prescription. Each country decides which medicines are OTC, so check your local rules with a pharmacist. Give OTC doses only as written on the label. For what each common OTC medicine does, see Over-the-Counter Medicines. Sort every medicine into one of three groups GroupExamplesHow to get moreWho decides the dose OTCThe kit ointments and aspirinPharmacy or storeYou, by the label Prescriptions you take nowBlood pressure, diabetes, thyroidYour prescriber and pharmacyYour prescriber Prescriptions you might needAntibiotics, strong pain reliefOnly through a clinicianA clinician Never self-prescribeDo not take prescription medicines that were not prescribed for you. Do not use veterinary, fish or aquarium antibio

Size your kit from your own use, not from a guess. We could not find an official kit list sized for decades without power. So use arithmetic on two numbers you control: how many people, and how much you actually use. Count your peopleList adults, children, babies, elders and dogs separately. Each group needs different items. Set the baselineOne Red Cross list per 4 people, rounded up.1 A family of 6 needs 2 lists. Log your use for 3 monthsWrite down every bandage, glove, wipe and dose you use. Real numbers beat guesses. Multiply to a year3 months × 4 = 1 year. Example: 10 bandages in 3 months is 40 a year, or 1,200 over 30 years. Do the medicine math1 tablet a day is 365 a year and 10,950 over 30 years. Show that number to your prescriber and plan together. Split durable from consumableBuy durable tools once, plus a spare. Buy consumables in bulk and rotate them. Durable versus consumable Durable: buy once, plus a spareConsumable: buy in bulk and rotate TweezersAdhesive bandages ThermometerSterile gauze pads and compress dressings Scissors and splintsGloves Instruction bookletTape, wipes and ointments The medicine math, in one lineThe Red Cross kit holds 2 packets of 81 mg aspirin and 5 packets of antibiotic ointment.1 Compare that with your usage log before you assume it will last. Medicines also expire: see Medicines: Shelf Life & Expiration Facts. This weekCheck your home kit against the Red Cross list. Put a second kit in the car.1 First 72 h This monthBuild one personal bleeding kit per adult. Book a Stop the Bleed class. First 30 days Month 3Finish your usage log. Scale your household kit to one year. Month 6Set up the group store and the medicine plan with a clinician. Year 1 Every check dateCount, date, replace. Repeat for as long as you need the kit. Long haul

A kit you cannot find, cannot open or that has expired is the same as no kit. The Red Cross says to check expiration dates and replace any used or out-of-date contents.1 Follow the storage line on each label. Read it on every medicine and sterile pack, and copy any temperature limit onto your inventory sheet. If a medicine got too hot or too cold, do not guess. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) says to check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, health care provider or the manufacturer.10 Insulin without a fridgeThe FDA says insulin vials and cartridges, opened or unopened, may be left unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days.11 Pens and other products can differ, so check each leaflet, and replace insulin exposed to extreme conditions as soon as you can.11 See Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies. Review the whole kit at least once a year. Ready.gov says to replace expired items as needed and to re-think your needs every year as your family changes.12 Count what you have, label it with the earliest expiry date, store it safely, then check and replace. The Red Cross advice to check dates and replace used items is the core of this loop.1 Use hard, sealed containersUse tubs with tight lids to keep out water, insects and rodents. Label the outsideWrite the tier, the contents and the earliest expiration date on the lid. Lock medicines away from childrenStore them high and locked. Keep the key where every adult knows to find it. Keep boxes off the floor and away from heatNot by the stove, not in the sun, not on a damp floor. Follow each label's storage line. First in, first outNew stock goes to the back. Use the oldest first so nothing expires unseen. Keep the log with the boxEvery item in or out gets a line: what, how many and the date. DoKeep a kit at home and in the car1Pick one fixed check date and stick to itKeep sterile packs sealed and dryRead the storage line on every label Don'tStore medicines where children can reach themMix loose pills in unlabeled bagsUse a sterile pack that is wet or torn as if it were sterileLeave the only kit in a car that might be gone Child safetyChildren explore boxes and bags. Keep every medicine, including the kit aspirin, in a locked box. Aspirin is never for children.7

Training turns a box of supplies into care. The Army rebuilt its kit from soldier feedback.2 Your family's kit should follow the same rule: carry what you know how to use. The American College of Surgeons (ACS) Stop the Bleed program has trained more than 5 million people worldwide. It teaches three techniques: direct pressure, wound packing and tourniquets.5 Training options, in a sensible order CourseWhat you learnWhen Stop the BleedPressure, wound packing, tourniquets5Before you buy a tourniquet CPR and first aidCPR, choking, everyday injuriesEvery adult and teen, first year Wilderness first aidCare when help is hours or days awayAfter the basics Pharmacist or doctor reviewYour family's medicine planBring your medicine lists For CPR steps and the current guidelines, see CPR & Choking. The Red Cross includes a first aid instruction booklet in its kit list, so keep a printed guide in every kit.1 Practice with your own kitEmpty the kit on a table. Name every item and say what it is for.Repack it with your eyes closed. Then repack it in the dark.Ask each adult to find the tourniquet in under 10 seconds.Teach children where the kit lives and how to bring it to an adult. Download while the internet works WHO Model Lists of Essential Medicines: the current adult and children's lists.9 Red Cross: Anatomy of a First Aid Kit: print it and tape it inside your kit lid.1 Buy these firstThe full Red Cross family list, times your household sizeOne tourniquet per adult, after a Stop the Bleed classExtra gloves, gauze and tapeHard, sealable tubs and a notebook for the log

Print the Red Cross family-of-four list and check your home kit against it Put a second kit in the car Build one personal bleeding kit per adult and decide where each person carries it Book a Stop the Bleed class for every adult and teen Write a medicine card for every person: names, doses, allergies, prescriber Ask your doctor and pharmacist how to get a longer supply of regular prescriptions Make separate labeled pouches for children's medicines and for the dog Start a 3-month usage log Label every box with its contents and earliest expiration date Pick one fixed date each year to review the whole kit Download the WHO 2025 Essential Medicines Lists while the internet works

What are the three kit tiers?Personal (on you), household (home and car), group (shared store). What starts the Red Cross family-of-four kit?25 adhesive bandages, 2 compress dressings (5 × 9 in) and 1 roll of cloth tape. Why does the Army IFAK II carry two tourniquets?The Army added a second one after soldier feedback. Severe bleeding and airway problems are leading battlefield killers. How many medicines are on WHO's 2025 lists?523 for adults and 374 for children. Who should never take the kit aspirin?Children. Adults with an aspirin allergy, a bleeding problem or on a blood thinner should ask a clinician first. What does Stop the Bleed teach?Direct pressure, wound packing and tourniquets. 1 tablet a day for 30 years is how many tablets?10,950. Plan it with a prescriber. How long can insulin vials stay out of the fridge?Up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F), per the FDA. Check each product's leaflet.

t: Assessing a Sick or Injured Person

s.x: Protect yourself first. Check the scene for safety, form a first impression, ask permission and put on gloves if you have them.1 Not responding and not breathing, or only gasping? Start CPR now. Spend no more than 10 seconds on that check.319 In an injury, heavy bleeding comes first. Military medicine works in the order MARCH: Massive bleeding, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia.5 Count, don't guess. A resting adult: pulse 60–100, breathing 12–20 a minute, nail refill under 2 seconds.91012 Children run faster. A newborn's resting pulse is 70–190.10 WHO counts 50 or more breaths a minute as fast breathing in babies aged 2–11 months.1617 Write the time next to every number. Then check again and compare. 10 seclongest you should take to check if a collapsed person responds3 60–100normal resting pulse for adults and children aged 10 and up10 12–20breaths per minute for a resting adult9 <2 secnormal time for a pressed nail bed to turn pink again12

s.h: 🧭 The whole check at a glance
s.x: Work in the same order every time, so you never have to stop and decide what comes next. The chart shows the order this chapter teaches. Each step has its own section below. Spend no more than 10 seconds deciding whether CPR is needed.3 In injuries, MARCH puts massive bleeding first.5 Then keep repeating the vital signs and writing them down.

Stop before you rush in. The American Red Cross starts every emergency the same way: check the scene for safety, form an initial impression, get consent and put on personal protective equipment (PPE) such as gloves.1 Keeping yourself safe is what lets you help others.2 If you get hurt too, your family has two patients and one less helper. Look for anything that could hurt you Fire, smoke or fumes from a stove, heater or generator Walls, roofs, trees or vehicles that could fall or roll Fast or deep water Broken glass, sharp metal and needles Blood, vomit and other body fluids: glove up first A frightened or protective animal An angry or violent person: back away and get help Stop and lookScan the whole area before you step in. Is anything still dangerous?1 Form a first impressionAs you walk up, notice: Is the person moving? Making sounds? Bleeding heavily? Is the skin an odd color?1If blood is pooling or spurting, control it first.5 Ask permissionSay your name and "I know first aid. Can I help?" Get consent before you touch them.1 For a child, ask a parent or caregiver if one is there. Protect your hands and eyesPut on gloves and eye protection if you have them.1 Get help and gear movingShout for help and send someone for the medical kit. The Red Cross says to get equipment and give care based on what you find, within your training.1 Collapsed and not breathing? Do not finish this chapter firstCheck for a response and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing, or only gasping, that is cardiac arrest: start CPR and use an AED (automated external defibrillator) right away.319 See CPR & Choking.  DoPause and scan before you go inAsk "Can I help?" firstWear gloves for any body fluidSend someone for the kit Don'tRun into smoke, water or a collapse zoneTouch blood with bare handsSpend more than 10 seconds deciding about CPR3Leave the person alone to fetch gear if someone else can go

s.h: 🔺 The primary survey: find the fastest killer
s.x: The primary survey is a quick first check for the most urgent problems. Fix each problem as you find it, then move to the next one. ABC: the classic order The Canadian Red Cross builds its first check around the ABCs: Airway, Breathing and Circulation.4 Airway: Is it open? Can they talk or cry? Breathing: Is the chest rising and falling? Circulation: Is there a pulse? Any major bleeding? What color is the skin? MARCH: when there is heavy bleeding Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) is the accepted standard for prehospital care on the battlefield.5 It divides care into three phases: Care Under Fire, Tactical Field Care and Tactical Evacuation Care.5 MARCH sets the order of care. While still in danger, the only treatment is control of life-threatening bleeding. Once you are safe, you work through all five letters.6 The five MARCH parts were shaped by battlefield limits such as delayed evacuation and limited supplies.7 Those are the same limits a household faces when no ambulance is coming. MARCH guides priorities in Tactical Field Care, starting with massive bleeding.56 The red frame steps through the order. M: Massive bleedingLook and sweep your gloved hands over the body for pooling or spurting blood. Stop it now: see Stopping Severe Bleeding. A: AirwayCan they talk or cry clearly? If not, look in the mouth for anything blocking it. See CPR & Choking. R: RespirationWatch both sides of the chest rise. Count breaths for a full minute. Look for wounds on the chest and back. C: CirculationFeel the pulse, press a nail bed and look at the skin. A slow nail refill can point to shock.13 H: Hypothermia and head injuryGet them off cold ground and covered. Note how alert they are. See Hypothermia, Frostbite & Heat Stroke and Head & Spine Injuries. First aid always starts with the airway. It depends on the emergency. For a person who is unresponsive and not breathing, the Red Cross says to start CPR and use an AED immediately.3 The American Heart Association's 2025 guideline starts CPR with chest compressions.19 For an injured person, TCCC's MARCH puts massive bleeding before the airway.56

Vital signs are numbers you can count with a watch, your fingers and your eyes. Normal values change with age, sex, weight, fitness and overall health.8 So compare every reading with two things: that person's own normal, and the last reading you took. Pulse Find the pulseUse your index and middle fingers. Press gently with flat fingers on the inner wrist below the base of the thumb, or at the side of the neck beside the windpipe.10Check one side of the neck only. Pressing both sides at once can slow blood flow to the head and cause fainting.10 Count for a full minuteUse a watch or clock that shows seconds. Count every beat for 60 seconds. Judge rhythm and strengthWrite "regular" or "irregular", and "strong" or "weak". CompareCheck the number against the age table below and against the person's own normal.10 Breathing Watch or feel the chest. One rise and one fall is one breath. Count for a full 60 seconds. Also note how hard they work to breathe: noisy breaths, flaring nostrils, or skin pulling in between the ribs. WHO uses fast breathing and chest indrawing as signs of pneumonia in young children.16  Short counts multiply your mistakesCounting for 15 seconds and multiplying by 4 is quick, but miss just one breath and your answer is off by 4 per minute. When the number matters, count the full minute. Count breaths without movingKeep your fingers on the wrist after you finish the pulse, and watch the chest. You can count breathing straight away without a break. Capillary refill (the nail-bed test) Press a fingernail until it turns white, then let go. Normal pink color should return in under 2 seconds.12 A time over 2 seconds can be a sign of dehydration, hypothermia, narrowed arteries in the limbs (peripheral vascular disease) or shock.1213 Normal refill is under 2 seconds.12 Slower refill can mean dehydration, hypothermia, poor circulation in the limbs or shock.13 Cold hands give slow resultsHypothermia is one of the listed causes of slow refill.13 If the hand is cold, warm it and test again, and test more than one finger. Remove colored nail polish first, or you cannot see the color change.12 Skin, alertness and the rest Skin: write three words. Color (pink, pale, gray, blue, flushed), temperature (warm, cool, hot) and moisture (dry or sweaty). Alertness: write one letter of AVPU. A = alert and talking. V = responds only to your voice. P = responds only to

Babies and children have faster pulses than adults. Use the row that matches the person in front of you.1011 Normal resting pulse by age (MedlinePlus) AgeBeats per minute Newborn, 0–1 month70–190 Infant, 1–11 months80–160 1–2 years80–130 3–4 years80–120 5–6 years75–115 7–9 years70–110 10 years to adult, including seniors60–100 Well-trained athletes40–60 The younger the child, the higher and wider the normal range.1011 Breathing rates at rest, and WHO "fast breathing" levels for children aged 2 months to 5 years AgeTypical at restWHO: fast breathing 2–11 months30–45 (age 3–6 months)50 or more 12 months to 5 yearsn/a40 or more 6–11 years18–25n/a 12–18 years12–18n/a Adults12–20n/a Table sources: WHO fast-breathing levels;1617 ages 3–6 months and 12–18 years;15 ages 6–11 years;14 adults.9 "n/a" means our sources did not list a figure for that age. Children's "normal" ranges are softer than they lookA 2011 systematic review in The Lancet found that the reference ranges in common use for children were not based on evidence. It pooled 69 studies, with heart rate data from 143,346 children and breathing data from 3,881 children, to build new age charts.18 A pulse under 60 always means something is wrong. Well-trained athletes can have a normal resting pulse of 40–60.10 That is why you record each person's own baseline while they are well. Babies and children Count breaths when the child is calm, for a full minute, and write down if they were crying. Sleeping children run slower. One school-age chart lists an awake pulse of 75–118 and a sleeping pulse of 58–90 for ages 6–11.14 Write down whether the child was awake or asleep. Know the WHO fast-breathing levels: 50 or more breaths a minute at 2–11 months, 40 or more from 12 months to 5 years.1617 Babies under 2 months have their own danger signs. For the full lists, see Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs.

Once the urgent problems are handled, ask questions. If the person cannot answer, ask family or bystanders, and look for medical ID tags, notes or medicine bottles. Use the six letters of SAMPLE as a checklist. Write each answer down as you go. The SAMPLE history: what to ask and write LetterAskWrite down S: Signs and symptoms"What is wrong? Where does it hurt?"What you see, and what they feel, in their words A: Allergies"Are you allergic to any medicine, food or insect stings?"The allergy and what happened last time M: Medicines"What do you take? When was the last dose?"Names, doses and times, including herbal products P: Past history"Any heart, lung, diabetes, seizure or other health problems? Could you be pregnant?"Conditions, past operations, pregnancy L: Last in and out"When did you last eat, drink and pee?"Times and amounts; for babies, last feed and last wet diaper E: Events"What happened just before this started?"A short story of the event, with times Ask about pain the same way every timeAsk them to rate their pain from 0 (none) to 10 (the worst they can imagine). Write the number and the time. Repeat the same question later so you can compare like with like. Women and girlsAsk about a possible pregnancy and the date of the last period in private, without family listening. Explain each step before you touch, offer a woman helper if one is there, and keep the person covered as much as you can.

Look, ask, then gently feel, working from the head down. Compare the left side with the right side as you go. Do this after the primary survey, and only once any heavy bleeding is controlled.5 Tell the person what you are about to do before every step. Head and faceLook for cuts, bumps, bruises, and blood or clear fluid from the ears or nose. Look at both pupils: are they the same size? NeckLook and feel for wounds and swelling. If they fell, were hit or have neck pain, keep the head still and read Head & Spine Injuries. ChestWatch both sides rise together. Press gently on the ribs and ask about pain. BellyPress gently in each of the four quarters. Note pain, hardness or swelling. HipsLook for wounds and ask about pain. If they fell or were crushed, do not rock or squeeze the hips: keep them still. Legs and armsCheck each limb for wounds, swelling or odd shape. Ask them to wiggle fingers and toes, and test feeling and nail refill on each side. BackSlide a gloved hand under the back where you can, then look at your glove for blood. Older and disabled peopleNormal vital signs change with age and overall health.8 Ask a caregiver or family member what is normal for this person: their usual alertness, speech, mobility and pulse. Make sure hearing aids and glasses are in place before you judge confusion. DogsA dog guarding a hurt owner can stop you helping. Ask someone the dog knows to hold it away while you work. Dogs have their own normal ranges and checks: see Dog First Aid.

Some findings mean you stop assessing and start treating. These are the ones this chapter covers. Act on these straight away You findIt can meanDo No response, and no breathing or only gaspingCardiac arrest3Start CPR and use an AED now Pooling or spurting bloodMassive bleeding, the first letter of MARCH5Stop the bleeding before anything else Nail refill over 2 secondsDehydration, hypothermia or shock1213Look again for bleeding, keep them warm, recheck often Young child breathing at or above the WHO level, or chest pulling inSigns WHO uses for pneumonia16Follow the child danger-sign chapter Pulse or breathing outside the range for the ageA change from normal10Recount for a full minute, look for the cause, recheck soon Learn the official warning-sign lists nowThis chapter teaches you how to measure. Stroke, heart attack and sepsis each have their own official warning-sign lists. Print them from your national health service while the internet works, and keep them with your notes. For sepsis, also read Infections, Sepsis & Antibiotic Facts. For babies and children, read Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs. Print and save while the internet works American Red Cross: Adult Ready Reference Cards (PDF) MedlinePlus: Vital Signs Canadian Red Cross: Check, Call, Care poster (PDF) The Canadian Red Cross notes that its poster does not replace formal first aid and CPR training.4

Write everything down, with the time. A written record shows whether the person is getting better or worse, and lets another caregiver take over without starting again. Keep one page per patient. Start a new line every time you recheck. What goes on a patient note SectionWhat to write WhoName, age, rough weight, date What happenedThe SAMPLE answers, in short lines Vital signsTime, pulse, breaths, nail refill, skin, AVPU, temperature if known FindingsWhat the head-to-toe check found, side by side Care givenEvery treatment and medicine, with dose and time ChangesBetter, worse or the same, compared with the last check Write the time firstEvery line starts with the clock time. Numbers without times cannot show a trend. Write what you counted, not what you guessed"Pulse 112, regular, weak" beats "fast pulse". Use their words for symptomsWrite "crushing pain in chest" in quotes, exactly as they said it. Recheck and add a new lineRepeat the vital signs and write them under the last set, so the change is easy to see. Keep the note with the patientIf they move or a new caregiver takes over, the note goes with them. The 30-year viewBattlefield care was shaped around delayed evacuation and limited supplies.7 In a long grid-down life, your notebook becomes the only medical record. Keep a binder with one section per family member: allergies, medicines, past illnesses, baseline vital signs and every illness or injury. Record everyone's baseline nowVital signs vary with age, sex, weight, fitness and health.8 Once a year, sit each family member down at rest. Count pulse and breathing for a full minute, test nail refill, and write the numbers with the date. A sick person's numbers mean far more when you know their healthy ones. Get hands-on trainingThe Red Cross teaches that you should give care based on what you find, within your level of training.1 Take a first aid and CPR course while classes still exist, and practice this whole chapter on each other.

Learn the order: scene safe, response and breathing (10 seconds), MARCH, vitals, SAMPLE, head-to-toe, notes Practice finding a pulse at the wrist and neck on every adult and child in the house Record each person's resting pulse, breathing rate and nail refill, with the date Put a mechanical watch with a second hand, notebooks and pencils in the medical kit Copy the patient-note table onto 20 blank pages and keep them with the kit Print the pulse and breathing tables from this chapter and tape them inside the kit lid Print official warning-sign lists for stroke, heart attack and sepsis Print the Red Cross reference cards Book a hands-on first aid and CPR course Learn your dog's resting pulse and breathing rate (see Dog First Aid)

What do you check before you touch anyone?That the scene is safe for you. Then get consent and put on gloves. How long do you spend checking a collapsed person for a response?No more than 10 seconds. Not breathing or only gasping: start CPR. What does MARCH stand for?Massive bleeding, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia (and head injury). Normal adult resting pulse and breathing?Pulse 60–100. Breathing 12–20 a minute. Normal nail refill time?Under 2 seconds. WHO fast breathing for a baby aged 2–11 months?50 or more breaths a minute. What does SAMPLE stand for?Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medicines, Past history, Last in and out, Events. What goes next to every number in your notes?The time.

Not responding and not breathing normally? Start CPR now. Gasping is not normal breathing. Shout for help, then push.1 Push hard and fast in the center of the chest. Aim for 100–120 a minute, at least 5 cm (2 in) deep in adults but not more than 6 cm (2.4 in).1 Babies, children, drowning, overdose: give breaths too. Use 30 compressions, then 2 breaths.51 Choking adult or child who cannot cough or speak: alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out. If they go limp, start CPR.3 Choking baby under 1: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand. Never abdominal thrusts.3 100–120chest compressions per minute, every age12 5–6 cmadult push depth (2–2.4 in)1 30:2compressions to breaths for one rescuer1 5 + 5back blows, then thrusts, for choking (2025)3

This chapter follows the newest rules. The American Heart Association (AHA) published its 2025 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care (ECC) on October 22, 2025, in the journal Circulation.318 CPR means cardiopulmonary resuscitation. It is chest compressions, with or without rescue breaths, for a person whose heart has stopped pumping.1 The guideline for babies and children was written by the AHA together with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).2 International experts in the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) reviewed the same science in 2025.7 What is new in 2025 (AHA and AAP) Topic2025 rule Choking, awake adult or childAlternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts3 Choking, infant5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand32 Infant CPR hands2 thumbs with your hands around the chest, or the heel of one hand. The 2-finger method was removed.9 Chain of survivalOne chain for all ages, in and out of hospital3 Opioid overdoseGuidance now includes naloxone use by the public3 Keep a paper copyGuidelines change. The 2025 version replaced earlier advice on choking and on infant CPR.3 Print this chapter now, while you can still check it against the official pages.

s.h: 🔎 Spot cardiac arrest and get help
s.x: Check fast, then act. A person in cardiac arrest does not respond and is not breathing normally, or is only gasping.1 Make sure the scene is safeLook for danger to you first: traffic, fire, live wires, deep water, smoke. The AHA choking algorithm starts with this check too.10 Tap and shoutTap their shoulders hard and shout, "Are you OK?" No answer means unresponsive.1 Look at the chest and faceNo breathing, or only gasping, means start CPR.1 Shout for helpSend one person for help and for an automated external defibrillator (AED), if one exists.5 Start pushing right awayDo not wait for help to arrive. Begin chest compressions now.5 Gasping is not breathingSlow, noisy gasps can happen after the heart stops. Treat "only gasping" the same as "not breathing" and start CPR.1 Do not hunt for a pulseThe public is not asked to check a pulse. Unresponsive and not breathing normally is enough to start.1 Feeling for a pulse wastes seconds. In a long outage, "call for help" may mean a two-way radio, a whistle or a runner. Plan this now in Radios: Ham, GMRS, CB & Listening. If the person is breathing, use Assessing a Sick or Injured Person instead.

Your hands do the pumping. Good CPR is deep, fast, steady and has very few pauses.14 Lay them on their back on something firmA floor or flat ground works. Compressions work best on a firm surface.1 Place your handsPut the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone, in the center of the chest. Put your other hand on top.1 Lock your armsKneel close. Keep your elbows straight and your shoulders right over your hands, so your body weight does the work. Push deep and fastPush at least 5 cm (2 in) but not more than 6 cm (2.4 in), 100 to 120 times a minute.1 Let the chest rise all the wayDo not lean on the chest between pushes. Full recoil lets the heart refill.1 Add breaths if you canIf you are trained and willing, give 2 breaths after every 30 pushes.1 If not, keep pushing without stopping.5  Push to a songThe AHA says people remember the right pace better when they train to the beat of "Stayin' Alive" or another familiar song at 100–120 beats a minute.6 Push down to the red line, then let the chest rise fully. The hands move at 110 per minute, inside the 100–120 range. For children and babies, push at least one third of the chest depth.12 Do Push on the lower half of the breastbone Use a firm floor or the ground Let the chest come all the way back up Swap pushers about every 2 minutes Keep pauses for breaths very short Don't Lean on the chest between pushes Push shallow "polite" compressions Push deeper than 6 cm (2.4 in) on an adult Stop to check for a pulse Do CPR on a soft mattress Every item above comes from the 2025 adult guideline.1 Keep any pause under 10 seconds.1  Swap pushers about every 2 minutes. That keeps compressions strong as people tire.1 Swap fast, during the breaths if you can. UK guidance matchesThe Resuscitation Council UK 2025 adult guideline also sets a depth of at least 5 cm and no more than 6 cm.8 CPR on women and girlsThe hand position is the same for everyone: the center of the chest.5 Do not let worry about touching a woman's chest delay CPR. Push on the breastbone, between the breasts.

s.h: 🫁 Hands-Only CPR or CPR with breaths?
s.x: Hands-Only CPR has two steps. Call for help (or send someone), then push hard and fast in the center of the chest.5 The AHA recommends it for teens and adults who suddenly collapse outside a hospital, such as at home, at work or in a park.5 Some people need breaths as well. The AHA recommends compressions plus breaths for all infants (up to age 1), children (up to puberty), drowning victims, drug overdose victims and people who collapse from breathing problems.5 If you are trained and willing, give 30:2 to adults too.1 ILCOR still suggests the 30:2 ratio in its 2025 review.7 Hands-Only CPR is for teens and adults who suddenly collapse. Babies, children and anyone who stopped breathing first (drowning, overdose, breathing problems) need breaths as well.52 How to give rescue breaths Open the airwayTilt the head back with one hand on the forehead. Lift the chin with two fingers of the other hand.1 Seal your mouth over theirsFor an adult or child, pinch the nose shut. For a baby, cover the mouth and nose with your mouth.2 Breathe for 1 secondBlow just enough to see the chest rise.1 Give a second breath, then push againGo straight back to compressions. The two breaths should take less than 10 seconds.1 Opioid overdoseFor a suspected opioid overdose, the 2025 guidelines include naloxone use by the public.3 Give naloxone if you have it, and give CPR with breaths.5 See Poisoning & Toxic Exposures. You need a certificate before you are allowed to do CPR. Hands-Only CPR is two steps: call for help, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest.5 An AHA consumer survey found many people still wrongly believe CPR requires special training.13 CPR on TV shows you how it is done. The AHA reports that TV depictions of Hands-Only CPR are often misleading.12 Learn from the official guideline numbers and hands-on practice instead. Get these before you need them A CPR face shield or pocket mask for every first aid kit A CPR training manikin, adult and infant if you can Naloxone, if anyone in your group uses opioids, through a doctor or pharmacy where it is legal A printed copy of this chapter in each kit

s.h: 👶 Children and babies: what is different
s.x: Babies and children need breaths with compressions. The AHA recommends CPR with breaths for all infants and for children up to puberty.5 CPR by age (AHA 2025) WhatAdultChildInfant AgeAfter puberty1 year to pubertyUnder 1 year Rate100–120/min100–120/min100–120/min Depth5–6 cm (2–2.4 in)About 5 cm (2 in)About 4 cm (1.5 in) Hands2 hands1 or 2 hands2 thumbs around chest, or heel of 1 hand 1 rescuer30:230:230:2 2 rescuers30:215:215:2 Adult figures come from the adult guideline.1 Child and infant figures come from the pediatric guideline, which sets the depth at at least one third of the chest's front-to-back depth.2 Alone with no phone? If you did not see the child collapse, give about 2 minutes of CPR before you leave to get help.2 Infant CPR (under 1 year) Lay the baby on a firm, flat surfaceA table or the floor works. Compressions need a firm surface.2 Wrap your hands around the chestPut both thumbs side by side on the center of the chest, just below the nipple line. Wrap your fingers around the back.2 Or use the heel of one handIf your hands cannot reach around the chest, push with the heel of one hand.2 Push about 4 cm (1.5 in)That is at least one third of the chest depth, at 100–120 a minute. Let the chest rise fully.2 Give gentle breathsCover the mouth and nose. Puff just enough to make the chest rise. Use 30:2 alone, 15:2 with two rescuers.2 Push on a baby's chest with two fingers. The 2025 guidelines removed the two-finger method because it often failed to reach the right depth.29 Use two thumbs with your hands around the chest. If you cannot reach around, use the heel of one hand.2 Newborns at birth are differentA baby who needs help in the first minutes after birth follows a separate neonatal guideline. There, the two-thumb method with hands wrapped around the chest is preferred.11 See Newborn Care: The First 28 Days. Practice on a doll, not a babyNever practice compressions or back blows on a real child. The AHA's Infant CPR Anytime kit has a practice infant manikin and was updated for the 2025 guidelines.15

Severe choking is silent. The person cannot speak, cough or breathe. They may clutch their throat with their hands.1 Mild choking is noisy. If they can cough hard or speak, let them keep coughing and stay with them. Act if the cough becomes weak or stops.8 Ask "Are you choking?"If they nod and cannot speak, act now. Tell them you are going to help. Shout for helpSend someone for help. Do not leave the person.10 Give 5 back blowsStand behind and to the side. Support their chest with one hand and lean them forward. Strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand.8 Give 5 abdominal thrustsStand behind them and wrap your arms around the waist. Put a fist just above the belly button, well below the breastbone. Grab it with your other hand and pull sharply in and up.1 Repeat 5 and 5Keep alternating until the object comes out or the person stops responding.3 If they go limp, start CPRLower them to the ground and begin compressions. Each time you open the airway, look in the mouth. Remove an object only if you can see it.117 The highlighted box shows the order: 5 back blows, then 5 thrusts, over and over. Infants get chest thrusts with the heel of one hand, never abdominal thrusts.32 Back blows are outdated. Only use abdominal thrusts (the "Heimlich"). Since 2025 the AHA says to alternate 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts for awake adults and children.3 The UK guideline also starts with back blows.8 Pregnant and chokingDo not press on a pregnant belly. Give chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts: hands on the center of the breastbone, pulling straight back.110 Larger or seated peopleIf you cannot get your arms around someone's waist, use chest thrusts instead.1 See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People. No blind finger sweepsDo not poke your fingers into the throat to search for the object. You can push it deeper. Remove it only if you can see it.12

Babies get back blows and chest thrusts only. Abdominal thrusts are not recommended for infants.3 Lay the baby face down on your forearmHold the jaw with your hand to support the head. Keep the head lower than the chest. Rest your arm on your thigh.2 Give 5 back blowsStrike firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.3 Turn the baby face upSupport the back of the head and sandwich the baby between your arms. Keep the head lower than the chest.2 Give 5 chest thrustsUse the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, just below the nipple line.32 Repeat 5 and 5Keep going until the object comes out or the baby stops responding.3 If the baby goes limp, start infant CPRUse the infant CPR steps above. Look in the mouth before each set of breaths and remove only what you can see.2 Never give abdominal thrusts to a babyFor any baby under 1 year, use back blows and chest thrusts only.3 The chest thrusts now use the heel of one hand, not two fingers.2 Prevent it firstRescue is the backup plan. The prevention side (food sizes, small objects, supervision at meals) is in Keeping Kids Safe: Drowning, Fire, Poison, Strangers. Dogs are not small peopleAll the numbers in this chapter come from human guidelines.12 Dog CPR and dog choking use different positions and methods. A frightened, choking dog may also bite. Learn the dog methods in Dog First Aid, and keep children back.

s.h: ⏱️ How long to keep going, and when to stop
s.x: Keep pushing until help takes over. The AHA tells the public to continue chest compressions until help arrives.5 If an AED arrives, turn it on and follow the voice prompts.5 Keep pushing while someone else sets it up. If the person wakes, moves with purpose or starts breathing normally, stop compressions. Stay with them and watch their breathing closely.1 A breathing person who is not awake can be rolled onto their side in the recovery position.8 You may stop CPR when The person shows clear signs of life, such as normal breathing or purposeful movement1 A trained helper takes over5 An AED is ready: follow its voice prompts5 The scene becomes unsafe for you10 You are too exhausted to continue and no one can take over8 The public guidance gives no time limit. It says to keep going until help arrives.5 It does not set a rule for a place where no help can come. Decide in advance, as a household, who will make that call. Use teams. Swap pushers about every 2 minutes so compressions stay strong for as long as you continue.1 The 30-year viewCPR is one link in a chain of survival that the AHA now uses for every age and setting.3 If no ambulance or hospital can be reached, the links after CPR are not available. Back blows, thrusts and CPR need nothing but trained hands, so train every capable person. Talk about wishes nowSome older or very ill people have clear wishes about resuscitation. Ask while they can tell you, and write it down. When CPR does not work, see Death, Dying & Handling the Dead Safely.

Train your older kids. The 2025 AHA guidelines say children 12 years old or older can learn CPR.3 Choking can turn into cardiac arrest. The AHA says knowing how to help someone who is choking, and when to start CPR, can prevent a heart crisis.17 Practice while help still exists Use an AHA Hands-Only CPR kiosk if one is near you.14 Use the AHA Family & Friends CPR course materials, updated for 2025.16 Practice infant CPR and choking on a manikin with Infant CPR Anytime.15 Push to the metronome above for 2 full minutes. Feel how tiring it is. Watch and download while the internet works AHA: Learn Hands-Only CPR (video and pace guide) AHA: Hands-Only CPR kiosk locations AHA: 2025 adult choking algorithm (PDF) AHA: Highlights of the 2025 Guidelines (PDF) Never practice on a real personDo not push on the chest, or give real back blows or thrusts, to anyone who is breathing and well. Use a manikin, a doll or a firm cushion. Run a two-minute family drillOne person lies on the floor as the patient. Others practice: check, shout, send a runner. Then push on a manikin or firm cushion beside them, and swap at 2 minutes. For choking, only mime the hand positions on a standing adult.

Learn the two steps of Hands-Only CPR: call for help, push hard and fast Push on a firm cushion or manikin to the metronome for 2 full minutes Take a hands-on CPR and first aid class while classes still run Teach CPR and choking rescue to everyone 12 and older Put a CPR face shield or pocket mask in every first aid kit Print the choking diagram and tape it up near where you eat Practice infant back blows and chest thrusts on a doll if you have a baby Ask a doctor or pharmacist about naloxone if anyone uses opioids Agree who calls for help, who pushes and who swaps in at 2 minutes Ask older relatives about their wishes for CPR and write them down

How fast do you push?100–120 times a minute, for every age. How deep for an adult?At least 5 cm (2 in), but not more than 6 cm (2.4 in). Who needs breaths with compressions?Babies, children, drowning, overdose and breathing problems. 30:2. Choking adult who cannot cough or speak?Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts. Choking baby under 1?5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand. Never abdominal thrusts. How do you push on a baby's chest since 2025?Two thumbs with your hands around the chest, or the heel of one hand. Not two fingers. Pregnant and choking?Chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. The choking person goes limp?Lower them down and start CPR. Look in the mouth before breaths. No blind finger sweeps.

Older people face the highest risk when the grid fails. After Hurricane Maria, poor and elderly people had the highest risk of dying, and older men had a 35% higher death risk than expected.1 Interrupted care kills slowly. A survey after Maria linked about one third of excess deaths to delayed or interrupted medical care.2 List every powered medical device now. Over 3 million US Medicare patients use electricity-dependent equipment. Ask each person's provider for a power outage plan.34 Name a main helper and a backup for every person who cannot move fast, and practice twice a year, by day and by night.5 Pack the small aids people forget: hearing aids with extra batteries, glasses, contact lenses, a cane and a written medicine list.6 35%higher death risk for older men after Hurricane Maria1 1 in 3Maria excess deaths linked to interrupted medical care2 3M+US Medicare patients on electricity-dependent equipment3 26%of adults with disabilities had nowhere to go (vs 15%)9

s.h: 📉 Who dies first when the power fails
s.x: The disaster record points one way. Older and chronically ill people carry the most risk when power, water and medical care stop.18 This chapter covers what that means for the people in your care. It gives the documented facts first, then the actions. Hurricane Maria, Puerto Rico, 2017 Surveyed households went an average of 84 days without power, 68 days without water and 41 days without cell phone service.2 In remote areas, 83% of homes had no electricity for the whole period studied, from landfall to December 31, 2017.2 The first official death toll was 64.2 A George Washington University study, commissioned by the governor, estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018.1 Many of those people were not killed by wind or water. The household survey linked about one third of excess deaths to delayed or interrupted medical care.2 Poor and elderly people faced the highest risk.1 The official death toll shows who a disaster killed. After Maria the first official count was 64.2 The George Washington University study estimated 2,975 excess deaths, with poor and elderly people at highest risk.1 Deaths from missed care kept coming for months: the study counted through February 2018. Texas winter storm, February 2021 Texas health officials counted 246 storm-related deaths. About two-thirds were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia (dangerously low body temperature).7 The final count rose from 210 to 246.7 Cold exposure killed more people than every other cause combined. The Hurricane Rita evacuation, 2005 The evacuation killed more people than the storm did. Over 100 of the at least 119 deaths attributed to Rita were linked to the evacuation itself.8 At least 10% of evacuation deaths were linked to overheating in vehicles. Medical examiners suspected overheating or a worsened chronic illness in about another 50%.8 A bus carrying nursing-home residents caught fire in the evacuation traffic, and about two dozen people died.8 More on this in Stay or Go? The 30-year view: everyone becomes the elderOver 30 years, a 45-year-old parent becomes 75 and a 60-year-old becomes 90. Plan as if every adult in your group will need this chapter one day.Write each person's needs down now, while they can tell you, and update the list at every family drill. See Building Your Group.

s.h: 🔌 Oxygen, CPAP and other powered equipment
s.x: Many people stay alive or mobile on machines that plug into the wall. In the US, over 3 million Medicare patients have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment.3 Over 4.6 million rely on that equipment or on services such as dialysis, oxygen or home health care.3 Oxygen concentrators, powered wheelchairs and home dialysis all depend on electricity.3 Other common examples are continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machines for sleep apnea, electric hospital beds, and feeding or suction pumps. Each one stops when its battery is empty. Make the plan before the outage. Ready.gov says to talk to your medical provider about a power outage plan for medical devices that run on electricity.4 List every device and every userInclude your family and your street. Write the person's name, the device, and what the provider says happens if it stops. Find the real battery timeRead the manual and write the hours on a label on the device. Then test a full charge while the device runs, and write that time too. Ask the provider for an outage planCover each device and each refrigerated medicine.4 Ask what to do if the device cannot run at all. Choose one safe power sourceA generator runs outdoors only, more than 6 m (20 ft) from windows, doors and vents.10 Decide where to goIf the home gets too hot or too cold, and it is safe to travel, go to a place with heat or cooling.4 Choose it now, with a route. Generator distance from the CDC; the garage warning from the US Consumer Product Safety Commission; the move-early rule from Ready.gov.10114 Generators kill families who run them indoorsNever use a generator inside a home or garage, even if the doors and windows are open.11 In the April 2025 Spain blackout, police in Galicia investigated carbon monoxide from a generator after an older couple and their adult son died at home.12Put a battery-powered carbon monoxide (CO) alarm near every sleeping area, and replace it every 5 years.10 See Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer. Oxygen and open flamesLight the house with flashlights, not candles. Ready.gov lists candles as a fire risk during outages.4Keep every flame, stove and smoker away from oxygen equipment. Ask the oxygen supplier now for its written fire-safety rules and keep them with the equipment. Label every oxygen cylinderAsk the supplier how long each cylinder lasts at the person's prescribed flow rate. Write that

s.h: 💊 Medicines: the clock starts when the power stops
s.x: Start with a written list. The Red Cross lists a medication list and medical information among the documents to copy for your kit.6 Write each medicine's name, dose, times and what it is for. Keep at least 7 days on hand. The current Red Cross survival kit list says a 7-day supply of medications and medical items.6 An older Red Cross checklist says a 1-month supply.15 Ask the doctor or pharmacist how to build a larger emergency supply legally. Ready.gov also lists non-prescription medicines: pain relievers, anti-diarrhea medicine, antacids and laxatives.16 Medicines that need a fridge The one-day rule: if the power is out for more than a day, throw away medicine that should be refrigerated, unless the label says otherwise.4 If a life depends on that medicine, talk to a doctor or pharmacist and use it only until a new supply is available.4 Insulin has its own rule. Vials and cartridges, opened or unopened, may be left unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days. Pens and other products differ, so read the label.13 Replace insulin that has been exposed to extreme heat or cold.13 For any other medicine kept at the wrong temperature, check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, provider or the maker.14 One-day rule from Ready.gov; 7-day supply from the Red Cross; 28-day insulin limit from the FDA; 84 days from the Hurricane Maria household survey.46132 Long-term medicine plansMedicines for heart disease, diabetes, lung disease and other long-term conditions are covered in Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies. How long stored medicines stay good is in Medicines: Shelf Life & Expiration Facts.

s.h: 🌡️ Heat and cold hit older bodies hardest
s.x: Older adults and young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures, says Ready.gov.4 The record agrees. In the 2021 Texas storm, about two-thirds of 246 deaths came from cold exposure.7 In the Rita evacuation, at least 10% of evacuation deaths were linked to overheating in vehicles.8 Move early, not late. If the home becomes too hot or too cold and it is safe to travel, go to a place with heat or cooling.4 Decide while roads and daylight still allow it. Never heat a home with a gas oven or stove. Ready.gov warns against it because of carbon monoxide.4 Do Use flashlights, not candles4 Move frail people early to a place with heat or cooling4 Check on older neighbors in person4 Keep a battery CO alarm by each bed area10 Don't Heat the house with a gas oven or stove4 Run a generator inside, even with doors open11 Leave a frail person in a hot, stuck car8 Wait until the roads are full to leave Babies and elders in one roomReady.gov names both older adults and young children as especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures.4 Keep them together in the warmest room in winter, or the coolest in summer, so one adult can watch both.See Staying Warm Without Heat and Staying Cool Without Air Conditioning. Visit, do not just callReady.gov puts checking on neighbors on its list of things to do in an outage.4 Knock on the doors of older people who live alone or use medical devices. A dead phone tells you nothing.Signs and treatment of hypothermia and heat stroke are in Hypothermia, Frostbite & Heat Stroke.

s.h: 🦯 Mobility, hearing, vision and communication aids
s.x: Small aids decide whether someone can walk, hear a warning or read a label. The Red Cross kit list includes hearing aids with extra batteries, glasses, contact lenses, syringes and a cane.6 Ready.gov adds prescription eyeglasses and contact lens solution.16 It also says to replace expired items and to re-think your needs every year.16 Aids to pack for each older or disabled person ItemPack thisListed by Hearing aidsThe aids plus extra batteriesRed Cross6 GlassesPrescription eyeglassesRed Cross, Ready.gov616 Contact lensesLenses plus lens solutionRed Cross, Ready.gov616 CaneThe cane the person usesRed Cross6 SyringesThe syringes they needRed Cross6 Medicines7-day supply and a written listRed Cross6 Communication Make the plan usable by the person it is for. The CDC says accessible planning and communication may help close the preparedness gaps for people with disabilities.9 Write a card for each person. Put their name, conditions, medicines, allergies and devices on it, and how they communicate best: speech, writing, sign language or pictures. Keep one copy on them and one in the kit. Know what is normal for them. Normal vital signs change with age and overall health.17 Ask family what this person's usual alertness, speech and walking look like, and write it on the card. Before you decide someone is newly confused, check that their hearing aids and glasses are in and working. How to check a sick person step by step is in Assessing a Sick or Injured Person. Light, water and a toilet within reach Give each person their own flashlight with extra batteries, and keep it within reach of the bed. Ready.gov says to use flashlights, not candles.4 Water is heavy. One liter weighs 1 kg and one US gallon weighs 8.33 lb.18 So a full 19 L (5-gallon) jug weighs about 19 kg (42 lb). Keep small containers within reach of anyone who cannot lift that. Put a toilet within reach of anyone who cannot walk far, with its own handwashing water. See Toilets Without Water. Learn the hands-on skills nowAsk the person's nurse, doctor or therapist to show you, while help still exists:How to move them from bed to chairHow to prevent pressure soresHow to make their home safer against fallsHow to handle dementia day to dayWrite down what they teach and keep it with this book. Bed care and pressure sores are also in Nursing the Sick at Home.

s.h: 🚪 Moving people who cannot move fast
s.x: People with disabilities face disasters more often. In a June 2024 CDC survey, 80% of adults with disabilities had lived through at least one natural disaster, against 70% of adults without disabilities.9 They also have fewer ways out. 26% said they had nowhere to go, against 15%. 20% named the cost of evacuating, against 14%.9 Plans were rare on both sides: only 48% of adults with disabilities and 46% without had an emergency plan.9 Adults with disabilities live through more disasters and face more barriers to leaving, but plan at about the same rate.9 Name a main helper and a backupNFPA says to plan for anyone with a disability and to assign a backup in case the main helper is not home.5 Check every meeting placeFEMA says to make meeting places accessible for household members with disabilities.19 Check steps, slopes and distance. Keep the car readyKeep at least half a tank of gas at all times, and a full tank if an evacuation seems likely.20 Leave earlyGo early enough that severe weather cannot trap you.20 Long waits in traffic were where Rita evacuees overheated.8 Pack for a long, hot waitCarry water and a way to stay cool for every person in the car, plus the aids and medicines listed above.86 Practice with themRun the drill twice a year, by day and by night, as NFPA advises for fire escape plans.5 Two ways out of every roomNFPA's escape plan asks for two ways out.5 For someone who uses a wheelchair or walker, check that both ways are actually usable: no steps, no narrow gaps, nothing stacked in the way.Full family plans are in The Family Emergency Plan, and grab-and-go lists in Go-Bags for Every Family Member. Assistance dogs and petsPack the dog's own kit. The Red Cross lists a collar, leash, ID, food, carrier and bowl.6Temporary public shelters may not allow animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay before you need them.21 See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

Older adults get sicker from food poisoning. Adults 65 and older are in the CDC's higher-risk group.22 Get care early for severe signs: bloody diarrhea, a fever over 38.9°C (102°F), frequent vomiting, signs of dehydration, or diarrhea that lasts more than 3 days.22 Safe food without a fridge is in Food Safety Without a Refrigerator. Give them your best-treated water. In people with weak immune systems, the parasite Cryptosporidium can cause diarrhea for weeks to months, with wasting.23 See Disinfecting Water. Protein does not shrink with age The adult recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for protein stays at 0.8 g per kg of body weight from age 19 to over 70.24 For a 60 kg (132 lb) person, that is 48 g of protein a day. For calories and special diets, see Calories & Nutrition and Special Diets. Choking in a chair or wheelchair If you cannot get your arms around someone's waist, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.25 Full adult choking steps are in CPR & Choking. Download these pages while the internet worksSave or print these official pages and keep them with this book:Ready.gov: Power OutagesHHS emPOWER Program: FAQNFPA: How to Make a Home Fire Escape Plan

List every person in your home and street who uses a powered medical device Write the battery time on each device, then test a full charge Ask each person's doctor for a power outage plan for devices and cold medicines Pack at least 7 days of medicines and a written medicine list for each person Add spare hearing-aid batteries, spare glasses, lens solution and a cane to the kit Name a main helper and a backup for everyone who cannot move fast Check that every meeting place and both ways out work for a wheelchair or walker Put a battery CO alarm near every sleeping area Put a flashlight with spare batteries beside every bed Ask a nurse or therapist to teach you transfers, pressure-sore prevention and dementia care

Who had the highest risk of dying after Hurricane Maria?Poor and elderly people. Older men had a 35% higher death risk than expected. What share of Maria's excess deaths was linked to interrupted care?About one third. Refrigerated medicine after more than a day without power?Throw it away unless the label says otherwise. If a life depends on it, ask a doctor or pharmacist and use it until new supply arrives. How long can insulin vials stay out of the fridge?Up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F). Pens differ: read the label. Where does a generator go?Outdoors, more than 6 m (20 ft) from windows, doors and vents. Never in a garage, even with the door open. How many helpers for each person who cannot move fast?A main helper and a backup. Which small aids do people forget?Hearing aids with extra batteries, glasses, contact lenses and solution, a cane, and the medicine list.

Build the kit in three tiers: 2 weeks, 3 months, 1 year. The Red Cross advises a 2-week supply at home, and Puerto Rico households averaged 84 days without power after Hurricane Maria.12 Measure first, then multiply. Count what your child really uses in a day, then multiply by 14, 91 and 365. Your child's own count beats any average. Formula needs safe water and fuel. CDC says to use bottled water until tap water is declared safe, and water at about 70°C (158°F) for young or vulnerable babies.3 Children's medicines get their own pouch. Never give aspirin to children. Pack a non-mercury, non-glass thermometer.45 Every bucket and basin needs a lid. Of the children under 5 who drowned at home in a CPSC count, 82% were under age 2.6 2 weekshome supply the Red Cross advises1 84 daysaverage time without power, Puerto Rico 20172 70°C(158°F) water to mix formula for young babies3 82%of child drownings at home were under age 26

s.h: 🎒 The kit at a glance: eight bins
s.x: Pack the kit by job, not by store aisle. When you are tired and it is dark, you want to grab "the diaper bin", not search five boxes. Start from the official lists. Ready.gov names infant formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream.8 The Red Cross adds baby food and says to copy important documents.1 Ready.gov also says to keep supplies in airtight plastic bags, packed in one or two easy-to-carry containers.8 One bin per job does that for a baby. Feeding, diaper and paperwork items follow the Ready.gov and Red Cross lists. Sorting them into bins is a packing method.81 Bin 1, Feed: formula or nursing supplies, bottles or cups, brush, soap, pot, fuel Bin 2, Diapers: diapers in two sizes, wipes or washcloths, rash cream, soap, lidded pail Bin 3, Clothes: current size, next size up, warm layer, sun layer Bin 4, Sleep and night: sleep space, headlamp, spare batteries, battery CO alarm Bin 5, Medicine: children's pouch, thermometer, ORS packets, dose card Bin 6, Carry: carrier, car seat manual, photos of car seat labels Bin 7, Papers: child ID card, copies of records, health card, cash Bin 8, Water: bottled water marked "formula only" Label the outside, three timesWrite the bin number, its job and the clothing size or date on two sides and the lid. You should be able to read it by flashlight from across the room. A 3-year kit, not a 3-day kitA newborn becomes a 3-year-old who walks, eats family food and may be out of diapers. Ready.gov says to re-think your needs every year and update the kit as your family changes.8In a long outage there is no calendar reminder. Tie the full review to a fixed date, such as the child's birthday.

Use three tiers, and tie each one to a real event. 2 weeks: the Red Cross advises a 2-week supply for home and 3 days for evacuation.1 3 months: after Hurricane Maria in 2017, surveyed Puerto Rico households averaged 84 days without power and 68 days without water.2 1 year: power came back to the whole island about 11 months after the storm.9 Short outages happen too. In the February 2021 Texas freeze, more than 4.5 million Texans lost power, some for up to 4 days.10 Bars are to scale: the full axis is 1 year. Your tiers (2 weeks, 3 months, 1 year) match these real durations.10129 Measure, then multiply Your child's real daily count is the only number that fits your child. Get it in 3 days. Count for 3 daysTally every diaper, wipe, feed, outfit and bib. Tape the tally sheet inside a cupboard door. Find the daily averageAdd the three days and divide by 3. Round up, never down. Multiply for each tierTimes 14 for 2 weeks, times 91 for 3 months, times 365 for 1 year. Fill the 2-week tier firstFinish one tier before you start the next. A full 2 weeks beats a half-filled year. Re-count every monthWrite the new count and date on the tally sheet. Adjust the next purchase. Daily count times days (arithmetic only: use your own child's count) Used per day2 weeks (14 d)3 months (91 d)1 year (365 d) 11491365 4563641,460 6845462,190 81127282,920 101409103,650 121681,0924,380 A year of single-use items is a large pile. At 8 diapers a day, a year is 2,920 diapers. Compare that with a reusable stash (see the diaper section below). Water for the baby Count the baby as a full person in your water plan. CDC advises at least 4 liters (1 gallon) per person per day, for 2 weeks if possible, and more for pregnant women, sick people and hot climates.11 University of Florida Extension says to store more water when children or nursing mothers live in the home.12 Ready.gov says very hot weather can double water needs.13 The arithmetic per person: 4 liters (1 gallon) a day is 53 liters (14 gallons) for 2 weeks, 344 liters (91 gallons) for 3 months and 1,382 liters (365 gallons) for a year. Storage methods are in Storing Water for Months & Years.

Pack for how your baby eats today, and pack a backup. Feeding changes fast between birth and age 3. Breastfed babies Direct breastfeeding needs no mixing water, no bottles and no fuel. The nursing mother does need extra water, so plan more for her.12 The facts on supply, latch, blocked ducts and relactation are in Breastfeeding: The Survival Superpower. The mother is part of the baby kitPut her water bottle, snacks, breast pads and nursing clothes in the feeding bin, within reach of where she feeds. UF Extension lists nursing mothers among the people who need more stored water.12 Formula-fed babies Formula is only as safe as the water you mix it with. CDC says to prepare formula with bottled water until officials say tap water is safe.3 If you must boil water, CDC says to boil it for 1 minute. For young or vulnerable infants, mix powdered formula with water at about 70°C (158°F).3 Boiling does not remove chemicals. CDC says chemically contaminated water cannot be made safe by boiling, disinfecting or filtering.3 So the formula bin holds more than formula: Formula of the exact type your baby uses, with the use-by date written on the lid Bottled water marked "formula only" A pot with a lid, a stove and fuel to boil water Bottles or cups, a bottle brush, dish soap and a washing basin A clean towel and a lidded box for drying clean parts The full method, and what to do when formula runs out, is in Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out. Stored water has a dateCDC says to label and date stored water and replace it every 6 months. Keep it at 10–21°C (50–70°F), out of sunlight.11 Rotate the "formula only" water on the same day you rotate the rest. Toddlers and solid food The Red Cross lists baby food in the kit.1 Add spoons, bowls and an open cup your child can hold. First foods and foods to avoid are in First Foods for Babies Without Stores. Learn infant choking first aid before solids start. The 2025 AHA guidelines use back blows and heel-of-hand chest thrusts for infants.25 Practice the steps in CPR & Choking. DoKeep a separate stock of bottled water for formula3Store fuel for boiling with the feeding binPack two of every bottle partEmpty and turn over the washing basin after use Don'tMix formula with water that may hold fuel or chemicals, even boiled3Leave a basin of wash water standing where a toddler can reach it7Switch formula types in a crisis without a reaso

Diaper supplies are health supplies. Ready.gov lists diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream in the basic kit.8 A healthy-looking child can still spread germs. CDC says hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route, and 70% of infections in children under 6 cause no symptoms.16 So wash your hands with soap after every change. WHO estimates that poor hand hygiene caused 384,000 diarrhea deaths in 2019.17 Unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene caused 395,000 deaths in children under 5 that year.17 What goes in the diaper bin: Diapers in the current size and the next size up Wipes, or washcloths and a small water bottle Diaper rash cream8 Bar soap and a handwashing jug A wipeable changing mat A pail with a tight lid, plus trash bags If the baby seems well, you can skip handwashing after a diaper change. Most hepatitis A infections in children under 6 (70%) have no symptoms, and the virus spreads by the fecal-oral route.16 Wash every time. A diaper pail can drown a toddlerCPSC counted 434 in-home drowning deaths of children under 5 in 2006–2010. 82% were under age 2, and 81% involved bathtubs or bath products.6KidsHealth says drowning can happen in less than 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water. Never leave water containers unattended.7 Put a lid on every pail and empty basins straight away. More in Keeping Kids Safe. Cloth stash math, washing with little water and rash treatment are in Cloth Diapers & Baby Hygiene.

s.h: 👕 Clothes that grow with the child
s.x: Children grow out of clothes, so store sizes ahead. Ready.gov says to re-think kit needs every year and update the kit as your family changes.8 Temperature is the reason clothes matter. Ready.gov notes that young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures during power outages.14 A size ladder keeps the next size ready. Ready.gov's yearly review is the minimum. The monthly fit check is this book's packing method.8 How many outfits Outfits needed = outfits used per day times days between washes, plus spares for wash day. Example: 3 a day, washing every 3 days, is 9 outfits plus spares. Use your 3-day tally for the "per day" number. If you wash less often, the outfit count goes up by the same arithmetic. Sizes, by fit Pack by fit, not by the age on the label. Try clothes on the child when you can. Weigh and measure monthly. Write the numbers on the health card. Keep outgrown clothes clean and labeled. They serve a younger child, a trade or cloth for repairs. Warm layers and sun layers both. Cold-house methods are in Staying Warm Without Heat. Every dayDress the child for the room you are in, not for the season on the calendar. Every monthWeigh, measure and check fit. Shift bins when clothes get tight. Every seasonBefore the cold or hot season, check the layers you need. Every birthdayDo the full kit review Ready.gov advises each year.8 Buy bigger sizes while stores existSecondhand children's clothes in the next sizes up cost little now. Wash, label by size and pack them in airtight bags, as Ready.gov advises for kit supplies.8

s.h: 😴 Sleep, light and air at night
s.x: Night feeds and changes need light that cannot start a fire. Ready.gov advises flashlights, not candles, in a power outage.14 A headlamp keeps both hands free for the baby. What goes in the night bin: A headlamp and a flashlight, with spare batteries The baby's own sleep space, set up to the safe-sleep rules Sleep clothing for the season A battery carbon monoxide (CO) alarm Put a battery CO alarm near where the baby sleeps. CDC advises battery-operated CO alarms and says to replace them every 5 years.15 Generators stay outsideCDC says to run generators outdoors, more than 6 m (20 feet) from windows, doors and vents, and never in a home or garage.15 A baby cannot tell you they feel ill. Read Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer. Safe-sleep facts on the sleep surface, position and bedding are in Newborn Care: The First 28 Days. Read them before you choose what goes in this bin.

s.h: 🚗 Car seats, carriers and moving with a child
s.x: Your car kit is a second baby kit. Ready.gov advises keeping kits at home, at work and in the car.8 Car seats Photograph every label on the seat. Keep the photos with your kit papers. Keep the manual in a zip bag in the car kit. It is the only instruction book written for that exact seat. Write the seat's limits on the health card, next to the child's latest weight and height. Compare them at each monthly weigh-in. If a used seat has no labels or manual, you cannot check its limits. Do not rely on it. Carriers and loads A carrier keeps your hands free, but the baby counts as load. Military research recommends loads of 30% of body mass or less to avoid a drop in performance.22 Weigh yourselfUse a bathroom scale. Write the number down. Weigh the full loadStep on again holding the baby in the carrier and wearing the bag. Subtract and divideThe difference divided by your weight is your load share. Lighten if over 30%Move items to another adult or a cart.22 Example arithmetic: 30% of 60 kg (132 lb) is 18 kg (40 lb). A 9 kg (20 lb) baby plus a 9 kg (20 lb) bag reaches that line. A walking toddler can carry a little. The National Safety Council says a child's backpack should weigh no more than 5–10% of the child's weight.23 For a 14 kg (31 lb) child, that is 0.7–1.4 kg (1.5–3 lb). What a toddler can carryA small water bottle, a snack, a comfort toy and a copy of their ID card. Keep it within the 5–10% line.23 Full family bags are in Go-Bags for Every Family Member.

s.h: 💊 Infant medicines, thermometer and health card
s.x: Give children's medicines only as the label or a clinician says. Doses depend on the product and the child, so this chapter lists none. Use professional care whenever it exists. Never give aspirin to children.4 Keep the adult kit's aspirin out of the children's pouch. The children's medicine pouch ItemWhy Non-mercury, non-glass thermometer, plus a spareThe type the Red Cross specifies for first aid kits5 Oral rehydration solution (ORS) packetsWHO and UNICEF advise low-osmolarity ORS for children with diarrhea19 Zinc, as a clinician directsWHO and UNICEF pair zinc with ORS and continued feeding19 Diaper rash creamOn the Ready.gov kit list8 The child's own prescriptionsRed Cross: pack a 7-day medication supply1 Children's fever or pain medicine labeled for the child's ageDose only by the label Dose card and penRecords each dose, time and who gave it Why ORS is in every baby kitWHO lists diarrheal disease as the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months, with about 443,832 deaths in children under 5 each year.18 How to use ORS is in Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration. WHO keeps a separate Essential Medicines List for children (EMLc). The 2025 edition lists 374 medicines.20 Use it as a map when you talk with your clinician, not as a shopping list. See Building a Long-Term Medical Kit. Store and check Check dates at every kit review. The Red Cross advises checking expiration dates and replacing used or out-of-date items.5 If a medicine was not stored at the right temperature, FDA says to check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist.21 Ready.gov says to throw out refrigerated medicine after an outage of more than a day, unless the label says otherwise.14 The health card Write one card per child and keep it in the medicine pouch. Name, date of birth, latest weight and the date it was taken Allergies and medical conditions Each medicine: name, strength, label dose for this child, times given Normal temperature and breathing rate, measured when the child is well Vaccine dates and clinician contacts Car seat limits and the latest height Record "normal" while the child is healthy, so you can compare when they are sick. Danger signs are in Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs. Fever care is in Fever, Coughs & Common Childhood Illnesses. Practice with the thermometer nowTake your child's temperature while they are well, by daylight and then by head

Pack proof of who your child is and who they belong to. After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, 5,192 children were reported missing. Reuniting all of them with family took more than six months.24 A child ID card: recent photo, name, parents' names and an out-of-area contact Copies of the birth certificate and vaccination record (the Red Cross says to copy important documents)1 The health card Extra cash, which the Red Cross includes in its kit list1 A familiar comfort toy for awake time Update the photo at every kit review.
