Reunification planning is in Keeping Kids Safe. Download these while the internet works Ready.gov: Build a Kit: the official basic kit list, including infant items. CDC: Prepare and Store Powdered Infant Formula in an Emergency: print it and put it in the feeding bin. WHO Model Lists of Essential Medicines: the adult and children's lists.

Tally your child's diapers, wipes, feeds and outfits for 3 days Work out your 2-week numbers and fill that tier first Set aside bottled water marked "formula only" and fuel to boil water Buy a non-mercury, non-glass thermometer and spare batteries Make a children's medicine pouch with a dose card, and take out any aspirin Pack the next clothing size up, labeled by size Put lids on every bucket, pail and basin in the house Put a battery CO alarm near where the baby sleeps Photograph the car seat labels and put the manual in the car kit Make a child ID card with a current photo Set the yearly kit review for the child's birthday

What are the three kit tiers?2 weeks, 3 months and 1 year. Why plan for 3 months?After Hurricane Maria, Puerto Rico households averaged 84 days without power. How do you size the kit?Count 3 days of real use, average it, then multiply by 14, 91 and 365. What water goes in formula?Bottled water until tap water is declared safe. About 70°C (158°F) for young or vulnerable babies. Aspirin for children?Never. Which thermometer?Non-mercury and non-glass, plus a spare. How much can a toddler carry?No more than 5–10% of their body weight. Biggest water danger to toddlers at home?Baths, buckets and basins. 82% of child drownings at home were under age 2.

t: Preparing Your Home for a Long Outage

s.x: Choose one warm, safe room now. Few windows, two ways out, and space for everyone, pets included.12 Never heat with a gas stove or oven. Never run a generator indoors. A generator goes outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.34 Use flashlights, not candles. Fit carbon monoxide (CO) alarms with battery backup. Replace each CO alarm every 5 years.35 Practice your fire escape twice a year, by day and by night. You may have only 1–2 minutes to get out.2 Find your main water valve today. To empty the pipes, close it, open the highest tap and drain from the lowest.67 After a flood, wear rubber boots, gloves and goggles. Floodwater can carry sewage and chemicals.8 246deaths in the Texas freeze of February 2021, about two-thirds from cold9 84 daysaverage time without power for Puerto Rico homes after Hurricane Maria10 1–2 minmay be all the time you get to escape a home fire2 6 m(20 ft): the least distance from a generator to doors, windows and vents4

s.h: 🏠 Your house has to stand on its own First 72 h
s.x: In a long outage, your home must keep you warm, keep fire out and hold your water. This chapter shows how to set it up before you need it. In February 2021, more than 4.5 million people in Texas lost power, some for up to 4 days.11 Texas later linked 246 deaths to the storm. About two-thirds were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia.9 The water failed too. Water system problems affected more than 14 million Texans during the same storm.12 Outages can last for months. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, a survey of 3,299 Puerto Rico households found that homes went 84 days without power on average.10 Household averages from the 2018 Harvard survey published in the New England Journal of Medicine.10 The same study linked about one third of deaths to interrupted medical care.10 Hurricane Helene, 2024Helene left 5.9 million customers without power across 10 states.13 That was one storm, in one recent year. Plan to live at home for at least 2 weeks. The American Red Cross advises a 2-week supply for home and a 3-day supply if you must leave.14 For a 30-year outage, that is only the base you build on. Water comes first: see Storing Water for Months & Years. If your house is not safe to stay in, read Stay or Go?

s.h: 🛋️ Choose one warm, safe room First 72 h
s.x: Live, sleep and keep watch in one room. Close off the rest of the house and use it for storage. For chemical and radiation emergencies, the CDC's shelter-in-place advice is an interior room with no or few windows, with everyone inside, pets included.1 Pick your warm room by the same rule, and one room can do both jobs. Add one rule from fire safety: know two ways out of every room.2 In a small room, plan on the door plus a window that opens. What to look for in your warm room Look forWhy Few windowsThe CDC's shelter-in-place room has no or few windows1 Two ways outNFPA's escape rule for every room2 Space for everyone, dogs tooThe CDC brings pets into the shelter room with you1 Far from the generator spotA generator must sit at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents4 A place for a CO alarmReady.gov advises CO alarms with battery backup3 Above the flood lineFloodwater can carry sewage and chemicals8 Pick a room with few windows and two ways out, and bring everyone in, pets too.12 Use flashlights and a CO alarm with battery backup.3 Any generator stays outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows and doors, exhaust pointed away.415 Set up the room Pick it todayWalk the house with the table above. Write the room into your Family Emergency Plan. Close off the restShut the doors to rooms you are not using. Lay rolled towels along the gaps under them. Cover the windows at nightHang blankets or heavy curtains, but keep the exit window easy to open. Ready.gov's basic kit includes plastic sheeting and duct tape.16 Insulate the floorPut rugs, mats or folded blankets under every sleeping place. Fit the alarmsAdd a CO alarm with battery backup.3 Add a battery smoke alarm too. Move everyone inBabies, elders and sick people get the warmest spots. Dogs sleep inside too. Any flame changes the rulesNever seal a room around a flame or an engine. Before you use any stove, heater, lamp or generator for warmth, read Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer. For warmth with no heat at all, see Staying Warm Without Heat. Babies and small childrenReady.gov warns that young children and older adults are vulnerable to extreme temperatures.3 Give small children a warm place in the warm room, where an adult can see them.For safe sleep and keeping newborns warm, see Newborn Care. Elders and people on medical devicesCheck on older neighbors. Ready.gov lists older adults as vulnerable t

s.h: 🔥 Heat and light without fire or fumes First 72 h
s.x: Use flashlights, not candles. It is one of Ready.gov's basic power outage rules.3 For lamps and lanterns that last for decades, see Light Without the Grid. Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Ready.gov and the CDC both say so.34 Fit CO alarms with battery backup.3 The CDC says to replace each CO alarm every 5 years.5 Write the date you fitted it on the back. Generators kill, even outsideNever run a generator inside a home or garage, even with the doors and windows open.15 The CDC adds carports, and says to keep it at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.4After the 2005 hurricanes in Alabama and Texas, at least 78 people were poisoned by generator CO and 10 died. Most cases involved generators placed outside, but near the home.20 Do Use flashlights for light3 Fit CO alarms with battery backup3 Run a generator outside, 6 m (20 ft) from openings4 Point generator exhaust away from buildings15 Unplug electronics during the outage3 Check on older neighbors3 Don't Light the house with candles3 Heat with a gas stove or oven34 Run a generator in a home, garage or carport4 Trust open doors or windows to clear the fumes15 A generator in the garage is fine if the garage door is open. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission says never use a generator inside a home or garage, even if doors and windows are open.15 For wood stoves, see Heating With Wood. For fuel storage and running a generator safely, see Generators & Fuel Storage.

s.h: 🚪 Fire safety: alarms and two ways out
s.x: A home fire can leave you as little as 1–2 minutes to escape.2 Every flame you add for heat, light or cooking is one more way for a fire to start. Plan as if no fire truck is coming. Prevention, working alarms and a practiced escape are your fire service now. Know two ways out of every roomUsually a door and a window. Check that both open from the inside.2 Practice twice a yearRun the drill by day and by night.2 Get low and close doorsCrawl low under smoke. Close doors behind you to slow the fire.2 Meet outsideGo straight to your outside meeting place and count heads. Never go back inNot for people, pets or things.2 Tell rescuers who is missing instead. Alarms that work without the grid Put a battery smoke alarm in the warm room and outside every sleeping area. Press the test button at every drill so everyone knows the sound. Keep spare batteries for every alarm, sealed and dated. Store them with your flashlight batteries. Keep a fire extinguisher near where you cook and heat. Learn to use it from your local fire service while classes still run. Babies, children and anyone who needs helpAssign one adult to each baby and to anyone who cannot get out alone, plus a backup.2 Carry them in the night drill too. Print these while the internet works NFPA: How to Make a Home Fire Escape Plan (PDF) NFPA Sparky: Home Fire Escape Plan grid for kids Ready.gov: Power Outages CDC: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics

s.h: 🚰 Pipes: protect the water inside your walls
s.x: Your pipes and water heater hold water you can use. FEMA and the Red Cross explain how to get it out.7 In Texas in 2021, water system problems hit more than 14 million people.12 Learn your own pipes before the taps stop. Find the main water valve and learn to close it. If the public water may be contaminated, closing it keeps dirty water out of your pipes.6 Emptying the pipes before a hard freeze If you cannot keep the house above freezing, empty the pipes into clean containers. Water expands as it freezes. That is why stored water needs 5–8 cm (2–3 inches) of space at the top of the container.21 A full pipe has no space at all. Close the main valveThis stops outside water from flowing in.6 Open the highest tapOpen the faucet on the top floor to let air into the pipes.7 Drain the lowest tapCatch the water from the lowest faucet in clean containers.7 Label and store itWrite the date on each container. Use plastic, not glass, where it may freeze.21 The water heater holds more. For the safe order (power off first, then drain), see Storing Water. Gas turned off? Call a professionalIf the gas to the water heater was shut off, a professional needs to turn it back on.7 Refill the tank before the power or gas goes back on.7 Shelves must be strong. Water weighs over 8 lb per gallon (about 1 kg per liter), so stored containers need sturdy shelving.21 A full bathtub is your drinking supply. The National Weather Service says to use bathtub water for cleaning and flushing only, not for drinking.22 Tubs and buckets drown toddlersFrom 2006 to 2010, 434 children under 5 drowned in US homes. 82% were under age 2, and 81% of the deaths involved bathtubs or bath products.23Drowning can happen in less than 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water. Never leave water containers unattended, use toilet-lid locks and keep bathroom doors closed.24

s.h: 🌀 After a storm: check the house before you trust it
s.x: Check the house from outside first, in daylight, before anyone moves back into damaged rooms. Keep children and dogs back until you are done. Look from outsideWalk all the way around. Look for a sagging roof, cracked or leaning walls, and trees resting on the building. Stay away from fallen wiresKeep everyone, children and dogs included, well back. Smell gas? Get outLeave the house. Do not light flames or use switches. Stay out until it has been checked. Dress for floodwaterWear rubber boots, gloves and goggles.8 Check your waterAsk about boil water advisories. A private well must be tested and disinfected after floodwater goes down.25 Clean what floodwater touchedDisinfect children's toys. Wash clothes in hot water with detergent.8 Floodwater can contain sewage. Swallowing contaminated water or food causes diarrheal disease.8 Floods also move chemical containers.8 Do not bathe in floodwaterThe CDC says not to bathe in water that may be contaminated.8 Keep children from playing in it. If you run a generator during cleanup, the same rule applies: outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.4 Hazard by hazard, see Floods and Hurricanes & Tornadoes. For collapse and debris dangers, see Salvage Hazards. Walk the house nowDo the outside walk-around today, while the house is fine. Photograph the roof, walls and nearby trees so you can spot changes after a storm.

Do the slow jobs now. Leave only quick jobs for the storm warning and the outage itself. NowChoose the warm room. Fit CO alarms with battery backup.3 Find the main water valve.6 Practice the fire escape.2 Storm warningFill the bathtub and large containers for washing and flushing.22 Charge phones and keep gas tanks full.3 Power outFlashlights on, no candles, no gas oven for heat.3 Generator outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) away.4 Hard freezeIf the house cannot stay above freezing, empty the pipes: main valve closed, top tap open, drain the lowest.67 After the stormBoots, gloves and goggles for floodwater.8 Test and disinfect a private well.25 Fumes first, then alarms, then warmth, then the pipes. Never heat with a gas oven or run an engine indoors.315 Fit CO alarms with battery backup.3 To empty the pipes, close the main valve, open the highest tap and drain the lowest.67 Get these before you need them CO alarms with battery backup3 A flashlight for every person3 Plastic sheeting and duct tape16 Rubber boots, gloves and goggles8 Battery smoke alarms, spare batteries and a fire extinguisher Food-grade water containers: see Storing Water The 30-year viewCO alarms need replacing every 5 years.5 Over 30 years, that is 6 alarms for each spot in the house. Count them into your long-term plan.Two drills a year2 adds up to 60 drills in 30 years. Ready.gov says to re-think your needs every year and replace expired items.16 Children grow, elders age and dogs change.

Where does a generator go?Outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents. Never in a home, garage or carport. Can you heat the house with a gas oven?No. Never.
