Never run a generator, grill, camp stove or car engine inside a home, garage or carport. Open doors and windows do not make it safe.146 Put the generator outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents. Point the exhaust away from buildings.14 Fit a battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarm near every sleeping area. Sleeping people can die before they feel any symptoms.2 Alarm sounding, or headache and dizziness? Get everyone outside into fresh air first. Then get medical help.1 Never heat your home with a gas oven or stove. It is a carbon monoxide risk.61 6 m(20 ft) minimum from a generator to doors, windows and vents1 78+people poisoned by generator CO in Alabama and Texas after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita (2005); 10 died3 5 yrsreplace every CO alarm after this long2 3family members died at home in Galicia during Spain's 2025 blackout; police investigated generator CO7

s.h: 💨 The killer you cannot see or smell First 72 h
s.x: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a gas with no color and no smell, and it can kill you.2 You will not notice it building up. Every flame and every engine makes it. CO is in the fumes whenever fuel burns in cars and trucks, small engines, stoves, lanterns, grills, fireplaces, gas ranges and furnaces.2 Indoors, it collects. CO builds up in enclosed or partly enclosed spaces and poisons the people and animals who breathe it.2 With no grid power, generators, grills, camp stoves, gas ovens and car engines become the tools for power, cooking, charging and heat. Official outage guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Ready.gov (FEMA) warns against each of them used the wrong way.16 Outside is not automatically safeAfter Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005, portable generators poisoned at least 78 people in Alabama and Texas and killed 10. Most of those generators were outside, but near the home.3

Generators have killed people after hurricanes, and police investigated a generator CO case after the 2025 blackout in Spain. Below are documented events and the scale of recent outages. Every entry is a recorded fact, not a forecast. 2005Alabama and Texas, after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita: portable generators poisoned at least 78 people with CO and killed 10. Most of the generators were outside but near homes.3 2017Puerto Rico, after Hurricane Maria: surveyed households went an average of 84 days without power.11 Long outages mean the rules in this chapter apply for months, not days. Feb 2021Texas winter storm: more than 4.5 million Texans lost power, some for up to 4 days.9 The state counted 246 storm-related deaths, about two-thirds of them from cold.10 Sep 2024Hurricane Helene left 5.9 million customers without power across 10 states.12 Apr 2025Spain and Portugal: a widespread blackout on April 28 stopped subways, traffic lights and ATMs.8 In Galicia, police investigated CO from a generator after an older couple and their adult son died at home.7 The lesson from 2005: outside was not enough. Most of those generators were outdoors but near the home.3 The CDC rule is outdoors and at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.1 In a cold outage, choose only safe heat. Staying Warm Without Heat shows how to keep warm without burning anything.

s.h: 🤒 Symptoms, and why sleeping people die
s.x: The warning signs are headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion.1 The CDC notes that people often describe them as "flu-like".2 Breathing in a lot of CO can make you pass out or kill you.2 People who are asleep or drunk can die from CO before they have any symptoms.2 No headache wakes them up. A CO alarm can. The CDC warns that people who are sleeping or drunk can die from CO before they have symptoms. At night, the alarm is the warning.2 Who is at higher risk Everyone is at risk. Infants, older people, and people with chronic heart disease, anemia or breathing problems are more likely to get sick from CO.2 Do not try to tell CO from fluCO can poison every person and animal who breathes it in the same space.2 If several people, or the dog, feel unwell at once while an engine, grill, stove or heater is running, treat it as CO. Get everyone outside first.1 Babies and childrenInfants are more likely to get sick from CO.2 A baby cannot tell you about a headache, so put a CO alarm near where the baby sleeps, as you would for every sleeping area.2Let older children hear the CO alarm's test sound. Teach them one rule: when it sounds, go straight outside to the family meeting spot. Older and disabled peopleOlder people and anyone with heart disease, anemia or breathing problems are more likely to get sick from CO.2 During an outage, check on older neighbors.6If someone cannot get out of bed alone, decide now who helps them outside when the alarm sounds.

Run a portable generator outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.1 Never run one in a home, garage or carport. Open doors and windows do not make it safe.14 Point the exhaust away from your house and any other building.4 Distance matters as much as "outside". Most generator poisonings after Katrina and Rita involved generators placed outdoors but close to homes.3 Distance from the CDC (20 ft from doors, windows and vents), exhaust direction from the CPSC, and the long cord and battery CO alarm from the California Department of Public Health.145 Set up a generator, step by step Choose the spot nowOutdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from every door, window and vent.1 Mark it with a stake or paint so nobody guesses in the dark. Aim the exhaust awayPoint it away from your home and from any other building.4 Run a long cordUse an extension cord longer than 6 m (20 ft), so the generator can stay far away.5 Switch on a battery CO alarm insideKeep a battery-powered CO alarm running in the home whenever the generator runs.5 Never move it closerNot into the garage or carport, not even in rain or to stop theft.14 A generator is fine in the garage if the big door is open. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) says never use a generator inside a home or garage, even if doors and windows are open.4 If the generator is outside the house, everyone inside is safe. Most generator CO poisonings after Katrina and Rita involved generators outside but near homes.3 Keep it at least 6 m (20 ft) from openings.1 Agree on generators with your neighborsYour neighbors' doors and windows count too. Agree as a street that nobody runs a generator within 6 m (20 ft) of any home's doors, windows or vents.1 See Organizing Neighbors: Mutual Aid & Watch. Dogs and other petsCO poisons animals as well as people.2 Keep dogs away from generator exhaust, and never keep a pet in a garage or carport with an engine running.If your dog seems weak or sick at the same time as people, take everyone, dog included, into fresh air. Then see Dog First Aid. For fuel storage, refueling, cords and transfer switches, see Generators & Fuel Storage.

s.h: 🔥 Grills, camp stoves, ovens and cars
s.x: Use charcoal grills and camp stoves outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.6 Never heat your home with a gas oven or stove.61 A gas range burns fuel, and burning fuel makes CO.2 Never run a car or truck in a garage or carport.1 If you charge phones from a car, park it in the open first. Fuel-burning devices: the rules (CDC, CPSC, Ready.gov) DeviceSafe useNever Portable generatorOutdoors, 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents; exhaust pointed away14In a home, garage or carport, even with doors open14 Charcoal grill, camp stoveOutdoors, 6 m (20 ft) from windows6Indoors Gas oven or stovetopCooking, then turn it offHeating the home6 Car or truckEngine on only in the open airIn a garage or carport1 Fireplace, wood stoveMakes CO too2; follow the chimney rules in Heating With WoodBurning when fumes stay in the room, where CO builds up2 Fuel lantern or lampMakes CO too2; battery lights burn no fuelLeft burning while people sleep, since sleepers get no warning2 Tents, campers and cars are enclosed spaces tooCO builds up in enclosed and partly enclosed spaces.2 A grill or camp stove inside a tent, camper, boat cabin or parked car is the same danger as one inside your kitchen. Cook outdoors with the methods in Cooking Without Power. For stove installation, clearances and chimney care, see Heating With Wood. For safe light at night, see Light Without the Grid.

Use a battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarm.26 An alarm that runs only on mains power goes silent in a blackout. Put one near every sleeping area.2 That is where people are when they cannot notice symptoms.2 Ready.gov also advises alarms in central locations on every level of the home.6 Replace every alarm after 5 years.2 Keep one switched on whenever a generator is running.5 Alarms near every sleeping area (CDC) and on every level (Ready.gov). No gas oven for heat, no grill or camp stove indoors, no engine in a garage, even with the door open.2614 Set up your alarms Check the labelIt must say carbon monoxide. A smoke alarm is a different device unless its label says it detects both. Choose battery powerBattery-powered, or plug-in with battery backup. Nothing that dies with the grid.2 Mount one near each sleeping areaInclude the places where babies and older relatives sleep.2 Write two dates on itThe install date, and a replace-by date 5 years later.2 Test it and teach the soundPress the test button as the manual says. Let every family member, including children, hear what it sounds like. Run a night-time get-out drillThe National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) advises practicing a home escape plan twice a year, during the day and at night, with two ways out of every room.13 Use the same drill for the CO alarm: wake up, get out, meet outside, count heads. Get these before you need them Battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarms, one per sleeping area2 Spare batteries in the size each alarm takes One extra battery CO alarm to run whenever the generator runs5 An extension cord longer than 6 m (20 ft)5

s.h: 🩺 If someone may be poisoned: fresh air first
s.x: Fresh air is the first treatment. If the alarm sounds, or anyone feels dizzy, sick or confused, get everyone outside into fresh air. Then get medical help.1 Get everyone out nowPeople and pets, straight outside into fresh air.1 Do not stop to hunt for the source. Keep yourself safeDo not go back in for belongings. The Red Cross notes that keeping yourself safe helps you take care of others.15 Get medical helpCall emergency services, or get the person to medical care as fast as you can.1 Check anyone who does not respondCheck quickly. If they do not respond and are not breathing normally, or are only gasping, start CPR and use an automated external defibrillator (AED) as soon as one is available (AHA, 2025).14 Stay out while the source runsDo not go back in while the engine, grill or stove is still burning. Where responders exist, let them say when it is safe. Learn CPR before you need it: see CPR & Choking: Adults, Children, Infants. Do Get everyone outside first1 Take the pets too2 Get medical help1 Start CPR if a person does not respond and is not breathing normally, or only gasping14 Don't Search the house for the source Go back in for belongings15 Put a sick person to bed in the same house Shrug it off as flu while engines or burners are running When no ambulance is comingFresh air is the one first step every household can always take.1 In a long grid-down life, prevention is the whole plan: correct placement, working alarms and a family that gets out fast.

Night is when CO kills quietly. Sleeping people can die before they notice symptoms.2 Do this check every night that anything has burned fuel. Walk the houseNo generator, grill, camp stove or engine running inside, in the garage or in the carport.16 Check the generator spotOutdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents, with the exhaust pointed away.14 Put out lanterns and fuel lampsLanterns make CO too.2 Switch to battery lights for the night. Check every alarmOne near each sleeping area, battery in, working.2 Agree who does whatName the adult who wakes the children, who carries the baby, who helps older relatives and who takes the dog. Make it a habit, not a decisionTie the check to something you already do every night, such as locking the door. A routine you do without thinking still happens when you are exhausted.

CO risk lasts as long as you burn anything. Fireplaces, stoves, lanterns and furnaces all make CO, not just generators.2 If your heat, cooking and light come from wood, charcoal or oil, the same rules apply every single day. Burn outdoors, or in a stove with a properly installed, clean chimney. See Heating With Wood. Alarms wear out on a schedule. Replace them every 5 years,2 so a 30-year plan needs several generations of alarms. 30 years of alarms: the mathAt one replacement every 5 years,2 each sleeping area needs 6 alarms over 30 years. A home with 3 sleeping areas needs 18.Store spares with the batteries they take. Check the date printed on each spare before you fit it. The rules never expire. Teach them to every child in the household, so the next generation runs the home the same way. Save these official pages while the internet worksCDC: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics, CDC: Avoiding Carbon Monoxide Poisoning, CPSC: What to Know About Generators and Ready.gov: Power Outages. Save each one as a PDF and print the generator rules.

Buy a battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarm for every sleeping area Write the install date and a replace-by date 5 years later on each alarm Buy spare batteries for every alarm Mark a generator spot at least 6 m (20 ft) from all doors, windows and vents Buy an extension cord longer than 6 m (20 ft) Tell everyone: no engine, grill or camp stove in the house, garage or carport, ever Choose an outdoor meeting spot and run a night-time CO drill Decide who helps the baby, older relatives and the dog get out Agree on generator distances with your neighbors Save or print the official CO and generator pages

Where does a generator go?Outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents, exhaust pointed away from buildings. Is the garage OK with the big door open?No. Never in a home, garage or carport, even with doors and windows open. Why do sleeping people die of CO?They can die before they have any symptoms. A CO alarm is their warning. Where do CO alarms go?Near every sleeping area. Battery or battery backup. Replace every 5 years. Alarm sounds or everyone has a headache. First move?Everyone, pets too, outside into fresh air. Then get medical help. The CO symptoms?Headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, confusion. Can a gas oven heat the house?No. Never heat your home with a gas oven or stove.

Check on your neighbors first. Ready.gov puts it on the power outage to-do list, because older adults and young children are most at risk from heat and cold.1 Hold a block meeting in week 1. Write one paper sheet: who lives where, who needs help, who has which skills, and one meeting place everyone can reach.10 Register anyone who depends on powered medical equipment. After Hurricane Maria, about 1 in 3 excess deaths was linked to delayed or interrupted health care.2 Watch in pairs. Observe, write it down, report. Never chase or confront. Six 4-hour shifts of 2 people need 12 person-shifts a day. Shared kitchens: keep hot food at 60°C (140°F) or hotter. Bacteria grow fastest between 4°C and 60°C (40°F–140°F) and can double in 20 minutes.15 Generators, grills and camp stoves stay outdoors, more than 6 m (20 ft) from any window, door or vent, including your neighbor's.121 84 daysaverage time without power for surveyed Puerto Rico homes after Hurricane Maria (2017)2 1 in 3Maria excess deaths linked to delayed or interrupted health care2 3M+US Medicare patients with claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment12 37%US adults who made an emergency plan in the past year (2023)5

s.h: 🏘️ Why your neighbors are your first backup
s.x: In a long outage, outside help is slow and far away. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, a survey of 3,299 households in Puerto Rico found they went an average of 84 days without power, 68 days without water and 41 days without cell service.2 Hurricane Helene left 5.9 million customers without power across 10 states in 2024.6 In Asheville, North Carolina, the water crisis that followed lasted 53 days.7 Without electricity, fuel pumps do not work. Outages also knock out lighting and payment systems.8 Driving away to find help is often not an option. The people who die are often the ones nobody checked on. In the February 2021 Texas winter storm, 246 people died. About two-thirds of those deaths came from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia (dangerously low body temperature).4 After Maria, the poor and the elderly had the highest risk of dying, and older men had a 35% higher risk of death.3 Those are the neighbors a street can reach on foot every day. Every service was out for weeks. Plan as if phones, taps and power all fail at once.2 Most households are not readyFEMA's 2023 national survey found that only 37% of US adults made an emergency plan in the past year, down from 41% in 2022.5 Expect most of your neighbors to start with little. Organizing early turns their gaps into a shared plan. For what research shows about how people behave in disasters, see How People Really Behave in Disasters. For group size and roles, see Building Your Group.

s.h: 🗺️ Map your block: the first meeting First 72 h
s.x: Start with the homes you can walk around in a few minutes. A small block that actually meets beats a big network that only exists on paper. Everything you learn goes on one paper block sheet and one hand-drawn map. Paper works when phones are dead. Knock and introduce yourselfGo in daylight, with a partner. Give your name and house, and invite them to a short block meeting. Pick one meeting placeChoose a spot everyone can reach. FEMA's family plan includes a neighborhood meeting place and says meeting places should be accessible to people with disabilities.10 Hold a 30-minute meetingAgree on three jobs: check on each other, share news, keep watch. Keep it short so people come back. Fill in the block sheetFor each home: adults, children, babies, elders, pets, medical needs, skills, and tools they are willing to lend. Draw the mapHouses, the meeting place, water sources, and who checks on whom (buddy pairs). Choose a block captain and a backupThe captain keeps the sheet. The backup keeps a copy in a different house. Set the next dateMeet often at first, then settle into a fixed weekly time. Each home has a buddy across the street. Priority homes get checked first, and every check is reported at the meeting place. Keep the block sheet privateMedical details and supply lists stay on paper with the captain and the backup. Do not post them on the notice board or online. See Keeping a Low Profile. Ask, do not demandLet each household choose what to share. People who feel respected at the first meeting come to the second one.

Text instead of calling while the network still works. The FCC and FEMA advise texting for non-emergency messages, keeping calls short and not redialing again and again, because networks get congested in emergencies.9 Limiting calls also saves your phone battery.9 Then plan for no phones at all: after Maria, homes averaged 41 days without cell service.2 Block communication methods, from most to least dependent on power MethodNeeds power?Best for Text messagePhone battery and a working networkShort updates while networks last Two-way radioBatteriesWatch posts talking to each other Runner (2 people)NoUrgent messages inside the block Notice boardNoRotas, news, lost and found, meeting times Window signNo"OK" or "HELP" seen from the street WhistleNoAlarms using a code you agree on Agree on a window sign. A green "OK" sheet or a red "HELP" sheet in the front window lets the morning check-in walker see at a glance which doors to knock on first. A whistle is on Ready.gov's basic kit list.11 Agree on a short block code, write it on the notice board, and teach it to the children. For licenses, ranges and batteries, see Radios: Ham, GMRS, CB & Listening. Communication kit for the blockA whistle for every adult and older childA notice board, pins, and a waterproof coverClipboards, pencils and a sharpenerRed and green sheets of paper or card for window signsSpare batteries for any radios Print these while the internet worksFEMA Family Emergency Communication Plan (PDF): print one for each household on the block. FCC/FEMA tips for communicating in an emergency.

s.h: 🔦 Watch rotas people can keep up First 30 days
s.x: A block watch is eyes and ears, not a fighting force. Its job is to notice, write it down, report, and wake people up when something is wrong. The rota must be fair and simple, or it falls apart within weeks. Do the math before you start. Arithmetic, not a rule: fewer adults means longer gaps between shifts or fewer posts. Recount every month. Rota math for your block Person-shifts per day = number of shifts × people per shift. Six 4-hour shifts × 2 people = 12. Shifts per adult = person-shifts per day ÷ adults on the rota. 12 ÷ 24 adults = 0.5, so one shift every 2 days. With only 12 adults, everyone stands one 4-hour shift every day, on top of water, food and child care. Choose your postsOne or two spots that see the street entrances and the meeting place. Fewer posts means a lighter rota. Always work in pairsOne watches while the other writes or goes for help. Nobody stands a night shift alone. Keep a logbookTime, what you saw, what you did. Plain facts, no guesses about people. Hand over properlyThe next pair arrives a few minutes early and reads the log before the old pair leaves. Report, then restTell the captain anything unusual. Nobody stands two shifts in a row. DoWatch, write it down, reportWork in pairs with a whistleWake the captain when unsureRotate shifts fairly, including weekendsGive tired people a night off Don'tChase, follow or confront anyonePunish or detain people yourselvesStand a post alone at nightTalk about supplies at the postWarm up with a grill or heater in a closed shed Observe and report: never confrontThe watch calls people together; it does not fight. Avoidance and calm talk come first. See De-escalation & Avoiding Violence. Cold watch posts and carbon monoxideNever run a generator, grill, camp stove or fuel heater in a shed, garage, tent or car to stay warm. Carbon monoxide (CO) is colorless and odorless, and sleeping people can die before they feel symptoms.21 Dress warmly instead, and swap shifts more often in the cold. Women and girlsPut women on the planning team and let them say which posts, paths and pairings feel safe. Nobody, and especially no woman or girl, should walk alone at night to a post, water point or latrine. See Personal Safety for Women & Girls.

s.h: 🧰 Sharing tools, skills and supplies Year 1
s.x: Not every house needs every tool. One shared, logged collection keeps each saw, ladder and wheelbarrow working for the whole block. The same goes for skills. A nurse, a mechanic and a gardener on one street can cover gaps that no single household could. Set up a tool library List what people will lendEach household writes down tools it is willing to share. Owners keep ownership. Mark every toolPaint, scratch or tag the owner's house number on the handle. Keep a sign-out logOne notebook, kept by one keeper. Every loan gets a line. Set three rulesReturn it clean. Report damage the same day. Bring it back by the due date. Hold a repair dayOnce a month, sharpen, oil and fix the shared tools together. Tool library sign-out log (copy this into a notebook) ToolOwnerBorrowerDue backCondition Bow sawHouse 5House 2FridaySharp, clean LadderHouse 3House 1Today, 5 pmGood Share skills and trips Skills board: list who can give first aid, fix bikes, mind babies, read a map or repair a roof. Pool trips: fuel pumps stop working without electricity,8 so one cart or car trip should carry errands for several homes. Child care rota: one adult minds several children so other parents can haul water or stand watch. For trading with people outside the block, see Barter, Trade & Money.

One kitchen for several homes means one fire, one cook rota and one set of hygiene rules. It also means one mistake can make everyone sick at once. Food safety numbers for a shared kitchen (USDA, FoodSafety.gov) RuleMetricUS Danger zone: bacteria grow fastest154–60°C40–140°F Hold hot food at or above1560°C140°F Keep cold food and coolers at or below164°C40°F Bacteria in the danger zone can double in as little as 20 minutes.15 Cook in batches you can serve hot, right away. Plan portions with real numbers. Humanitarian food aid uses 2,100 kcal per person per day as its minimum planning figure.17 A kitchen feeding 30 people needs 30 × 2,100 = 63,000 kcal a day.  Cook outdoors, away from homesReady.gov says camp stoves and charcoal grills belong outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1 Wash hands at a set stationSoap and water before cooking, after the latrine and after handling raw meat. See Handwashing & Personal Hygiene. Sick cooks stay outAnyone with diarrhea or vomiting does not cook or serve until they are well. Serve hot, serve fastKeep food at 60°C (140°F) or above until it is served.15 Do not keep risky leftoversPerishable food that sat out more than 2 hours, or 1 hour above 32°C (90°F), gets thrown out.16 Clean and dry everythingWash pots, ladles and boards with hot soapy water and let them dry in the air. Disasters always cause epidemics. A review in the CDC journal Emerging Infectious Diseases found that disasters which do not displace people rarely lead to outbreaks. The risk rises with crowding, poor water and sanitation, poor nutrition and lost access to health care.19 A clean, uncrowded shared kitchen helps keep that risk low. Shared toilets need numbers too. UNHCR's target is 1 latrine per 20 people (or 1 per household), and no latrine should serve more than 50 people in the first phase of an emergency.20 Put latrines well away from the kitchen and water. See Toilets Without Water. Babies, children and pregnant womenChildren under 5, pregnant people and adults 65 and older are at higher risk from food poisoning.18 Serve them first, straight from the hot pot. Rope off the fire area so toddlers cannot reach it, and give one adult the job of watching children during cooking. Dogs at the kitchen and meeting placeKeep dogs leashed and out of the cooking area. Feed them separately, away from people eating. Carbon monoxide poisons animals as well

Make a private list of every neighbor who could die without help. Then make sure someone checks on each of them every day. More than 3 million US Medicare beneficiaries have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment. Counting dialysis, oxygen and home health services, it is more than 4.6 million.12 In a June 2024 CDC survey, 26% of adults with disabilities said they had nowhere to go in an evacuation, against 15% of adults without disabilities. 20% named the cost of evacuating, against 14%.13 Moving frail people can kill them too. Nearly 3.7 million people evacuated ahead of Hurricane Rita in 2005. Over 100 of at least 119 deaths were linked to the evacuation itself, including heat in vehicles and a nursing-home bus fire.14 The vulnerable-neighbor register: what to ask and what the block does NeedAsk aboutBlock plan Oxygen, CPAP, dialysis or other powered deviceBackup power, the provider's outage planFirst on the morning check; first call on any shared power Lives alone, or has dementiaWho has a spare key; usual routineDaily knock and talk; buddy sleeps over in extreme heat or cold Cannot walk far, or uses a wheelchairCan they reach the meeting place?Two named helpers; plan routes early Babies and toddlersFormula, diapers, medicinesShared "baby shelf" of spare supplies Pets and service dogsFood, leash, vaccination papersPet buddy who can feed and walk them The daily check-in walk Walk the route every morningTwo people, same time each day. Look for the OK or HELP sign in each window. Knock at priority homes firstElders living alone and anyone on powered equipment. Ready.gov names older adults and young children as most at risk from extreme temperatures.1 Talk, do not just waveAsk about warmth, water, food, medicines and sleep. Look inside if you can. Write it on the sheetName, time, how they are, what they need. Act the same dayBring in the medic, move the person somewhere warmer or cooler, or call help if it exists. Elders and disabled neighborsAfter the 2021 Texas freeze, about two-thirds of the 246 deaths came from cold exposure.4 A warm shared room at night and a daily visit cost little. See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People. Children: ID and a reunion planAfter Hurricane Katrina, 5,192 children were reported missing; the last were reunited with family by March 2006.25 Give every child a card with their name, parents' names, house and the bloc

s.h: 🩹 Train the block and keep it going Long haul
s.x: Every adult on the block should know how to stop bleeding and do CPR. Teach it at block meetings and practice it on a schedule. See CPR & Choking. You need a certificate before you are allowed to do CPR. An American Heart Association survey found many people still wrongly believe CPR requires special training.23 Learn it now, but never hold back in an emergency because you lack a card. A generator is safe as long as it is outside. After two 2005 hurricanes, at least 78 people were poisoned and 10 died from portable generators, and most cases involved generators outside but near the home.22 Keep them more than 6 m (20 ft) from every window, door and vent on the street.21 Day 1Check on the neighbors on each side and across the street. Put up OK or HELP signs. Week 1First block meeting. Block sheet, map, captain, backup, meeting place. Week 2Watch rota starts. Daily check-in walk. Notice board up. Month 1Shared kitchen and latrine rules. Tool library log. Skills board. Year 1Monthly first aid practice. Rotate captains. Recount adults and redo the rota math. Year 5 and beyondTeenagers learn each role. Written rules and records outlast any one leader. Practice this now while help still existsAsk your local emergency management office or Red Cross chapter what volunteer disaster and first aid training they offer, and go with a neighbor. Then run one practice: a 30-minute block meeting and one full day of the check-in walk. The 30-year viewOver decades, people tire, fall ill, move away and die. Rotate every role, write the rules down, and keep the block sheet updated each season. When disputes come, use agreed rules, not the loudest voice. See Group Rules, Decisions & Resolving Disputes.

Introduce yourself to the neighbors on each side and across the street Agree on a block meeting place that a wheelchair user can reach Print a blank block sheet and draw a one-page map of your street Ask privately who uses oxygen, CPAP, dialysis or other powered equipment Buy whistles, a notice board, clipboards and pencils Make red "HELP" and green "OK" window signs for every home Work out your watch rota math: shifts × people ÷ adults Start a tool library notebook with three items each Book a first aid and CPR class with at least one neighbor Make an ID card for each child with the block meeting place on it

After Maria, how long were homes without power on average?84 days. Also 68 days without water and 41 without cell service. What share of Maria's excess deaths was linked to interrupted health care?About 1 in 3. Register neighbors on powered equipment and check them first. How do you work out a watch rota?Shifts × people per shift = person-shifts. Divide by the adults on the rota. What does the watch do when it sees trouble?Observe, write it down, report and wake people up. Never chase or confront. What temperature should shared hot food stay at?60°C (140°F) or hotter until served. How far must generators and grills be from windows?More than 6 m (20 ft) from any window, door or vent, including your neighbor's. How many people per latrine?Target 1 per 20 people; never more than 50 in the first phase.

t: What to Salvage First: The Priority List

s.x: Salvage only what you have the right to take. Your own things, things people give or trade you, and items covered by a community agreement. Taking without permission is theft. See Scavenging vs Looting. Water containers first, medical supplies second, warmth third. After Hurricane Maria, homes averaged 68 days without water, and about one third of excess deaths were tied to interrupted health care.1 In the 2021 Texas freeze, about two-thirds of deaths were from cold.2 Only food-grade containers hold drinking water. Never use one that held bleach, pesticides or other toxic chemicals.4 Leave what has spoiled. Fridge food is safe for only about 4 hours without power. Refrigerated medicine is thrown out after more than a day unless its label says otherwise.1816 Weigh before you carry. Water weighs 1 kg per liter. Keep loads at or under 30% of body weight.823 Log every item, where it came from and who allowed it. Date it, check it, and replace what is used or out of date.1213 68 daysaverage time without water after Hurricane Maria1 53 daysAsheville's water crisis after Hurricane Helene, 20243 1 kgweight of 1 liter of water (8.33 lb per gallon)8 ≤30%of body weight: the load ceiling for fit adults23

s.h: 📋 The priority list: what to look for first First 30 days
s.x: Salvage in the order that things kill. Records from long outages point to three big killers: no safe water, missed medical care and cold.12 After Hurricane Maria in 2017, a survey of 3,299 Puerto Rico households found they averaged 68 days without water and 84 days without power (NEJM, 2018).1 About one third of excess deaths were tied to delayed or interrupted health care.1 Texas linked 246 deaths to the February 2021 winter storm. About two-thirds were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia.2 After Hurricane Helene in 2024, Asheville, North Carolina, went through a 53-day water crisis before its boil-water notice was lifted.3 So this book ranks salvage in that order: hold water, treat injury and illness, stay warm. Light, tools and materials come next. The ranking is guidance built from those records. Tiers 1 to 3 follow the main causes of death recorded after Hurricane Maria and the 2021 Texas freeze.12 Tier 4 follows Ready.gov and CDC outage advice.1622 Tier 5 items appear on the Ready.gov and Red Cross kit lists.1314 The salvage priority list RankLook forWhy it ranks here 1Food-grade water containers with lidsMaria homes averaged 68 days without water1 2First aid supplies, medicines, soapAbout 1 in 3 Maria excess deaths: interrupted care1 3Blankets, sleeping bags, plastic sheeting, duct tapeAbout 2 in 3 Texas 2021 storm deaths: cold2 4Flashlights, batteries, battery CO alarmsCandles are a fire risk; CO alarms need battery power1622 5Wrench, pliers, multi-tool, manual can openerListed in the Ready.gov and Red Cross kits1314 6Fasteners, wire, rope, clothing, glass jarsRepairs, clothing and storage for the long haul

A clean container is worth more than the water in it. Rain, streams and wells can refill it again and again. Without one, you cannot carry, treat or store water. Use only food-grade containers. The CDC says never to use a container that held toxic substances such as bleach or pesticides.4 Look for the number 2 inside the recycling triangle. Utah's emergency management agency calls food-grade high-density polyethylene (HDPE #2) the best choice.5 It also says milk jugs break down and become brittle.5 A lid and a tap beat an open bucket. CDC safe-storage guidance favors a small opening, a lid and a tap or spout. Hands, cups and dippers carry germs into wide-open containers.10 How many containers? The Sphere humanitarian standard is 15 L (about 4 gallons) per person per day for drinking, cooking and hygiene.9 For a family of 4, that is 60 L (about 16 gallons) every day. Arithmetic: two 20 L (5.3 gallon) jugs per person hold 40 L. That is about 2.5 days at the Sphere amount. Aim for enough containers to carry today's water and store tomorrow's. Ask what it heldRead the label and smell it. Reject anything that held bleach, pesticides, fuel or other chemicals.4 Check the plasticLook for HDPE #2.5 Reject milk jugs and anything brittle or cracked. Light makes containers brittle and leaky.6 Wash and rinseWash with soap and water, then rinse well.4 SanitizeStir 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of unscented liquid bleach into 1 quart (about 1 L) of water. Pour it in, cap, shake to coat every surface, wait at least 30 seconds, then pour it out.4 Fill and labelFill with safe water. Write "drinking water" and the date on it.4 Fumes pass through plasticNebraska Extension warns that vapors from gasoline, kerosene and pesticides can penetrate plastic containers.7 Treat a jug found sitting beside fuel or pesticides as a non-drinking container. Store your water away from them.4 Lids on, always, around toddlersDrowning can happen quickly in less than 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water. Never leave a bucket or any container of water unattended.24 Salvaged buckets need tight lids before they come home. Any big plastic jug or drum is fine for drinking water. Only food-grade containers are safe, and never one that held bleach or pesticides.4 Milk jugs break down and turn brittle.5 Full storage rules are in Storing Water.

Use the American Red Cross first aid list as your salvage list. It is written for a family of 4.12 Dressings: 2 absorbent compress dressings, 25 adhesive bandages, 10 sterile gauze pads, 2 roller bandages and 2 triangular bandages12 Tape and protection: 1 roll of adhesive cloth tape, 2 pairs of nonlatex gloves and a breathing barrier12 Ointments and wipes: antibiotic ointment, antiseptic wipes, hydrocortisone ointment and 81 mg aspirin12 Tools: tweezers, an emergency blanket, an instant cold compress, a non-mercury nonglass thermometer and an instruction booklet12 Most of the list is dressings and protection. Only four items are medicines or antiseptics.12 Sealed bandages, gauze and gloves are light, compact and worth taking in bulk. See Building a Long-Term Medical Kit. Hygiene supplies prevent illness. Ready.gov lists soap, hand sanitizer, moist towelettes, garbage bags and plastic ties in its basic kit.13 Found medicines: read the storage line first Insulin: the FDA says vials, opened or unopened, may be kept unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days. Replace insulin that was exposed to extreme heat or cold.15 Other refrigerated medicines: Ready.gov says to throw them out if the power has been out for more than a day, unless the label says otherwise.16 The safety rules for found medicines, including expiration dates, are in Found Food & Medicine. Prescription medicines belong to one patientA prescription was written for one person's body and illness. Before anyone takes a found prescription medicine, ask a doctor, nurse or pharmacist whenever one can be reached. Antibiotic facts are in Infections, Sepsis & Antibiotic Facts. Babies and childrenNever give aspirin to children.17 Keep salvaged aspirin with adult supplies only.Ready.gov's baby items are infant formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream.13 Put them at the top of the list for any household with a baby. Elderly and disabled peopleThe Red Cross lists hearing aids with extra batteries, glasses, contact lenses, syringes and a cane.14 These are small, light and very hard to replace.In the US, more than 3 million Medicare patients have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment (HHS emPOWER).25 Batteries for that equipment are a top find.

s.h: 🔧 Tools, fasteners, fabric, glass and batteries
s.x: Hand tools Take tools that need no power. Ready.gov lists a wrench or pliers to turn off utilities and a manual can opener.13 The Red Cross adds a multi-purpose tool.14 Saws, hammers, axes, shovels and files let one person do far more work. Choosing and caring for them is in The Essential Hand Tools. Fasteners, tape and sheeting Nails, screws, bolts, wire and hinges are small and light. Sort them by size into lidded jars or tins so you can find them in the dark. Ready.gov lists plastic sheeting, scissors and duct tape in its basic kit for sheltering in place.13 Sheeting and tape also patch broken windows and leaking roofs until a proper repair. Fabric and clothing Blankets and sleeping bags come first. Ready.gov lists a sleeping bag or warm blanket, a complete change of clothes and sturdy shoes for each person.13 The Red Cross first aid list includes an emergency blanket.12 Wash anything that touched floodwater. CDC says to wash clothes that touched floodwater or sewage in hot water and detergent. Disinfect toys before children use them.19 Clean cotton cloth is the raw material for reusable pads and cloth diapers. See Periods Without Stores. Glass Glass jars and bottles store dry food, seeds and liquids. Do not use glass for water that may freeze. Use freezer-safe plastic instead.7 The Red Cross specifies a non-mercury, nonglass thermometer for first aid kits.12 Handle old glass thermometers and broken glass as hazards: see Salvage Hazards. Batteries and light Light the house with flashlights, not candles. Ready.gov lists candles as a fire risk in power outages.16 Ready.gov also lists extra batteries in its basic kit.13 Battery CO alarms are high-value finds. The CDC advises battery-powered or battery-backup carbon monoxide (CO) alarms, replaced every 5 years.22 Look for a date on the alarm before you trust it. Car batteries and damaged batteries need special handling. See Salvage Hazards. A generator is the best thing you can salvage. Fuel pumps do not work without electricity (FEMA, 2025).20 A generator must run outdoors, more than 6 m (20 feet) from windows, doors and vents, and never in a home or garage.22 See Carbon Monoxide. Women and girlsReady.gov lists feminine supplies and personal hygiene items in its basic kit.13 Sealed pads, tampons and menstrual cups are light and high value. The CDC says pregnant women need more stored water, so containers mat

Start with your own home. Walk it room by room before you go anywhere else. List what you already own before you ask anyone else. Then ask. This chapter covers lawful salvage only: your own things, things people give or trade you, and items covered by a community agreement. Taking from homes, stores or vehicles without permission is theft, and looting is a crime. The law is in Scavenging vs Looting. A water heater tank on the drinking line is a usable water source (FEMA, 2025).11 Fuel and pesticide vapors can pass into plastic jugs stored nearby.7 Where to look, and what to watch for PlaceLook forWatch for HomesFirst aid kits, blankets, containers, water heater water11Fridge food is unsafe after 4 hours without power18 Garages and shedsHand tools, fasteners, tarps, buckets, cartsFuel and pesticide vapors penetrate plastic7 FarmsDrums, tanks, fencing wire, feed bucketsAny container that held pesticides is not for drinking water4 Hardware and farm storesFasteners, tools, sheeting, containersStock belongs to the business: agree terms with the owner Vehicles (owner's permission)First aid kit, blankets, tools13Fuel pumps do not work without power20 Flooded buildingsMetal tools, glass, sealed itemsFloodwater can carry sewage and move chemical containers19 Vehicle parts have their own chapter: Useful Parts From Vehicles. Ready.gov advises keeping a kit in the car, so ask the owner about the trunk first.13 Get permissionWrite down the owner's name, the date and what they agreed to. If no one can give permission, follow your community's agreement. Go in pairsTell someone where you are going and when you will be back. Gear upWork gloves, a dust mask and sturdy shoes.13 In flood-damaged places add rubber boots, rubber gloves and goggles.19 Check before you enterLook for structural damage, gas smells and spilled chemicals. If in doubt, stay out. See Salvage Hazards. Work the list from the topWater containers, then medical supplies, then warmth. Stop when your load limit is reached. Log itRecord each item, the place and who allowed it, before it joins the group store. DogsLeave dogs at home or on a short leash during salvage. Floodwater can carry sewage and chemicals.19Worth finding for your dog: collar, leash, ID tag, food, carrier and bowl (Red Cross).14 Ready.gov adds extra water for your pet, so count the dog when you count containers.13

s.h: ⏳ What spoils fast and what lasts
s.x: Time decides value. Some finds are unsafe within hours. Others keep their value for years if you store them well. Food in a dead fridge is the fastest to go. USDA says a fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours if the door stays closed. A full freezer holds about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.18 Days later, that food is not a salvage find. Fridge and freezer with doors closed (USDA).18 Refrigerated medicine after more than a day without power, unless the label says otherwise (Ready.gov).16 Insulin vials unrefrigerated (FDA).15 Self-bottled water (CDC).4 Bleach under 1 year old (EPA).21 CO alarm replacement (CDC).22 Blue barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart within 5 years (Be Ready Utah).6 Bleach weakens with age. EPA's emergency method calls for bleach stored at room temperature for less than one year.21 Use a found bottle with no date for cleaning, not for treating drinking water. Plastic weakens in light. Be Ready Utah says sunlight, and even artificial light, makes containers brittle or leaky.6 A barrel that sat in a sunny yard is a lower-value find than one from a dark shed. Short-lived: use now or leaveFood from a fridge or freezer without power18Refrigerated medicines kept warm16Undated bleach21Milk jugs5 Keeps its value if stored wellMetal hand tools, kept dry and oiledGlass jars and bottlesFasteners in sealed tinsHDPE containers kept out of light6Wool and cotton kept dry and away from pests The 30-year viewEven good finds wear out. Containers in sun can start to fall apart within 5 years.6 CO alarms need replacing every 5 years.22 Stored bleach is a first-year tool.21Plan salvage as a cycle, not a one-time haul. Log a replace-by date for every item that wears out.

s.h: ⚖️ Weight vs value: carry it or leave it?
s.x: Water is the heaviest thing you will move. One liter weighs 1 kg (2.2 lb). One US gallon weighs 8.33 lb (3.8 kg).8 A 2018 study in Military Medicine notes that loads of 30% of body mass or less are recommended to avoid drops in performance.23 Those were fit soldiers. Treat 30% as a ceiling, not a target. The 30% ceiling, and how much water that equals (arithmetic) Body weight30% ceilingEquals this much water 50 kg (110 lb)15 kg (33 lb)15 L (4.0 gal) 70 kg (154 lb)21 kg (46 lb)21 L (5.5 gal) 90 kg (198 lb)27 kg (60 lb)27 L (7.1 gal) Do the family math. At the Sphere amount of 15 L per person per day, a family of 4 needs 60 L (60 kg) of water a day.98 A 70 kg adult at the 30% ceiling carries 21 kg.23 That is 3 full loads every day. Carts and wheelbarrows are high-value finds. See Bicycles, Carts & Moving Loads. Value per kilogram matters too. A pack of gauze, a pair of glasses or a box of batteries weighs little and is hard to replace. A heavy item you already own one of adds little. Is it ours to take?No permission, no agreement: leave it. Is it safe to handle?Chemicals, fuel, flood soaking or damaged batteries: leave it and mark the spot. Does it meet a top-4 need?Water, medical, warmth or safe light: take it first. Will it spoil before we use it?If yes, take only what you will use now. Check the chart above. Can we carry it safely?If it pushes anyone past 30% of body weight, come back with a cart or a second person.23 DoCarry containers empty and fill them close to where you use the waterUse carts, wagons and wheelbarrowsSplit heavy loads between peopleMark heavy finds and come back Don'tWalk long distances with full glass jarsGive children adult loadsCarry fuel or chemicals home in food containersTake more than you can store dry

If it is not written down, you do not have it. A log stops double counting, shows what is running out, and proves where each item came from. The Red Cross says to check first aid kit expiration dates and replace anything used or out of date.12 Ready.gov says to replace expired items and re-think your needs every year.13 The CDC says to label stored water with the date.4 Example salvage log (one line per item) Item and countFrom, and who allowed itCheck or replace by 2 HDPE #2 jugs, 20 LNeighbor's garage; owner, 3 MayRefill water every 6 months4 1 bottle liquid bleach, datedOwn home1 year from the date21 1 battery CO alarmGroup store, by agreement5 years from its date22 Every dayCheck lids, water levels and that every log entry has a place. Every 6 monthsReplace water you bottled yourself.4 Every yearReplace bleach that is a year old.21 Re-think the group's needs and replace expired items.13 Every 5 yearsReplace CO alarms.22 Inspect barrels and jugs for brittleness.6 Sharing by need Share water by need, drinking first. Sphere puts drinking and food at 2.5–3 L per person per day, within basic survival needs of 7.5–15 L.9 The CDC says pregnant women, sick people and hot climates need more.4 Share heavy tools, not just food. A group can keep one set of saws, ladders and carts with a sign-out sheet. That leaves more carrying capacity for water and medical supplies. Write the sharing rules before you need them. See Organizing Neighbors. Turning leftovers into tools is in Repurposing Junk. Do a salvage audit of your own home this weekWalk each room with the floor plan above. List every container, first aid item, blanket, tool and battery you already own. Then you know what is worth asking others for. Get these before you need themFood-grade water jugs with a tap or spout10Rubber boots, rubber gloves and goggles19Work gloves and dust masks13A waterproof marker, labels and a notebook for the log4 Print these while the internet worksRed Cross: Anatomy of a First Aid Kit, your medical salvage list12Ready.gov: Build a Kit, the basic supply list13CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply, container rules4

Walk your home room by room and list every water container, first aid item, blanket, tool and battery Check each plastic jug for HDPE #2 and throw out milk jugs used for water Move any water stored near fuel or pesticides Print the Red Cross first aid list and tick off what you have Date every bottle of bleach and every CO alarm you own Put rubber boots, gloves, goggles and dust masks in one salvage bag Start a salvage log notebook with columns for item, source, permission and check date Agree with neighbors, in writing, how shared salvage will be stored and split Read Scavenging vs Looting and Salvage Hazards before you collect anything that is not yours

What are the first three salvage priorities?Water containers, medical and hygiene supplies, then warmth: blankets, sleeping bags and sheeting. Which plastic number marks a good water container?HDPE #2, food-grade. Never one that held bleach, pesticides or fuel. How much water does Sphere set per person per day?15 L (about 4 gallons) for drinking, cooking and hygiene. How heavy is a liter of water?1 kg (2.2 lb). A US gallon is 8.33 lb. What is the load ceiling for a fit adult?30% of body weight. A 70 kg adult: 21 kg. How long is fridge food safe with no power?About 4 hours with the door closed. Full freezer: about 48 hours. What goes in the salvage log?Item, count, where it came from, who allowed it, and the check or replace date.

Know what it held before you reuse it. The CDC says a container that held toxic chemicals, such as bleach or pesticides, must never hold drinking water.1 For food and water, reuse only food-grade plastic. Look for the 2 in the recycling triangle: high-density polyethylene (HDPE). Heavy-duty, food-grade #1 (PETE) is also accepted.23 Milk and juice jugs get non-food jobs. Their residue lets bacteria grow, and they turn brittle.42 Boiling does not remove fuel or chemicals. If you do not know an item's past, keep it away from food, water and fire.5 Put a lid on every bucket and barrel. A child can drown in less than 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water.6 #2HDPE, the best plastic for stored water2 5 yrsblue barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart7 458 lba full 208 L (55 gal) drum, about 208 kg8 <1 in(2.5 cm) of water can drown a small child6

s.h: ♻️ Three questions before you reuse anything Year 1
s.x: Over 30 years, worn-out and salvaged things become your raw material. Repurposing works when the right material goes to the right job. It fails when the wrong material ends up next to food, water, fire or a child. Ask three questions every time, in this order. What is it made of? Plastic (find the code), glass, wood, metal, or something you cannot name. What did it hold or touch? Food, water, fuel, chemicals, pesticides or floodwater. What will it touch next? Drinking water, food, fire, skin, children or dogs. The answers decide the job. The CDC rule for drinking water is short: use food-grade containers, and never use containers that held toxic chemicals such as bleach or pesticides.1 Plastic picks up what sits near it. University of Nebraska–Lincoln (UNL) Extension warns that fuel and pesticide vapors penetrate plastic.9 The CDC says to store water containers away from gasoline and pesticides.1 Food-grade HDPE #2 or PETE #1 can hold water after cleaning. Anything that held toxic chemicals cannot.231 Chemical containers never hold food or waterThe CDC says not to use containers that held toxic chemicals for drinking water.1 Boiling does not remove fuel or toxic chemicals from water.5Mark these containers NOT FOR FOOD and give them a non-food job, or leave them. Salvage lawfullyRepurpose what you own, what you are given, or what you have clear permission to take. Taking other people's property is theft. Looting is a crime, and many places punish it more harshly during a declared emergency.The law and the ethics are in Scavenging vs Looting.

s.h: 🧴 Plastics: read the code, then clean it
s.x: Turn the container over and find the number inside the recycling triangle. Utah's Division of Emergency Management says to look for the 2. Food-grade high-density polyethylene (HDPE #2) is its best choice for stored water.2 Oregon State University Extension also accepts heavy-duty, food-grade containers stamped PETE (#1, polyethylene terephthalate) or HDPE.3 Resin codes and reuse for food or water CodeWhat it isFood or water? #2HDPEYes, if food-grade. The best choice for water.2 #1PETEYes, if heavy-duty and food-grade.3 #3 to #7Other plasticsNot named by the agencies cited here. Non-food jobs, unless the maker labels it food-grade.1 Any codeMilk or juice jugNot for water. Residue feeds bacteria.4 Any codeHeld chemicals, fuel or pesticidesNever for food or water.1 The number alone is not enough. The CDC asks for food-grade containers.1 A #2 bucket that once held paint or pool chemicals is still a chemical container. A well-rinsed milk jug is fine for storing water. Ready.gov says milk and fruit juice containers keep protein and sugar residue that lets bacteria grow.4 Utah's guide adds that milk jugs break down and become brittle.2 Sanitize a reused food-grade container This is the CDC method. You need soap, water and plain, unscented liquid chlorine bleach.1 Wash and rinseWash the container with soap and water. Rinse it completely.1 Mix the sanitizerStir 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of unscented liquid chlorine bleach into 1 quart (about 1 liter) of water.1 Coat every surfacePour it in, cap it and shake so the solution touches every inside surface.1 Wait, then emptyWait at least 30 seconds, then pour the solution out.1 Fill and capFill with safe water and close it tightly. Ready.gov's version of these steps is written for chlorinated tap water.14 Label itWrite "drinking water" and the date on it.1 Write the job on the containerUse a permanent marker: WATER, FOOD or NOT FOR FOOD. For water, the CDC asks at least for "drinking water" and the date.1 A clear label helps a tired family member grab the right jug.

A clean, food-grade HDPE drum becomes a water barrel. Utah's guidance names food-grade HDPE #2 as the best plastic for stored water.2 Place it before you fill it. Water weighs 1 kg per liter (8.33 lb per gallon).8 So a full 208 L (55-gallon) drum weighs about 208 kg (458 lb). UNL Extension advises sturdy shelving for stored water because of its weight.9 Raise it off concrete and keep it out of the sun. Be Ready Utah says to raise containers off concrete for air flow. It also says blue barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart within 5 years.7 Utah State University Extension adds that plastic on concrete or dirt absorbs odors.11 Give it a lid and a tap. CDC safe-storage guidance prefers a container with a small opening, a lid and a spigot (tap). Wide-mouth vessels let hands, cups and dippers contaminate the water.12 The CDC also says to keep treated water in clean, covered containers.13 Shade it, raise it off concrete, keep the lid on and draw water from a tap. Leave room for ice where it can freeze.71298 Turn a food-grade drum or bucket into a water station Check its historyIt must be food-grade and must never have held chemicals, fuel or pesticides.1 Wash and sanitizeUse the CDC steps in the plastics section above.1 Fit a lid and a tapKeep the lid on. Draw water from the tap so no hand or cup goes inside.12 Set it up high and dryPut it on a pallet or boards, in shade, away from fuel and pesticides.71 Fill with safe waterFor a full 208 L (55-gallon) drum, Oregon State gives 2 tablespoons (30 mL) of unscented household bleach.3 For other amounts, see Disinfecting Water. Leave room to freezeWhere it can freeze, leave 2–3 inches (5–8 cm) of headspace.9 Label and rotateWrite "drinking water" and the date. Replace water you stored yourself every 6 months.1 Rain barrels Rainwater must be treated before you drink it. The CDC lists rainwater among the outdoor sources that need treatment.5 Utah State University Extension says the same.11 A rain barrel is a food-grade drum under a downspout. Roof math, gutters, first-flush diverters, screens and mosquito control are in Rainwater Harvesting. Drum stoves and burn barrelsThis chapter gives no plans for drum stoves or burn barrels. For heat, see Heating With Wood. Never cut, weld or heat a drum unless you know it never held fuel or chemicals.If anything burns indoors, fit a battery-powered carbon monoxide (CO) alarm.

Match each item to a job the guidance supports. This table covers common household salvage. Common salvage and the use the guidance supports ItemBest useKey rule Food-grade HDPE (#2) drumWater barrel or rain barrelShade it.7 Treat rainwater before drinking.5 Food-grade bucket with lidCovered water container with a tapLid on, no dipping.12 Heavy-duty PETE (#1) drink bottleDrinking-water bottleFood-grade only, sanitized first.31 Wood pallet or boardsPlatform under water containersKeeps plastic off concrete.711 Milk or juice jugNon-food jobsResidue feeds bacteria.4 Chemical, fuel or pesticide containerNon-food jobs, clearly markedNever food or water.1 Glass jarDry food storageNot for water that can freeze.9 Pallets Use pallets and boards to lift water containers off concrete. Be Ready Utah and Utah State University Extension both advise it.711 Before you burn or build with any salvaged wood, read Salvage Hazards. Bicycles Keep bicycles whole and rideable. Do not strip a working bike for parts. Repairs, spare parts, trailers and handcarts are in Bicycles, Carts & Moving Loads. Tires and car parts Check the vehicle hazards first. Tires, wire, mirrors and seat fabric, plus battery acid and lead safety, are in Useful Parts From Vehicles. Glass Do not store water in glass where it can freeze. UNL Extension advises against glass for stored water. It says to leave 2–3 inches (5–8 cm) of headspace in containers that may freeze.9 Glass jars for dry foods are covered in Mylar, Buckets, Oxygen Absorbers & Pests. Handle broken glass with thick gloves and sweep it up at once. Metal Know the metal before it touches food or fire. Zinc-coated (galvanized) metal and its fumes are covered in Basic Blacksmithing & Metal Repair. Old paint is covered in Salvage Hazards.

s.h: ☠️ The red list: what not to reuse
s.x: When in doubt, keep it out of food, water and fire. Every rule below comes from the guidance cited in this chapter. Do Reuse food-grade #2 HDPE and #1 PETE for water23 Sanitize before the first fill1 Store water away from gasoline and pesticides1 Wear rubber boots, gloves and goggles for flood-soaked salvage10 Disinfect flood-soaked toys before children use them10 Don't Put water in a container that held bleach, pesticides or other toxic chemicals1 Store water in milk or juice jugs4 Trust boiling to remove fuel or chemicals5 Store water in glass where it can freeze9 Leave plastic water containers in direct sun7 Boiling or bleach will make water from a fuel or chemical drum safe. The CDC says not to use water that may hold fuel or toxic chemicals, because boiling will not remove them.5 Its infant-feeding guidance adds that chemical contamination cannot be removed by boiling, disinfecting or filtering.20 Floods move chemical containers. The CDC warns about this in its floodwater guidance.10 Treat any container that sat in floodwater as unknown until you know what it held. The CDC also says to wash flood-soaked clothes in hot water with detergent.10 Do that before cloth goes to rags, bedding or patches. Materials to identify first Do not sand, cut, burn or cook on these until you have read the chapter named. Old painted wood or metal: lead paint, in Salvage Hazards Building materials and insulation: asbestos, also in Salvage Hazards Zinc-coated (galvanized) metal: zinc fumes, in Basic Blacksmithing & Metal Repair Car batteries: acid and lead, in Useful Parts From Vehicles Wood of unknown treatment: do not burn it, and do not build food beds or animal feeders from it Dogs and salvageKeep salvaged chemical containers capped and out of a dog's reach. Disinfect anything that sat in floodwater before it becomes a dog bowl or toy, the same way the CDC advises for children's toys.10

Run every item through the same line. A fixed path keeps unknown and dirty things apart from food, water and children. Flood-soaked items need boots, gloves and goggles. Food and water containers stay away from fuel and pesticides.10117 QuarantineBring salvage to an outdoor holding spot first. Wear rubber boots, gloves and goggles for anything flood-soaked.10 IdentifyFind the resin code, the old label or the material. Ask what it held. If nobody knows, it is non-food. CleanWash everything. Sanitize anything headed for food or water with the CDC method.1 SortGreen bin: food and water. Yellow bin: non-food jobs. Red bin: marked NOT FOR FOOD, or discarded. Label and logWrite the job and the date on the item. Record it in a paper notebook so the group knows what exists. Store and shareKeep food and water containers away from fuel and pesticides.1 Share surplus through your group; see What to Salvage First. Workshop safety rules Keep generators outside. Never run one in a home, garage or carport. Place it at least 20 feet (6 m) from doors, windows and vents.17 The CPSC says never indoors, even with doors and windows open.18 Fit a battery-powered CO alarm anywhere a fire, stove or engine runs near people. Replace it every 5 years.16 Plan two ways out. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) home escape plan calls for two ways out.19 Keep both clear of stacked salvage. Practice this nowWhile hardware stores are open, sanitize one food-grade bucket and fit it with a tap. Then spend 10 minutes sorting your garage into green, yellow and red piles. Get this before you need it Food-grade buckets with tight lids, and drum taps (spigots) A bung wrench for drum caps Permanent markers and tape for labels Rubber boots, heavy gloves and safety goggles Battery-powered CO alarms, with spare batteries Plain, unscented liquid chlorine bleach

s.h: ⏳ Keeping plastic useful for 30 years Long haul
s.x: Shade protects plastic. Be Ready Utah says light makes containers brittle and grows algae in stored water.7 Every container you protect is one you do not have to replace. Keep plastic out of the sun, off bare concrete and away from fuel.71 Day 0Sanitize, fill and label with "drinking water" and the date.1 Month 6Replace water you stored yourself.114 Check each empty container for cracks. Every yearLook for brittle plastic and algae. Light causes both.7 Move brittle containers to non-food work. Year 5Blue barrels kept in direct sun can start to fall apart.7 Replace battery CO alarms.16 Years 5–30Down-cycle: water container, then dry non-food storage, then parts bin. Re-label it at every step. The 30-year viewYour stock of food-grade containers is limited, so guard it. Never let a food-grade drum be borrowed for fuel, paint or pesticide. Once it holds a chemical, the CDC rule takes it out of food and water use for good.1

Check every water container for the 2 or 1 in the recycling triangle and a food-grade label Move milk and juice jugs to non-food jobs Mark every container that held chemicals, fuel or pesticides NOT FOR FOOD Store food and water containers away from fuel and pesticides Put pallets or boards under water drums and move them out of the sun Put lids on every bucket and barrel a toddler can reach Buy a drum tap, a bung wrench and permanent markers Set up an outdoor quarantine spot with boots, gloves and goggles Install a battery CO alarm in any workshop where something burns Read Salvage Hazards before you sand, cut or burn painted wood or metal

Which plastic code is best for stored water?#2 HDPE, food-grade. Heavy-duty, food-grade #1 PETE is also accepted. Can a rinsed milk jug store water?No. Residue grows bacteria and the jug turns brittle. Can boiling fix water from a chemical drum?No. Boiling does not remove fuel or toxic chemicals. How do you sanitize a container?1 tsp (5 mL) unscented bleach per quart (1 L) of water. Shake to coat, wait 30 seconds, pour out. How heavy is a full 55-gallon drum?About 208 kg (458 lb). Place it before you fill it. Why a tap instead of a dipper?Hands, cups and dippers contaminate water in wide-mouth containers. How much water can drown a toddler?Less than 1 inch (2.5 cm). Lid every bucket.

Evacuate from the water, not the wind. Storm surge and large waves are the greatest threat to life on the coast.12 Inland is not safe either. Flooding is the major hurricane threat inland. Hurricane Helene killed at least 250 people in the US in 2024.13 Generators go outside, at least 6.1 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents. Never in a home, garage or carport.4 The deaths do not stop when the wind stops. Hurricane Maria's official toll was 64. A later study counted 2,975 excess deaths.56 Bathtub water saved before a storm is for flushing and cleaning only. Do not drink it, and keep small children away from a filled tub.78 49%of US hurricane and tropical storm deaths, 1963–2012, came from storm surge9 250+US deaths from Hurricane Helene, 20243 53 dayslength of the water crisis in Asheville, North Carolina, after Helene10 20 ft(6.1 m) minimum from a generator to doors, windows and vents4 Not yet in this editionTornado shelter, mobile homes, window protection, chainsaws and downed power lines are not covered here yet. Those sections are still being checked against official sources, and this book prints only checked facts.Until they are added, save your national weather service's tornado and hurricane safety pages while the internet works. Two official hurricane pages are listed in the "Download now" box below.

s.h: 🌊 Storm surge: the deadliest hurricane hazard
s.x: In a hurricane, water kills more people than wind.9 The National Hurricane Center (NHC) says storm surge and large waves are the greatest threat to life and property along the coast.1 Storm surge is an abnormal rise of seawater generated by the storm, over and above the normal tide.1 It is the sea itself coming onto the land. An NHC study by Edward Rappaport blamed 49% of US hurricane and tropical storm deaths from 1963 to 2012 on storm surge.9 That is why an NHC official put it so simply: "We evacuate from the water, not the wind, and we have evacuation zones."2 Learn your zone before the season starts. For the full decision, see Stay or Go? On the coast, storm surge and large waves are the greatest threat to life. Inland, flooding is the major threat.1 Helene killed at least 250 people in the US.3 Hurricane wind kills most people, so a strong house keeps you safe. Storm surge caused 49% of US hurricane and tropical storm deaths from 1963 to 2012.9 On the coast, surge and waves are the greatest threat to life.1 Download now, while the internet worksSave these official pages to your phone, then print them:NHC: Hurricane Hazards (storm surge and inland flooding)NWS: Hurricane Safety Checklist (printable PDF)

A late, crowded evacuation can kill too. When Hurricane Rita threatened Texas, nearly 3.7 million people evacuated in 4 days.11 More than 100 of at least 119 deaths were linked to the evacuation, not to the storm itself.11 At least 10% were heat illness (hyperthermia) in vehicles, and a bus carrying nursing-home residents caught fire.11 Do not let this keep you in a surge zone. The lesson is to leave early, with a plan and fuel in the tank.12 Know your zone nowFind out before the season whether your home is in a storm surge evacuation zone.2 Keep fuel in the carKeep at least half a tank at all times. Fill up when an evacuation seems likely.12 Plan where you will goDecide how you will leave and where you will stay.12 Check that the place accepts your dogs, since public shelters may not.13 Leave earlyGo early enough that severe weather cannot trap you on the road.12 Use official routesFollow the recommended evacuation routes. Do not take shortcuts.12 Carry water for the drivePack drinking water for every person and pet in the car. Heat in vehicles killed people during the Rita evacuation.11 Dogs and other petsTemporary public shelters may not allow animals.13 Find a pet-friendly place to stay before the season, not on the day you leave.Microchip your dog. Vet clinics and animal shelters scan for microchips.13 Store extra water for pets, too.14 See Dogs in a Long Emergency. Practice this nowDo a timed dry run on a calm day. Load the car with go-bags, water, medicines, dogs and leashes, and note how long it takes.Then drive your official evacuation route once, so you know it in the dark and in the rain.Next, test-run the generator at its marked spot with the CO alarms switched on, so the first time is not during a storm.

Hurricanes kill far from the beach. For people living inland, NHC says flooding is the major threat.1 Hurricane Helene came ashore as a Category 4 hurricane on September 26, 2024. It caused at least 250 deaths in the US, making it the deadliest hurricane on the US mainland since Katrina.3 Helene left 5.9 million customers without power across 10 states.15 In the mountain city of Asheville, North Carolina, a systemwide boil water notice followed, and the water crisis lasted 53 days.1610 Sept 26, 2024Helene comes ashore as a Category 4 hurricane.3 After landfall5.9 million customers lose power across 10 states.15 Asheville goes under a systemwide boil water notice.16 Nov 18, 2024After 120 water samples are tested, Asheville lifts the notice for all customers. The water crisis lasted 53 days.1016 How people die in sudden disastersIn rapid-onset disasters such as storms and floods, most deaths come from blunt trauma, crush injuries and drowning.17 The 30-year viewHelene left millions without power and a whole mountain city without safe tap water for 53 days.1510 With no grid for decades, your household has to store, collect and treat its own water.Build that system now. See Disinfecting Water.

Treat floodwater like sewage. It can carry sewage and chemicals. Swallowing water or food it has contaminated causes diarrheal disease, such as E. coli and Salmonella infections.18 Private wells must be tested and disinfected after floodwaters go down. Check with your water utility or health department about boil water advisories.19 Boiling, disinfecting and filtering cannot remove chemical contamination.20 If floodwater may hold fuel or chemicals, use a different water source. See Floods. Check the water noticeAsk the water utility or health department whether a boil water advisory is in force.19 Gear up before cleanupWear rubber boots, rubber gloves and goggles.18 Do not bathe in itDo not bathe in water that may be contaminated with floodwater.18 Wash what it touchedWash clothes in hot water with detergent. Disinfect children's toys before they play with them.18 Test the wellTest and disinfect a private well before anyone drinks from it.19 Dead bodies left after a storm will start an epidemic. There is no evidence that dead bodies cause epidemics after natural disasters.17 Outbreak risk comes from displacement, crowding, and unsafe water and sanitation.17 Disasters that do not displace people rarely lead to outbreaks. Diarrheal outbreaks can follow contamination of drinking water.17 Keeping your household housed and your water clean protects you most. Babies and formulaMix formula with bottled water until officials declare the tap water safe.20 Boiling cannot remove chemicals, so water touched by floodwater is not a safe base for formula.20Disinfect toys that touched floodwater before a baby mouths them.18

Generators poison people after hurricanes. After two major hurricanes in Alabama and Texas in 2005, portable generators poisoned at least 78 people with carbon monoxide (CO) and killed 10.21 Most of those generators were outside, but near the home.21 "Outside" is not enough. Distance matters. CO has no color and no smell. People who are asleep can die from it before they have any symptoms.22 Generators are not the only source. CO comes from burning fuel in cars, small engines, stoves, lanterns, grills, fireplaces, gas ranges and furnaces, and it builds up in enclosed spaces.22 After a storm, cook and run engines outdoors only. Run a generator outside, at least 6.1 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents, and never in a home, garage or carport.4 Point the exhaust away from buildings. Never run one inside, even with doors and windows open.23 Outside onlyNever run it in a home, garage or carport.4 Open doors and windows do not make it safe.23 Measure the distancePlace it at least 6.1 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.4 Use a tape measure the first time. Aim the exhaust awayPoint the exhaust away from every building.23 Alarm the sleeping areasPut battery or battery-backup CO alarms near sleeping areas. Replace each alarm every 5 years.22 Act on symptoms fastHeadache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain or confusion: get everyone into fresh air, then get medical help.4 DoGenerator outside, 6.1 m (20 ft) or more from doors, windows and ventsExhaust pointed away from the houseBattery CO alarms near sleeping areasAn extension cord longer than 6.1 m (20 ft) Don'tRun it in a garage or carport, even with the door openSet it just outside a door or windowHeat the home with a gas oven4Run a car in a garage or carport4 A generator is safe in the garage if the big door is open. Never use a generator inside a home or garage, even with doors and windows open.23 Keep it at least 6.1 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.4 Who is at higher riskInfants, older people, and people with heart disease, anemia or breathing problems are at higher risk from CO.22 CO poisons animals too, so dogs shut in with a running engine are in danger.22Full details are in Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer. Get these before storm seasonBattery or battery-backup CO alarms for each sleeping area22An extension cord longer than 6.1 m (20 ft), so the generator can stay far

s.h: 💧 Store water before landfall, then guard it
s.x: Fill your bathtub and large containers before the storm. Use the bathtub water for cleaning and flushing toilets only. Do not drink it.7 For drinking, store at least 3.8 liters (1 gallon) per person per day for at least 3 days, and for 2 weeks if you can.14 Helene showed why: Asheville's water crisis lasted 53 days.10 Use food-grade containers, never old bleach or pesticide bottles. Label and date them, and replace stored tap water every 6 months.14 Keep them out of sunlight and away from gasoline and pesticides.14 See Storing Water for Months & Years.  A filled tub can drown a toddlerFrom 2006 to 2010, 434 children under 5 drowned at home in the US. 82% were under age 2, and 81% of the deaths involved bathtubs or bath products.8Keep the bathroom door closed while the tub is full. Never leave a young child alone near a filled tub or bucket. Pregnancy and stored waterStore more water if anyone in the home is pregnant or sick, or if you live in a hot climate.14 Count the extra before the season, not after the taps stop. Food after the outageWhen the power has been off for hours, sort the fridge and freezer before anyone eats. Use the rules in Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

s.h: 🧓 The long tail: deaths after the storm passes
s.x: Most of a hurricane's deaths can come after the wind stops. After Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico in 2017, the official death count was 64.56 A study commissioned by Puerto Rico's governor found 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018.6 That is more than 46 times the official count.
