s.h: 🏝️ Puerto Rico after Maria: 11 months to reconnect Year 1
s.x: What happened Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico on September 20, 2017.2 About 11 months later, officials said every part of the island had power again.1 A Harvard-led team surveyed 3,299 randomly chosen households. From landfall to December 31, 2017, homes averaged 84 days without electricity, 68 days without water and 41 days without cell phone service (NEJM, 2018).2 Remote homes waited longest. In remote areas, 83% of homes had no electricity for the whole period studied.2 How many people died The first official death toll was 64. The household survey estimated 4,645 excess deaths from landfall to the end of 2017.2 A George Washington University (GWU) study, commissioned by Puerto Rico's governor, estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018.7 "Excess deaths" are deaths above the number normally expected. The first official count was 64. Two independent studies later estimated thousands of excess deaths.27 Missed care killed people for months. The survey linked about one third of excess deaths to delayed or interrupted medical care.2 The GWU study tracked excess deaths through February 2018, about five months after landfall.7 The GWU team found that poor and elderly people had the highest risk of dying.7 Older adults carried the most riskAfter Maria, older men had a death risk 35% higher than expected.7 Put the medicines, devices, warmth and cooling of older relatives at the top of your plan. See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People. First counts can be far too lowThe first Maria count was 64.2 The study commissioned by the governor found 2,975, about 46 times more.7 Texas raised its 2021 count from 210 to 246.3 Always check the date on a number. The 30-year viewPuerto Rico's island-wide restoration took about 11 months.1 Thirty years is about 33 times longer (360 months ÷ 11), and this book assumes no repair crews arrive. Plan the long haul with Year 1 to Year 30: A Phased Plan.

s.h: ❄️ Texas, February 2021: up to four days in the cold First 72 h
s.x: More than 4.5 million people in Texas lost power, some for up to 4 days. Federal regulators found that frozen generating equipment was the main cause.8 Texas linked 246 deaths to the storm. The count rose from 210 in an earlier report. About two-thirds of the deaths were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia, which means body temperature falling dangerously low.3 Water failed at the same time. Water system disruptions hit more than 14 million Texans.4 The lesson: a blackout of a few days can kill when it is cold. Most of the Texas deaths came from cold, not from the dark.3 Heat for the most vulnerable person in the house comes first. See Winter Storms & Extreme Cold. Babies and young childrenReady.gov warns that older adults and young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures. If your home gets too cold or too hot, go to a place with heat or cooling.17 Plan the warmest spot in your home for the youngest child first: see Staying Warm Without Heat. Never heat your home with a gas stove or ovenReady.gov says never to use a gas stove or oven to heat your home.17 Read Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer before winter comes.

s.h: 🚰 When the pumps stop, the water stops First 72 h
s.x: Tap water runs on electricity. Water and wastewater plants often use about 30–40% of a town's energy (EPA, 2024).18 Losing power for more than 30 minutes can disrupt wastewater treatment.18 Cleveland and Detroit, August 2003 On August 14, 2003, about 50 million people in the US and Canada lost power. The outage cut 61,800 megawatts of load across eight US states and Ontario.9 In Cleveland, the four major water supply pumps lost power. Taps gave only a trickle.10 Residents were then warned to boil their water.19 In Detroit, a boil-water alert covered 4.3 million customers. It was not lifted until August 19, five days after the blackout began.119 Asheville, North Carolina, 2024 After Hurricane Helene, Asheville did not lift its boil water notice for all customers until November 18, 2024.16 Local public radio called it a 53-day water crisis. The notice was lifted after 120 water samples were tested.15 Why it matters for health A review in a CDC journal found that diarrheal outbreaks after disasters can follow contamination of drinking water.20 Keep toilet waste far away from anything you drink. See Toilets Without Water. Fill clean containers at onceCleveland's taps dropped to a trickle when its pumps lost power.10 Fill every clean, lidded container while pressure lasts. Separate drinking water from washing waterLabel them. Keep drinking water covered and away from flushing and cleaning water. Treat tap water when it comes backBoil-water warnings followed the 2003 blackout in Cleveland and Detroit.1911 Boil or disinfect tap water until officials say it is safe. See Disinfecting Water. Count your days of waterAsheville's water crisis lasted 53 days.15 Write down how many days your stored water covers each person. When the water comes back on, it is safe to drink. Not always. Cleveland residents were warned to boil water after the 2003 blackout.19 Asheville's boil notice ran until November 18, 2024.16 Treat tap water until officials say it is safe.

s.h: 🏭 Ukraine, 2022 to 2025: a grid under repeated attack Long haul
s.x: Before 2022, Ukraine had about 38 gigawatts (GW) of dispatchable power capacity.6 Dispatchable plants are the ones operators can turn up or down on demand. Ukraine lost 19 GW to occupation, destruction and damage in the first year of the full-scale war. After more attacks in spring 2024, about 12 GW was left (IEA, 2025).6 About two-thirds of Ukraine's dispatchable capacity was gone after the spring 2024 attacks (38 GW down to about 12 GW).6 That is about two-thirds of the capacity gone (38 − 12 = 26 GW; 26 ÷ 38 ≈ 68%). The attacks continued. On September 7–8, 2025, Russia carried out its largest air attack on Ukraine since February 2022, with major damage to energy infrastructure.6 The lesson: repeated damage kept capacity far below its pre-war level from 2022 into 2024, and major attacks were still hitting energy infrastructure in 2025.6 The 30-year viewThis book plans for a grid with no repairs at all. Build household systems that need no grid: see Low-Tech Power for the Long Haul and What Fails When: The 30-Year Timeline.

s.h: 🏧 Spain and Portugal, 2025: 16 hours without cash or trains
s.x: On April 28, 2025, a widespread blackout hit Spain and Portugal. Subway networks, traffic lights and ATMs stopped.13 Full restoration took about 16 hours. The expert panel's final report (2026) found no single trigger, with voltage management at the center of the failure.12 Even a 16-hour blackout was linked to deaths. Early reports linked at least three deaths to it. In Galicia, police investigated carbon monoxide (CO) from a generator after an older couple and their adult son died at home.14 Money and fuel stop first Payments and fuel need power. FEMA lists fuel pumps, lighting and payment systems among the systems hit by power outages (2025).21 Ready.gov warns that ATMs and card machines may not work, and says to keep cash in your kit.17 Plan for a world without cards. See Barter, Trade & Money After Collapse. "Outside" is not far enough for a generatorAfter Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005, portable generators poisoned at least 78 people with CO and killed 10. Most of those generators were outside, but near the home.5Keep generators outdoors and at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows. Fit CO alarms with battery backup.17 See Generators & Fuel Storage.

s.h: 🩺 What studies measured: how long blackouts hurt health
s.x: The studies and official counts behind these cases point to five killers. Each one is documented: Missed medical care: about one third of Maria's excess deaths.2 Cold: about two-thirds of the 246 Texas deaths in 2021.3 Generator fumes: 10 deaths and at least 78 poisonings after Katrina and Rita.5 Unsafe water: diarrheal outbreaks can follow contamination of drinking water.20 Heat during evacuation: overheating in vehicles during the Hurricane Rita evacuation.22 The power cut is only the first failure. Water,10 heat,3 medical devices,23 fuel and payments,2113 generator safety5 and phones2 all failed in real events. Leaving can kill too Nearly 3.7 million people left the Texas coast in the 4 days before Hurricane Rita in 2005. Over 100 of at least 119 deaths linked to Rita came from the evacuation itself.22 At least 10% of those evacuation deaths were linked to overheating in vehicles. A bus carrying nursing-home residents caught fire in the evacuation traffic, and about two dozen people died.22 Weigh both risks in Stay or Go? People who need power to stay alive In the US, more than 3 million Medicare patients have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment. More than 4.6 million rely on that equipment or on services such as dialysis, oxygen or home health care (HHS emPOWER).23 Ready.gov says to make a plan for any medical device that needs power, and for medicines that must stay cold.17 It also says to discard refrigerated medicine after an outage of more than a day, unless the label says otherwise.17 Do not throw away life-saving medicineThe one-day rule has an exception. If a life depends on a refrigerated medicine, Ready.gov says to ask a doctor or pharmacist and to use it only until a new supply is available.17 Insulin vials and cartridges can stay at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days.25 Displacement drives outbreaks A review in CDC's journal Emerging Infectious Diseases linked disease outbreaks after disasters mainly to displacement. Disasters that did not displace people rarely led to outbreaks.20 The same review linked outbreak risk to crowding, water and sanitation, nutrition, vaccine immunity and access to health care.20 A safe home with clean water and a working toilet covers several of those. A blackout kills in the first day or two. After that, it is just an inconvenience. After Maria, excess deaths were counted from September 2017 to Fe

Restoration ranged from hours to years. Here are the documented times, shortest first. 16 hoursSpain and Portugal, April 2025: full restoration.12 Up to 4 daysTexas, February 2021: more than 4.5 million people without power.8 Parts of the US also waited 4 days in August 2003.9 5 daysDetroit, August 2003: boil-water alert for 4.3 million customers, lifted August 19.11 Over 1 weekOntario, 2003: rolling blackouts in parts of the province.9 41 daysPuerto Rico, 2017: average home without cell phone service.2 53 daysAsheville, NC, 2024: water crisis after Hurricane Helene.15 68 daysPuerto Rico, 2017: average home without water.2 84 daysPuerto Rico, 2017: average home without electricity, counted to December 31.2 About 11 monthsPuerto Rico: power restored to the whole island in 2018.1 2022 to 2025Ukraine: about 12 GW of 38 GW left after spring 2024; the largest air attack of the war came on September 7–8, 2025.6 In Puerto Rico, phones and water came back before power, on average. Homes averaged 41 days without cell service and 68 without water, against 84 without electricity.2 Even the longest repair was short next to 30 yearsPuerto Rico's whole-island restoration took about 11 months.1 That is about 3% of 30 years (11 ÷ 360 months). Every system in your plan has to last far longer than any outage on record.

t: Year 1 to Year 30: A Phased Plan

s.x: Plan in four phases, not one stockpile. Live on stores (year 0–1), build production (years 1–3), make it last (years 3–10), then rebuild and hand on (years 10–30). One person at 2,100 kcal a day eats about 23 million kcal in 30 years. No home can store that.10 Year 1 is the build year. Puerto Rico needed about 11 months just to restore power after Hurricane Maria.13 Start every long-term system while stored food still covers you. Everything stored has an end date. Fridge food about 4 hours, insulin out of the fridge up to 28 days, home-bottled water 6 months, bleach 1 year, CO alarms 5 years.35267 Protect the children born after the grid fails. Diarrhea is the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months worldwide.17 Clean water, toilets and handwashing are your child survival plan. Skills outlast supplies. The AHA says children 12 and older can learn CPR.18 Drill twice a year, every year.19 23 Mkcal one person eats in 30 years at 2,100 kcal a day10 11 moto restore power to all of Puerto Rico after Maria13 1 in 3Maria excess deaths linked to delayed or interrupted health care12 5 yrsuntil CDC says to replace a carbon monoxide alarm7

This chapter turns the whole book into a schedule. For each phase it shows what to work on, what runs out, which skills to master and how your family changes. Stored supplies are a bridge, not a plan. At the planning figure of 2,100 kcal a day, one person eats 22,995,000 kcal in 30 years.10 At the CDC minimum of 1 gallon a day, they need 10,950 gallons (about 41,450 liters) of water.2 Real outages already last months. Homes surveyed in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria averaged 84 days without power.12 In Ukraine, attacks cut dispatchable power capacity from about 38 GW before 2022 to about 12 GW after spring 2024.14 This book plans for the longer case: 30 years with no grid and no repair crews. For the real events in detail, read Real Long Blackouts. The four phases at a glance PhaseMain jobMove on when 1. Stores Year 0–1Live on stores. Ration food, never water. Start water, toilet and garden systems.Your water comes from a system you run, and the first harvest is in. 2. Production Years 1–3Grow, raise and preserve food. Replace each store before it runs out.Food you produce covers most meals, and you saved seed for next year. 3. Make it last Years 3–10Keep tools, health, soil and skills working. Teach the children.At least two people can do every critical job. 4. Rebuild Years 10–30Trades, records and community health. Hand everything on.People born after the grid failed can run the systems. Phase 1 limits come from official guidance: fridge and freezer (USDA),3 insulin (FDA),5 stored water (CDC)2 and bleach (EPA).6 CO alarms7 and plastic drums left in direct sun8 wear out around year 5. Long outages end in a few days, so a 3-day kit is enough. Puerto Rico homes averaged 84 days without power after Maria,12 and the whole island took about 11 months.13 The Red Cross 3-day supply is for evacuation; it advises 2 weeks at home.1 How to use this chapterFind your phase. Read that section. Tick its milestones at the end of this chapter. Then follow its links to the detailed chapters.

s.h: 📦 Phase 1 · Year 0–1: Live on stores, build systems Year 1
s.x: Your job in year 1 is to stretch what you have and start what replaces it. Do not wait for stores to run low. The first weeks are covered in The First 72 Hours and The First 30 Days. What runs out in Phase 1 Hour 0ATMs and card machines may not work. Ready.gov says to keep some cash.4 Hour 4Food in a closed fridge stays safe for about 4 hours.3 Day 1–2A full freezer holds about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.3 Refrigerated medicine: discard after more than a day without power unless the label says otherwise.4 Day 14The end of a Red Cross 2-week home supply.1 Day 28Insulin vials and cartridges can stay out of the fridge for up to 28 days, and only at 15–30°C (59–86°F).5 Month 6Water you bottled yourself is due for replacement.2 Month 12Bleach passes the 1-year age that EPA's water disinfection method uses.6 Ration food, never water. FEMA and the Red Cross say healthy people can live on half their usual food for an extended period, but children and pregnant women should not be rationed.11 A normally active person needs to drink at least 2 quarts (about 2 liters) a day. Drink what you need today and find more for tomorrow.11 Do the year math once, on paper. A family of 4 at 2,100 kcal each eats 3,066,000 kcal a year.10 Add up the kcal printed on your stored food, divide by your family's yearly number, and you know how much of the year your stores cover. s.h: 🔧 Phase 3 · Years 3–10: Make it last Long haul
s.x: Phase 3 is maintenance. Your systems now feed you. The danger shifts to things that wear out slowly: alarms, plastics, tools, skills and health. What wears out in Phase 3 CO alarms: CDC says to replace them every 5 years.7 The alarms you fit in year 0 are due in year 5. Plastic drums in the sun: Be Ready Utah says blue barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart within 5 years.8 Shade them from day one. Medicines: every medicine has a date. The WHO 2025 Model Lists name 523 essential medicines for adults and 374 for children.24 Read Medicines: Shelf Life. Kits: Ready.gov says to re-think your needs every year and update the kit as your family changes.23 A newborn from year 0 is a school-age child by year 6. Disease risk rises with crowding and poor sanitation. A CDC review of epidemics after disasters linked outbreak risk to displacement, crowding, water and sanitation, nutrition, vaccine immunity and access to health care.15 WHO reports that better water, sanitation and hygiene can save about 1.4 million lives a year (2019 estimates).16 Poor hand hygiene alone was linked to about 384,000 diarrhea deaths.16 Read Public Health for a Small Community. Write your group's rules early, while things are calm. Read Group Rules, Decisions & Disputes and Tool Maintenance.

s.h: 🏗️ Phase 4 · Years 10–30: Rebuild and hand it on Long haul
s.x: Phase 4 is about handing knowledge on. The adults who learned skills before the grid failed are aging. The children born after it failed are growing into the workforce. The math is simple addition. A baby born in year 1 turns 18 in year 19. An adult who is 50 at the start is 80 in year 30. Older people need planned care, not leftover care. After Hurricane Maria, the poor and the elderly were at highest risk of death.25 Ready.gov says older adults and young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures.4 Phase 4 jobs Trades with apprentices: Rebuilding Local Trades Power without the grid: Low-Tech Power Records that last: Preserving Knowledge & Records Teaching the next generation: Passing On Skills Year 30 is a checkpoint, not an endAt one replacement every 5 years,7 each sleeping area uses 6 CO alarms in 30 years. A home with 3 sleeping areas uses 18.Every habit in this chapter, from the daily water log to the twice-yearly drill, carries on past year 30.

s.h: 👶 Children born after the grid fails
s.x: Plan for babies to be born in your group. Treat pregnancy, birth and childhood as core systems, not surprises. For methods and how well each works, read Contraception & Family Planning. One example family. Swap in your own ages. The AHA says children 12 and older can learn CPR, so the baby born in year 2 can train by year 14.18 Add 10, 20 and 30 years to each person PersonYear 0Year 10Year 20Year 30 Grandparent65758595 Parent35455565 Child8182838 Baby born in year 2not born81828 Young children die mostly of preventable causes. WHO lists diarrhea as the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months, with about 443,832 deaths in children under 5 each year.17 WHO estimates that unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene caused about 395,000 deaths of children under 5 in 2019.16 Your water and toilet systems are your children's survival systems. Vaccinate everyone now and copy the records. After disasters, measles risk depends on vaccine coverage, especially among children under 15.15 The Red Cross says to keep copies of important documents.1 Read Vaccine-Preventable Diseases. A child's path through the 30 years Ages 0–5: safe water, clean hands, toilets, warmth and full food rations.11 Ages 6–11: reading, writing, math and safe chores. Read Teaching Kids Without Schools. s.x: Water, latrines and soap come first. WHO linked at least 1.4 million deaths in 2019 to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene.1 Count on paper, every week. Tally new cases by sign, plus every birth and death. After Hurricane Maria the first official death count was 64; a study for the governor later estimated 2,975.45 Train health helpers in a few danger signs. Start with fast breathing in a child and dehydration from diarrhea.92 Mothers and young children first. FEMA and the Red Cross say food may be rationed, but not for children and pregnant women.18 When cases jump: separate, treat, find the source, block the route. Cholera can kill within hours, and most cases can be treated with oral rehydration solution (ORS).11 1.4Mdeaths in 2019 linked to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene1 1 in 3Hurricane Maria excess deaths linked to delayed or interrupted care4 443,832children under 5 killed by diarrhea each year2 1 per 20people per shared latrine, the UNHCR target6

Public health is the work of protecting everyone at once. A doctor treats one person at a time. A community that guards its water, latrines, food and records protects everyone together, and none of it needs electricity. The numbers below come from WHO data and real disasters. They point to the same short list: dirty water, human waste, dirty hands, crowding and missed care. Water, waste and hands Unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) kill on a huge scale. A 2023 WHO report found that safe WASH could have prevented at least 1.4 million deaths in 2019. More than 1 million of them were from diarrhea.1 Hands alone matter. WHO linked about 384,000 diarrheal deaths and 356,000 deaths from respiratory infections in 2019 to poor hand hygiene.1 Young children pay the most. Diarrhea is the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months. It kills about 443,832 children under 5 every year.2 Cholera is a current disease. In 2024, 60 countries reported 560,823 cholera cases and 6,028 deaths to WHO.12 Cholera deaths rose for a second year in a row, and by September 2025, 31 countries had reported outbreaks that year.25 Disasters: crowding and missed care A review in the CDC journal Emerging Infectious Diseases studied outbreaks after natural disasters. Displacement was the main risk factor. Disasters that did not displace people rarely led to outbreaks.3 The same review tied outbreak risk to crowding, safe water and sanitation, nutrition, vaccination coverage and access to health care.3 A community can work on every one of these. Missed care kills slowly. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, a household survey linked about one third of excess deaths to delayed or interrupted health care.4 Poor and elderly people had the highest risk of dying.5 Each threat has a community job ThreatWhat the evidence showsCommunity job Unsafe waterDiarrheal outbreaks after disasters can follow drinking-water contamination3One protected, treated water point Waste and dirty hands384,000 diarrheal deaths linked to poor hand hygiene in 20191Enough latrines, with soap and water beside each Crowding, displacementThe main outbreak risk factor after disasters3Keep people housed and spread out Missed careAbout 1 in 3 Maria excess deaths4Health helpers, a register, a medicine plan

s.h: 🚰 Water, latrines and soap: the first medicine
s.x: Plan water by the head count. The Sphere humanitarian standard sets a minimum of 15 liters (about 4 gallons) per person per day for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene.7 Sphere splits basic needs into 2.5–3 L for drinking and food, 2–6 L for hygiene and 3–6 L for cooking.7 How to find and treat that much water is in Disinfecting Water. One protected water point No hands, cups or dippers in the water. CDC guidance says wide-mouth containers let hands, cups and dippers carry germs into treated water. Safe containers have a small opening, a lid and a tap.23 Big batches need measured bleach. The EPA dose is 2/3 teaspoon of 6% unscented bleach per 8 gallons (30 L) of clear water. Double it for cloudy, colored or very cold water, then wait 30 minutes.22 Chlorine does not stop every germ. CDC rates chlorine and iodine as not effective against Cryptosporidium, and boiling as very effective.21 Boil drinking water for babies and the sick whenever you have fuel. Latrines and handwashing Build enough latrines. UNHCR's target is 1 latrine per 20 people, or 1 per household. In the first phase of an emergency, no latrine should serve more than 50 people.6 Put soap and water beside every latrine. The Sphere standards call for handwashing facilities close to latrines.6 Building them is covered in Toilets Without Water. Keep waste away from water. Diarrheal outbreaks after disasters can follow contamination of drinking water.3 Site latrines and garbage pits well away from the water point and the kitchen. Draw your own version of this map. UNHCR's latrine target is 1 per 20 people, with handwashing close to every latrine.6 Field math for a community of 60 people NeedStandardFor 60 people Water per day15 L (4 gal) per person7900 L (238 gal) Shared latrines1 per 20 people63 latrines Hard limit, first phaseNo more than 50 per latrine6At least 2 latrines 6% bleach, clear water2/3 tsp per 8 gal (30 L)22About 20 tsp (100 mL) a day to treat all 900 L  Bleach is a first-year toolEPA's method uses bleach stored for less than one year.22 At about 100 mL a day, 60 people would use about 36 L (9.5 gallons) of 6% bleach a year. Plan boiling, filters and pool shock for the decades after. See Disinfecting Water. Dogs and the water pointKeep dogs out of latrines, the kitchen, the water point and the sick room. CDC says to store extra water for pets, so count every dog in the water math.19

s.h: 🧑‍⚕️ Train your own community health helpers
s.x: Pick helpers, not heroes. A health helper is a trusted neighbor trained to spot danger signs, start simple care, keep records and send people on to a clinic whenever one works. Teach a short list well. Drill the danger signs in the table below until every helper can recite them and act on them without looking. Choose at least two helpersPick calm adults the community trusts, who can read and count. Two means one can rest or fall sick. Include a womanWomen and girls can then choose a woman to talk to about periods, pregnancy and assault. Teach the danger signsUse the table below. Practice counting a child's breaths for a full minute. Teach a few safe actionsORS and continued feeding for diarrhea,8 CPR and bleeding control. Get formal courses while teachers exist. Give them toolsA watch with a second hand, a thermometer, ORS sachets, soap, gloves, the tally sheet and the register. Meet every weekReview each sick person, the tally sheet and the medicine count. Write down what you decided. s.h: 📋 Paper surveillance: count it, write it, compare it
s.x: Surveillance means counting the same things, the same way, every week. When one count jumps above your normal, that is your early warning. Paper and a pencil are enough. Use fixed case definitions. WHO defines diarrhea as 3 or more loose or liquid stools in a day, and acute bloody diarrhea as dysentery.2 If every helper counts the same way, the numbers can be compared. Cholera's typical sign is milky "rice-water" diarrhea, often with vomiting and leg cramps.10 Hepatitis A can cause yellow skin or eyes, dark urine and clay-colored stools.14 Copy this grid into a notebook. The diarrhea and dysentery rows use WHO's definitions;2 the fever row uses CDC's 102°F warning sign.17 Count new cases onlyMark each sick person once, on the day the sign starts. A child sick for 5 days is 1 mark, not 5. Write one line per caseThe line list holds the details the tally sheet cannot (see the table below). Add every birth and deathNo exceptions. These two rows matter most over 30 years. Send even the zerosA sheet of zeros proves someone looked. A missing sheet tells you nothing. Compare with past weeksAfter a few weeks you know your normal. A clear jump starts the outbreak loop below. Keep every sheet dryStore them in a sealed container. See Preserving Knowledge & Records. Line list: one line per sick person ColumnWhy it matters Date the first symptom startedLets you count back to the exposure. Cholera usually starts 2–3 days after exposure.10 HouseholdHepatitis A spreads by close contact,13 so cases cluster in homes Water source usedA shared source points to the water What they ate and drankTyphoid spreads through food, drinks and water contaminated by sewage15 Name, age, sex, signs, outcomeShows who is hit hardest and who died Count every birth and every death Death counts are easy to get wrong. After Hurricane Maria, Puerto Rico's first official death count was 64. A household survey estimated 4,645 excess deaths to the end of 2017.4 A study commissioned by the governor estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018.5 Excess deaths are deaths above the number normally expected.5 You can only see them if you have been counting. For each death, write the name, age, sex, date, household and the signs before death in plain words. For each birth, write the date, the mother, and whether the baby breathed and fed well. s.h: 🤰 Mothers, babies and young children first
s.x: Protect the people with the least reserve. CDC lists children under 5, pregnant people and adults 65 and older among those more likely to get seriously ill from food poisoning.17 Feed them first. FEMA and the Red Cross say healthy people can survive on half their usual food for an extended period. Food should not be rationed for children and pregnant women.18 Pregnant and breastfeeding women need more protein: 71 g a day in the US reference tables.20 CDC also says to store extra water for pregnant women.19 Pregnancy and water treatmentCDC does not recommend iodine-treated water during pregnancy.21 Give pregnant women boiled water, or water treated with bleach. Birth planning is in Emergency Childbirth: Step by Step. The child health basics Diarrhea: ORS, zinc and keep feeding. For children with diarrhea, WHO and UNICEF recommend low-osmolarity ORS, zinc supplements and continued feeding.8 Zinc shortens an episode of diarrhea by 25%.2 Take the zinc dose from a clinician or the package label. The full ORS method is in Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration.  Healthy-looking children can spread germs. About 70% of hepatitis A infections in children under 6 cause no symptoms.13 Wash hands with soap after every diaper change. Vaccination records are health records. Measles risk after disasters depends on how many people were already vaccinated, especially children under 15.3 Hepatitis A is also vaccine-preventable.13 See Vaccine-Preventable Diseases to Recognize. The mother-and-child register Every pregnant woman: due date, who will attend the birth, and the nearest working clinic Every baby under 1: birth date, feeding (breast or other), weight checks, illnesses Every child under 5: vaccination record and every episode of diarrhea or fast breathing Every new mother: date of birth and any warning signs (see After Birth: Bleeding, Recovery & Warning Signs) Babies and diarrheaDiarrhea is the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months.2 In 2019, unsafe WASH caused 395,000 deaths of children under 5, including 273,000 from diarrhea.1 Babies keep breastfeeding through diarrhea.8 See Breastfeeding: The Survival Superpower.

s.h: 🚧 Outbreak plan: isolation, quarantine and response
s.x: Write the plan before the first case. Decide now where the sick will stay, who will care for them, and who tells everyone what to do. Isolation separates people who are sick. Quarantine separates well people who were exposed, until the time when symptoms could start has passed. Infection control in the sick room is in Epidemics: Quarantine, Isolation & Infection Control. Run the loop again with every new case. Diarrheal outbreaks can follow drinking-water contamination, so check the water early.3 Spot itOne row of the tally sheet is clearly higher than your normal week. Check itVisit each family. Do the cases really match the case definition? Separate and treatMove the sick to the isolation room. For watery diarrhea, start ORS at once: cholera can kill within hours.11 Find the sourceCount back from each first symptom with the table below. Look for a shared water source, meal or latrine. Block the routeClose or treat the suspect water, fix latrines, add soap. Keep the sick out of food preparation. Tell everyoneOne short message from trusted people: what to watch for, what to do, where to bring the sick. Watch the windowKeep tallying. New cases can still appear up to the longest incubation time after the last exposure. Watch windows: when symptoms can still start DiseaseSymptoms start after exposureLongest wait CholeraA few hours to 5 days, usually 2–3105 days Typhoid6–30 days1630 days Hepatitis A15–50 days, average 281350 days Do the arithmetic. If the last exposure to a hepatitis A case was on day 10, a new case can still start as late as day 60 (10 plus 50).13 For cholera, that window closes on day 15 (10 plus 5).10 Cholera can kill within hoursWHO says untreated cholera can kill within hours, and most cases can be treated with ORS.11 About 1 in 10 people get severe symptoms. With early, proper treatment, even people with severe cholera can survive.10 Start ORS at the first watery stools. Setting up the isolation room Do Pick a room or tent away from the kitchen and water point Name one carer per patient, and a backup Put soap and water at the door Give the patient their own cup, plate and toilet bucket Write every patient on the line list Don't Let a person who had typhoid cook for others without a clinician's advice15 Let children visit or play near the room Share cups, towels or bedding Empty waste near the water point The carer is the person most expose

s.h: 💊 Medicines, chronic illness and records for 30 years
s.x: Missed care was a major killer after Maria. About one third of excess deaths were linked to delayed or interrupted health care.4 A community that knows who needs which medicine can act before supplies run out. Keep one health register. For each person write: medicines and days of supply left, long-term conditions, allergies, devices that need power, vaccination record and any pregnancy due date. Update it at the weekly meeting. Use the WHO Essential Medicines List as a planning map. The 2025 edition, published on 5 September 2025, lists 523 medicines for adults and 374 for children.24 Talk it through with a doctor or pharmacist while you can. See Building a Long-Term Medical Kit. Week 1Map the water point, latrines and isolation room. Start the health register. Month 1Two helpers trained in the danger signs. Weekly tally sheets start, zeros included. Year 1You know your normal week. Bleach bought before the outage is now over one year old.22 Year 5+Helpers train new helpers. Birth and death registers show whether children are surviving. The 30-year viewSupplies run out; skills and records do not. Over decades, the jobs that last are the cheap ones: a protected water point, enough latrines, soap, a trained helper, and a notebook that counts births and deaths. Teach them to teenagers. See Passing On Skills to the Next Generation. A baby's supplies run out fastest, and most cannot be improvised safely. Ready.gov lists infant formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream.1 The Red Cross adds baby food.2 Formula or baby food: 3 days in the go-bag, 2 weeks at home12 Bottles, and a pot and fuel to clean them Bottled water set aside only for mixing formula16 Diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream1 A thermometer that is non-mercury and nonglass, like the one in the Red Cross kit9 A sling or soft carrier, so your hands stay free Clothes in the current size and the next size up The baby's medicines and a copy of the vaccination record A warm layer and a blanket Safe water for formulaThe CDC says to use bottled water for powdered formula until officials say tap water is safe. With no bottled water, boil water for 1 minute and let it cool.16For babies under 2 months, premature babies or babies with weak immune systems, the water must still be at least 70°C (158°F) when you mix it. Then cool the bottle to body temperature before feeding.16 Boiling does not remove chemicals.16 See Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out. Count your own baby's numbersCount diapers and feeds for 3 days. Divide by 3 for the daily number. Multiply by 14 for 2 weeks, or by 365 for a year. Babies change sizes, so buy ahead in the next sizes. Full lists by age are in The Baby & Toddler Prep Kit.

Your dog eats and drinks from the same stores you do. Write the date on everything you store. Every limit in this chapter counts from a date or time you wrote down. The CDC says to label and date stored water.1 Replace water you bottled yourself every 6 months. Keep it at 10–21°C (50–70°F), in the dark, away from fuel and pesticides.12 No power: a closed fridge keeps food safe about 4 hours, a full freezer about 48. Perishable food above 4°C (40°F) for 2 hours goes in the trash.34 Insulin vials and cartridges last up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F). Other medicines labeled "refrigerate" are discarded after a day without power, unless the label says otherwise.56 Use bleach less than 1 year old for water. s.h: 📏 How to read a shelf-life number
s.x: A shelf-life number is a limit under stated conditions. It tells you how long something stays safe or useful when it is stored the way the source describes. Read the conditions, not just the number. EPA's bleach rule is for bleach stored at room temperature for less than one year.7 FDA's 28-day insulin rule is for 15–30°C (59–86°F).5 Outside those conditions, the number does not apply. Every clock needs a start time Label and date every water container when you fill it. The CDC asks for exactly that.1 Do the same for bleach, food boxes and medicine. A table cannot help you if you do not know when the clock started. In an outage, write down the time the power went off. The fridge, freezer and medicine limits below all count from that moment. The first hours are covered step by step in The First 72 Hours. Three kinds of numbers Replace-by schedules. Water you bottled: every 6 months.1 CO alarm: every 5 years.8 Put these on a paper calendar. Safety limits. Perishable food above 4°C (40°F): 2 hours.4 Past the limit, it goes. Printed dates. Find out what a date means before you act on it. A CDC planning guide says the sell-by date on bottled water is mainly for stock rotation.10 For medicine, the label winsReady.gov's one-day rule for refrigerated medicine applies unless the label says otherwise.6 If a medicine was stored outside its label temperature, the FDA says to check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, doctor or the maker.11 Ask the three questions in order for water, food, medicine and gear. USDA says never to taste food to test it, the CDC says when in doubt, throw it out, and the FDA says to check the storage instructions or ask a pharmacist when a medicine was stored wrong.31211 Tables for other suppliesDry staples, home-canned food, fuel, batteries and seeds each have their own chapter and storage rules: Long-Term Food Storage, Home Canning Safely, Generators & Fuel Storage, Small Solar & Batteries and Seed Saving & Seed Viability. Use the same three questions there.

Store-bought bottled water is your safest stored water. The CDC calls unopened, commercially bottled water the safest and most reliable water in an emergency.1 Water you bottle yourself gets replaced every 6 months. The CDC and Ready.gov give the same schedule.12 Water: how long it keeps and when to replace it (CDC, Ready.gov, Utah) ItemKeep forReplace sooner if Store-bought bottled water, unopenedThe sell-by date is mainly for stock rotation10It sat in light: plastic turns brittle or leaky13 Tap water you bottled in clean, food-grade containers6 months12You see green growth (algae) from light13 Water you disinfected and bottled yourselfNot forever: check it for leftover chlorine10No chlorine is left: treat it again10 Blue plastic drum kept in direct sunCan start to fall apart within 5 years13The plastic is brittle, cracked or leaking13 Old milk or juice jugDo not use for water14Always: residue lets bacteria grow,14 and milk jugs also turn brittle15 What makes water last, or not Cool: 10–21°C (50–70°F).1 Dark: out of sunlight.1 Light makes plastic brittle and lets algae grow.13 Away from fuel and pesticides: vapors from gasoline, kerosene and pesticides can pass through plastic.116 Off bare concrete or dirt: plastic absorbs odors there.17 Air flow underneath limits moisture and mold.13 Room to freeze: leave 5–8 cm (2–3 in) of headspace, and do not use glass.16 The right plastic: food-grade HDPE, marked with a 2 in the recycling triangle, is the best choice.15 Container choice, rotation and how much to store are in Storing Water for Months & Years. Babies, children and nursing mothersUniversity of Florida Extension says to store more water when there are children or nursing mothers at home.18 The CDC says to make powdered formula with bottled water until officials say the tap water is safe.19 Keep a few unopened bottles set aside for formula only. Count the dogThe CDC says to store more water if you have pets.1 Ready.gov's pet kit includes a water bowl and several days of water.20 Put the dog's water on the same 6-month calendar as yours, and read the labels on any pet medicines for the word "refrigerate".

Your disinfectants have time limits too. Put them on the same calendar as the water they treat. Water-treatment chemicals: time limits and checks (EPA, CDC) ItemTime limitStorage and checks Regular unscented liquid bleachEPA's method uses bleach stored at room temperature for less than 1 year7Write the purchase date. Scented, color-safe or "with cleaner" bleach is not for drinking water7 Chlorine dioxide tablets or dropsFollow the date on the packageKeep sealed and out of the sun: it is volatile and sensitive to sunlight21 Iodine tablets or solutionCDC does not recommend continuous use beyond a few weeks22Not for pregnancy, thyroid problems or iodine allergy22 Bleach keeps forever if the cap stays on. EPA's emergency water method calls for bleach stored at room temperature for less than one year.7 Older bleach is outside the official method. Date every bottle when you buy it. The smell test tells you the dose worked Measure the dose8 drops of 6% bleach, or 6 drops of 8.25%, per 3.8 L (1 gallon) of clear water.7 Double it for hard casesCloudy, colored or very cold water gets twice the dose.7 Stir and wait 30 minutesStir, then let the water stand for 30 minutes.7 Smell itA faint chlorine smell means it is ready.7 No smell? RepeatAdd the same dose again and wait another 15 minutes.7  Pregnancy and nursingThe CDC does not recommend iodine water treatment for pregnant women.22 The CDC also says to store more water during pregnancy,1 and Florida Extension says the same for nursing mothers.18 Other methods are in Disinfecting Water. Learn the smell nowDose 3.8 L (1 gallon) of tap water with fresh bleach, wait 30 minutes and smell it.7 Then you will know the faint chlorine smell when it matters, even in the dark.

s.h: 🥩 Fridge and freezer food without power First 72 h
s.x: Keep the doors shut. The safe times assume the fridge and freezer stay closed.3 Use appliance thermometers. Safe readings are 4°C (40°F) or colder in the fridge and −18°C (0°F) or colder in the freezer.312 Fridge and freezer food when the power is off (USDA, CDC, FoodSafety.gov) SituationSafe for aboutAfter that Closed fridge4 hours312Discard meat, fish, eggs, milk and leftovers12 Full freezer, kept closed48 hours3Refreeze or cook food that has ice crystals or is at 4°C (40°F) or colder3 Half-full freezer, kept closed24 hours3Same rule; check each package3 Full 510 L (18 cu ft) freezer with 23 kg (50 lb) of dry ice2 days3Never touch dry ice with bare hands3 Perishable food above 4°C (40°F)2 hours, or 1 hour when the air is above 32°C (90°F)4Throw it out4 Hard cheese, butter, whole fruit, raw vegetables, bread, peanut butter, condimentsCan be kept after an outage9Unless they smell, look or feel wrong9 Why the limits are so short: bacteria grow fastest between 4°C and 60°C (40°F and 140°F) and can double in as little as 20 minutes.23 Signs it has gone bad Throw out food with an unusual smell, color or texture, or food that feels warm.9 The CDC rule is short: when in doubt, throw it out.12 A small taste will tell you if food is still safe. USDA says never taste food to decide whether it is safe.3 Use the thermometer, the clock and the sign check instead.9 Each bar ends at an official limit. The scale is logarithmic so that hours and years fit on one chart. Food: USDA and FoodSafety.gov. Medicine: FDA and Ready.gov. Water and bleach: CDC and EPA. CO alarm: CDC.3456178 Print this chart while the internet worksFoodSafety.gov: printable chart of refrigerated food to keep or throw out after an outage.24 Tape it inside a cupboard door. The full method is in Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

To get °F, multiply °C by 1.8 and add 32. To get °C, subtract 32 from °F and divide by 1.8. That is the whole method. °C to °F: × 1.8, then + 32Example: 70°C × 1.8 = 126. Add 32 and you get 158°F. °F to °C: − 32, then ÷ 1.8Example: 40°F − 32 = 8. Divide by 1.8 and you get 4.4°C. Write both on your labelsYour thermometer, your book and your medicine box may use different scales. Danger zone 40–140°F (4–60°C), where bacteria grow fastest.17 Fridge 40°F, freezer 0°F.19 1-hour limit above 90°F.18 Insulin vials: 59–86°F for up to 28 days.14 Formula water: about 70°C.21 Keep food at 40°F (4°C) or colder, or 140°F (60°C) or hotter. Bacteria grow fastest between those two numbers.17 A cooler must stay at 40°F (4°C) or below.18 Insulin vials and cartridges can stay out of the fridge for up to 28 days at 59–86°F (15–30°C). Pens and other products differ, so read your own label.14 "Double it and add 30" converts °C to °F well enough. It is close near room temperature but wrong when it matters. At 70°C, the shortcut gives 170°F; the real answer is 158°F. That is the CDC's formula-water temperature.21 Use × 1.8 + 32. Formula water and boilingCDC advises boiling water for formula for 1 minute, and using water of about 70°C (158°F) for young or vulnerable babies.21 Above 6,500 ft (about 2,000 m), boil water for 3 minutes.20 See Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

s.h: 🪣 How much water is in that container?
s.x: Volume = area of the bottom × depth of the water. It works for any container with straight sides: drums, tanks, buckets, troughs. Measure the insideUse centimeters or inches. Measure inside the walls, not outside. Find the bottom areaBox: length × width. Round tank: 0.785 × diameter × diameter. Multiply by the water depthUse the depth of the water, not the height of the tank, to see what is left. Convert to liters or gallonscubic cm ÷ 1,000 = literscubic inches ÷ 231 = US gallonscubic feet × 7.48 = US gallons Write it on the containerLiters when full, liters per cm of depth, and the full weight. Example, round drum: 60 cm across, 80 cm of water. 0.785 × 60 × 60 × 80 = 226,080 cubic cm, so 226 L (60 gal). Each 1 cm of depth holds 2.8 L. Example, box tank: 100 × 80 × 50 cm = 400,000 cubic cm, so 400 L (106 gal). It weighs about 400 kg (880 lb) when full, because 1 L of water weighs 1 kg.1 Full containers are heavyA full 208 L (55 gal) drum weighs about 208 kg (458 lb).1 University of Nebraska Extension advises sturdy shelving for stored water because of its weight.3 Fill big containers where they will stay. Leave 5–8 cm (2–3 inches) of space at the top of any container that might freeze.3 Stored water at CDC's minimum of 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day PeoplePer day2 weeks1 year 13.8 L (1 gal)53 L (14 gal)1,382 L (365 gal) 415 L (4 gal)212 L (56 gal)5,527 L (1,460 gal) 623 L (6 gal)318 L (84 gal)8,290 L (2,190 gal) CDC sets 1 gallon per person per day as the minimum and asks for a 2-week supply if possible. Store more for pregnant women, sick people, pets and hot climates.2 See How Much Water You Really Need.  Ration drinking water to make it last longer. FEMA and the Red Cross say never ration water. Drink what you need today and find more for tomorrow. A normally active person needs at least 2 quarts (about 1.9 L) a day to drink.7 Every open container is a drowning riskA child can drown in less than 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water. Never leave water containers open and unattended.24 Keep lids on buckets and tanks. Count your dogs in the water mathA pet kit needs a water bowl and several days' supply of water.25 CDC says to store extra water for pets.2 Add a line for each dog in your table, and measure what each one drinks in a day.

1 mm of rain on 1 m² of roof gives 1 liter. The reason: 1 mm × 1 m² = 0.001 cubic meters, which is exactly 1 liter. In US units, 1 inch of rain on 1 square foot gives 0.62 gallon. 1 inch × 144 square inches = 144 cubic inches. A US gallon is 231 cubic inches. 144 ÷ 231 = 0.623. Rainfall is a depth measured on flat ground, so multiply it by the roof's footprint (seen from above, overhangs included), not the sloped surface. Water weight: 1 kg per liter.1 Measure the footprintLength × width of the roof as seen from above, overhangs included. Slope does not add area. Multiply by the rainfallmm × m² = liters. Inches × sq ft × 0.623 = US gallons. Compare with your need4 people at 1 gallon a day need 1,460 gallons (5,527 L) a year.2 Measure what you really catchAfter a measured rain, check how much the tank gained. Gained ÷ calculated = your roof's own ratio. Use it for future estimates. Metric example: a 10 × 8 m footprint is 80 m². A 25 mm storm can give at most 2,000 L (528 gal). For 4 people at CDC's minimum, that roof must capture about 69 mm (2.7 in) of rain a year.2 US example: a 30 × 40 ft footprint is 1,200 sq ft. 1 inch of rain gives at most 748 gallons (2,831 L). Make a free rain gaugeAny container with straight, vertical sides measures rainfall. The depth of water in it equals the rain that fell, whatever its width. Check it at the same time each day and write the number down. The 30-year view: keep a rain logOne year of daily rain numbers shows your wettest and driest months. Size tanks to carry you through your longest dry stretch, not your average month. Treat roof water before drinking it: see Disinfecting Water. For gutters and first-flush diverters, see Rainwater Harvesting.

Start from the EPA table, then multiply. Use only plain, unscented bleach that is less than 1 year old, and wait 30 minutes before drinking.5 Unscented bleach for clear water (EPA rates; bigger batches multiplied out) Water6% bleach8.25% bleach 1 quart or 1 liter2 drops2 drops 1 gallon (3.8 L)8 drops6 drops 5 gallons (19 L)40 drops30 drops 20 L jerrycan (5.3 gal)42 drops32 drops Cloudy, colored or very coldDouble itDouble it The first two rows and the doubling rule are EPA's.5 The 5-gallon and 20 L rows are the 1-gallon dose multiplied. For a 55-gallon (208 L) drum, Oregon State Extension gives 2 tablespoons (30 mL).4  A few extra drops make clear water extra safe. EPA gives a set dose per strength, and doubles it only for cloudy, colored or very cold water.5 Measure; do not pour by eye. To sanitize a container, use 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of bleach per quart (about 1 L) of water. Shake it to coat every surface, wait at least 30 seconds, then pour it out.2 The dilution formula Strength before × amount before = strength after × amount after. Written short: C1 × V1 = C2 × V2. It works for any dilution. EPA's dry-chlorine method: 1 heaping teaspoon (about ¼ oz, 7 g) of high-test calcium hypochlorite in 2 gallons (7.6 L) of water makes a stock of about 500 mg/L. You then add 1 part stock to 100 parts water.6 Check it with the formula: 500 mg/L × 1 part ÷ 101 parts = about 5 mg/L. Because 1 L of water weighs 1 kg (1,000,000 mg), 1 mg/L is the same as 1 part per million (ppm).1 Stock solution is not drinking waterAt about 500 mg/L, the stock is 100 times stronger than the treated water.6 Label it, cap it and keep it away from children. Never mix chlorine with other cleaners.

Plan 2,100 kcal per person per day. That is the minimum planning figure for humanitarian food rations.8 Adult women need about 1,600–2,400 kcal and men about 2,000–3,000, depending on age and activity.9 Calories at 2,100 kcal per person per day, and the same calories as dry white rice Peoplekcal per daykcal per yearAs rice per year 12,100766,500210 kg (463 lb) 48,4003,066,000840 kg (1,852 lb) 612,6004,599,0001,260 kg (2,778 lb) The rice column uses USDA's figure of about 365 kcal per 100 g of dry white rice, which is 3,650 kcal per kg.10 Rice is only an example. Calories are not a full diet: see Deficiency Diseases. Find kcal per kgFrom the label: kcal per serving ÷ grams per serving × 1,000. Find the total kcal you holdkg of food × kcal per kg. Divide by the daily needTotal kcal ÷ (people × kcal per day) = days of food. Example: a 25 kg (55 lb) sack of white rice holds about 91,250 kcal.10 A family of 4 at 2,100 kcal each uses 8,400 kcal a day. 91,250 ÷ 8,400 = about 11 days. Oil carries 2.4 times the calories of rice, kilo for kilo. Vegetable oil has about 884 kcal per 100 g; dry white rice has about 365.10 That matters when you carry food. See Calories & Nutrition.  Cutting everyone's food in half hurts everyone the same. FEMA and the Red Cross say healthy people can survive on half their usual food intake for an extended period. Food may be rationed safely, except for children and pregnant women.7 Protein by body weight Protein targets are grams per kilogram of body weight. The adult RDA is 0.8 g/kg.11 The Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030 set 1.2–1.6 g/kg a day.12 Daily protein by body weight (multiplication of the published g/kg figures) Body weight0.8 g/kg (RDA)1.2–1.6 g/kg (2025–2030)Pregnancy, breastfeeding 1.1–1.3 g/kg 50 kg (110 lb)40 g60–80 g55–65 g 60 kg (132 lb)48 g72–96 g66–78 g 70 kg (154 lb)56 g84–112 g77–91 g 90 kg (198 lb)72 g108–144 g99–117 g Pregnancy and breastfeedingProtein needs in pregnancy and breastfeeding are 1.1–1.3 g/kg a day.11 CDC says to store more water for pregnant women.2 Do not cut food for pregnant women or children when you ration.7 Older adultsThe 0.8 g/kg protein RDA applies from age 19 to over 70.11 Weigh older relatives each month. A falling weight is a number you can act on early.

s.h: 💊 Dosing and loads by body weight
s.x: Weight-based math needs a real weight. Guessing a child's weight puts every later number wrong. Weigh yourselfUse a bathroom scale on a hard, flat floor. Weigh yourself holding the baby or dogStand still and read the number. SubtractThe difference is their weight. Convert: lb ÷ 2.2 = kg. Write it down with the dateChildren and dogs grow. Re-weigh before any weight-based dose. Learn the unit ladder. 1 kg = 1,000 g. 1 g = 1,000 mg. 1 mg = 1,000 micrograms (mcg). 1 L = 1,000 mL. Mixing up mg and mcg is a 1,000-fold mistake. Get the weight in kgUse the steps above. Find the dose on the label or from a clinicianThe dose comes from the label's chart or a written instruction, never from your own guess. Read the strengthLabels give mg in a volume. "100 mg per 5 mL" means 20 mg in each mL. Measure in mL with the device that came with itNot a kitchen spoon. Write the time and amountCheck the label's daily maximum before every dose. DoWeigh, then convert to kgMeasure liquids in mLUse the device in the boxLog every dose and time Don'tGuess a child's weightDose with kitchen spoonsGive aspirin to childrenWork out a dog dose from a human one Never give aspirin to childrenMayo Clinic's first-aid guidance is plain: never give aspirin to children.13 Use professional care whenever it exists. For what each medicine does, see Over-the-Counter Medicines. Dogs are dosed by a vet, not by mathDo not convert a human dose for your dog. Weigh the dog with the hold-and-subtract method and give the weight to a veterinarian. See Dog Health. Loads by body weight A child's backpack should weigh 10–20% of the child's weight. An 80 lb (36 kg) child carries 8–16 lb (3.6–7.3 kg).15 For adults, a 2018 military study recommends loads of 30% of body mass or less.16 Loads scale with the bodyAt 30% of body mass, a 50 kg (110 lb) woman's limit is 15 kg (33 lb), and an 80 kg (176 lb) man's is 24 kg (53 lb).16 Split group loads by body weight, not evenly.

s.h: ⏱️ Estimating time: count it, don't guess
s.x: Count breaths and pulse for a full 60 seconds. WHO calls 50 or more breaths a minute fast breathing at 2–11 months, and 40 or more from 12 months to 5 years.22 See Assessing a Sick or Injured Person.  Calibrate your counting nowWhile you still have a watch, count "one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand" to 60 and check the clock. Repeat until you land within a few seconds. Then you have a timer that needs no battery. 1 minuteRolling boil makes water safe from germs; 3 minutes above 6,500 ft (about 2,000 m).20 20 minutesBacteria can double in food between 40°F and 140°F.17 30 minutesWait after adding bleach before drinking.5 1 hourPerishable food limit above 90°F (32°C).18 2 hoursPerishable food limit above 40°F (4°C).18 4 hoursA closed fridge keeps food safe with no power.19 24 / 48 hoursA half-full / full closed freezer.19 28 daysInsulin vials and cartridges out of the fridge at 59–86°F (15–30°C).14 6 monthsReplace water you bottled yourself.2 1 yearReplace bleach you use for water.5 Arithmetic from USDA's figure that bacteria can double in as little as 20 minutes in the danger zone: 2 hours is 6 doublings, so 1 becomes 64.17 The 1-hour and 2-hour limits are FoodSafety.gov's.18 A half-full freezer keeps food as long as a full one. A full closed freezer holds about 48 hours; a half-full one about 24 hours.19 Write down the time the power went off. See Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

Your pace count A pace count turns your legs into a tape measure. In this method, one pace is two steps: count each time the same foot lands. Mark a measured 100 mUse a tape measure on flat ground. In feet, 100 m is 328 ft. Walk it normally and countCount every time your left foot lands. Repeat 3 times and averageThat average is your pace count per 100 m. Recalibrate for real conditionsWalk the course again carrying your usual load, and on slopes, and keep a separate count for each. Use itDistance in meters = paces counted ÷ your pace count × 100. Example: your count is 64 per 100 m and you counted 320 paces. 320 ÷ 64 × 100 = 500 m. Use it for safety distances. CDC says to run a generator outdoors more than 20 feet (6.1 m) from windows, doors and vents.23 With a count of 64, 6.1 m is about 4 paces; pace it out and mark the spot. Map scales: what 1 cm or 1 inch on the map means on the ground Map scale1 cm on the map1 inch on the map 1:24,000240 m2,000 ft 1:25,000250 m2,083 ft (0.39 mi) 1:50,000500 m4,167 ft (0.79 mi) 1:100,0001 km1.58 mi The rule: ground distance = map distance × the scale number. For route finding, see Map & Compass Navigation. Height from shadows A stick and two shadows give a tree's height. At the same moment, every upright object casts a shadow in the same ratio to its height. Similar triangles: stick 1 m, stick shadow 1.5 m, tree shadow 15 m gives 15 × 1 ÷ 1.5 = a 10 m tree. Measure both shadows within a few minutes of each other. Stand a straight stick uprightMeasure the part above the ground. Measure both shadowsThe stick's shadow and the tree's shadow, base to tip, at the same time. Do the mathTree height = tree shadow × stick height ÷ stick shadow. No sun? Use the arm's-length stick method. Hold a stick upright at arm's length, with the part above your fist as long as the distance from your eye to your fist. Walk until the stick's tip lines up with the treetop and your fist with the base. Your distance to the tree now equals its height; pace it. Know the reach before you fellA tree that falls reaches as far as it is tall. Measure the height first, and keep people, dogs and roofs out of that circle.

Area is length × width for a rectangle. A triangle is base × height ÷ 2. A circle is 0.785 × diameter × diameter. These units are exact definitions. An acre is about 40% of a hectare. For how much land feeds a family, see the land-math chapter. Pace or tape every sideSketch the plot on paper and write each length on it. Split the shapeCut odd shapes into rectangles and right-angle triangles. Work out each piece and add themRectangles: length × width. Triangles: base × height ÷ 2. Convertm² ÷ 10,000 = hectares. m² ÷ 4,047 = acres. sq ft ÷ 43,560 = acres. Square corners with a 3-4-5 ropeMark a rope at 3 m, 4 m and 5 m (or 3, 4 and 5 ft). Pull it into a triangle: the corner between the 3 and 4 sides is a perfect right angle, because 3² + 4² = 5². Use it for beds, sheds and fences. Seed packets often give rates per 100 sq ft. 100 sq ft is 9.3 m², so "per 100 sq ft" is close to "per 10 m²". For yields and land per person, see Feeding a Family Forever. The 30-year view: keep your own standardsTools wear out, but water does not change. A 1-liter bottle full of water weighs 1 kg, so it can check a homemade balance scale.1 Keep one tape-measured 1 m stick, and recheck each child's pace count and weight every year. Pounds to kilograms?Divide by 2.2. Bleach for 1 gallon of clear water?8 drops of 6% or 6 drops of 8.25%. Double for cloudy, colored or very cold water. Find a word by its first letter. Short forms in capitals, like CDC, ORS and CPR, have their own tables. Every entry links to the chapter with the full steps. "Only gasping" means not breathing. That is cardiac arrest: start CPR and use an AED (automated external defibrillator).6 The Danger Zone is 4–60°C (40–140°F). Bacteria in that range can double in as little as 20 minutes.13 A rolling boil for 1 minute kills germs in clear water (3 minutes above 2,000 m or 6,500 ft).10 It does not remove chemicals.15 Carbon monoxide (CO) has no color and no smell. Fit battery CO alarms near sleeping areas and replace them every 5 years.1 100–120chest compressions per minute in CPR (AHA, 2025)3 40–140°Fthe food Danger Zone, 4–60°C13 < 2 secnormal nail-bed (capillary) refill9 523medicines on WHO's 2025 adult essential list19

Plain word meanings link to the chapter that covers the topic in depth, with its own sources. Spot the type of wordAll capital letters? Go to Short forms. An organization? Go to Who's who. Anything else: go to its first letter. Find the rowTerms run A to Z inside each table. The first column is bold. Read the one-line meaningA number in the meaning is a rule. Learn it together with the word. Follow the chapter linkThe last column takes you to the full steps, warnings and sources. Capital letters go to the Short forms tables. Everything else goes to its first letter. If someone is in danger, do the steps in the red box first. Five terms that mean act now, read later Cardiac arrest: no response and not breathing, or only gasping. Start CPR and use an AED.6 Choking: for an adult or child, alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts. For a baby under 1, use back blows and chest thrusts.4 Carbon monoxide: headache, dizziness, weakness, vomiting or confusion near burning fuel. Get to fresh air, then get medical help.2 Massive bleeding: in an injured person, MARCH puts it first.7 See Stopping Severe Bleeding. Cholera: untreated, it can kill within hours. Start oral rehydration solution (ORS).17 Search instead of scrollingIn the online book, press / to search every chapter at once. On paper, use the letter headings in this chapter. Do Look up every short form on a medicine or chemical label Use exact words with helpers, such as "not breathing, only gasping" Write new words and their meanings at the back of the book Don't Guess what letters on a label mean Call gasping "breathing"3 Use scented bleach on water just because the label says bleach11

s.h: 🌡️ Words that come with a number
s.x: Some words are rules with a number attached. Learn the number together with the word, because the number tells you what to do. The thermometer below gathers the temperature words from across the book. The timeline after it gathers the time words. Boil water 1 minute.10 CDC uses water at about 70°C for young babies' formula.15 The Danger Zone runs 40–140°F.13 Keep the fridge at 40°F and the freezer at 0°F or colder.14 Insulin vials can stay at 59–86°F for up to 28 days.16 Time words, from seconds to years 2 secondsCapillary refill: nail color should return in under this time.9 1 minuteRolling boil for clear water. Make it 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft).10 20 minutesBacteria in the Danger Zone can double this fast.13 30 minutesWait this long after adding bleach before you drink.11 2 hoursPerishable food above 4°C (40°F) for longer than this goes in the trash.14 4 hoursA closed fridge keeps food safe this long without power.14 24 or 48 hoursA half-full or full freezer, with the door shut.14 28 daysInsulin vials and cartridges out of the fridge at 15–30°C (59–86°F).16 6 monthsReplace water you stored yourself.22 5 yearsReplace carbon monoxide alarms.1 Gasping means the person is still breathing. Gasping can happen after the heart stops. Treat "only gasping" as not breathing and start CPR.36 Boiled water is safe from everything. Boiling kills germs. It does not remove chemicals.15 Hands-Only CPR is right for everyone. It is for teens and adults who suddenly collapse. Infants, children, and people who drowned, overdosed or had breathing problems need breaths too.5

What does "only gasping" mean?Not breathing. It is cardiac arrest: start CPR and use an AED. What is the Danger Zone?4–60°C (40–140°F). Bacteria can double in 20 minutes. What does ORS stand for?Oral rehydration solution: salts and sugar in clean water to replace fluid lost to diarrhea. What does MARCH stand for?Massive bleeding, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia and head injury. Bleeding comes first. What does SAMPLE stand for?Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medicines, Past history, Last in and out, Events. What is a normal capillary refill?Nail color returns in under 2 seconds. Which bleach goes in drinking water?Plain unscented bleach, less than 1 year old. How long can insulin vials stay out of the fridge?Up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F). Pens differ.
